Politics | The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, will land in Mumbai on 20 October for his second visit to India this year. Rubio will meet foreign minister S Jaishankar and then travel to Jamnagar, home to Reliance Industries’ massive refinery.

Imran Khan | Days after the Bollywood actor Imran Khan appeared at a Mumbai protest against the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, authorities asked him to leave the country by 28 October over what they described as a violation of the Foreigners Act. The action followed a complaint by BJP leader Kirit Somaiya against Khan, who is a US citizen.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste

blocks.caption: Media Ka Loktantra by Vineet Kumar. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: With the chief justice of India criticising citizen journalist covering the recent protests, veteran television reporter Ravish Kumar, who now hosts a YouTube show, recommends a relevant book.

“I had just finished reading Vineet Kumar’s book Media Ka Loktantra (Democracy of Media) when the chief justice’s statement came out, saying that if every citizen becomes a journalist, it will create problems for all of us. Published in 2024, Vineet’s book discusses the idea of do-it-yourself journalism. He shows how, when mainstream journalism began silencing the voices of ordinary people, they picked up cameras themselves and started practising journalism. They are becoming journalists to also assert their citizenship and rights guaranteed to them by the constitution. The mainstream media has a problem with journalism emerging on social media platforms because stories that it refuses to report – such as those concerning the electoral rolls – are being covered by others. The conflict between the media and DIY journalism has only now reached the courts. But it began a long time ago.”
Count it
A number worth knowing

blocks.caption: The National Thermal Power Corporation (NTPC) plant in Dadri. Photograph: Prakash Singh/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Close to 45% of thermal power plants in India – as many as 84 out of 191 – were critically low on coal stocks (£) as of early October. At the same time, the country’s demand for power grew by 10% this year, the highest year-on-year increase in the past 10 years.
Vibe check

blocks.caption: A felt sculpture by Sagarika Sundaram at the Henry Moore Institute. Photograph: Rob Harris

blocks.text: Artist Sagarika Sundaram has spent a decade working with wool, transforming it into felt for expansive sculptural pieces that feel almost otherworldly. Her latest exhibition, Reservoir recently opened at the Henry Moore Institute, in Leeds, and runs until 10 January.

“There’s a clearer commitment to sculpture in this body of work, even though I’m still working with felt. I’m thinking spatially and making large volumes that explore what cloth can do: bend, collapse, gather, turn inward and support or surrender to its own weight,” she said of her latest works. Among them is Blue Mountain, which stretches almost seven metres long, creating a cave-like space that viewers can move through. That’s what I find compelling in the way her works are presented: they are not static objects offering a single perspective.

The New York-based artist finds it exciting to give up a degree of agency during the making process, allowing the material to determine, in part, how the final form will unfurl. “Wool is a wonderfully responsive material. It can be soft and pliable but also dense, strong and structural. Wool takes dye exceptionally well and I can be quite expressive with colour and mark-making,” she said.
Get in touch

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

articles.title: Surprise drop in UK unemployment to 4.7%
articles.summary: ONS data shows rate down from 4.9% but number of job vacancies continues to shrink

blocks.text: Unemployment in the UK fell unexpectedly in the three months to August, to 4.7% from 4.9%.

The Office for National Statistics figures, which provide a backdrop to the budget on 28 October, also showed that the number of payrolled employees rose by 13,000 between August and September, to 30.3m.
However, the number of job vacancies fell by 21,000 to 691,000 in the three months to September, the lowest since 2021 during the Covid pandemic.
Economists had expected the unemployment rate to rise to 5%.
Average wage growth, including bonuses, has fallen to 3.7% from 3.9%. Stripping out bonuses, average pay growth rose to 3.7% from 3.6%.
after newsletter promotion

Average pay growth remains above the 3.1% headline rate of inflation, which is of concern to Bank of England interest rate setters, who fear higher-than-expected inflation will translate into higher wage awards, fuelling future prices rises recorded by the consumer prices index (CPI).

articles.title: A young life ‘dominated by gambling’: Victorian coroner delivers stinging findings on death of 22-year-old
articles.summary:
Online betting was the ‘direct and paramount’ cause behind Kyle Hudson’s decision to take his own life, inquest finds

  • Get our

blocks.text: Kyle Hudson was “a young man brimming with promise”, with a loving and supportive partner, family and friends, and prospects.
“It was a near ideal picture – except for the grip that online sports betting had upon him,” the Victorian coroner Paul Lawrie said on Tuesday.
“Ultimately, he lost everything.”

Lawrie, delivering his findings into the 22-year-old Werribee man’s death, said Hudson’s online gambling was “the direct and paramount causative factor underlying his decision to take his own life” on 6 July 2021.
“Kyle’s case reveals, in the sharpest relief, the human cost of online gambling,” Lawrie said.

The inquest, held in May, examined the immediate circumstances and likely contributing factors to Hudson’s death, his personal and financial history, his online gambling history, and whether some of Australia’s largest betting companies accurately assessed Hudson’s risk of gambling-related harm in the years prior to his death.

Hudson opened his first online gambling account with Sportsbet on his 18th birthday in 2017. He gambled $895,733 through Sportsbet and other online betting platforms run by Entain and Bet365 over four years, with the last bets placed hours before he took his own life.

Hudson’s online betting was also the “indisputable” direct cause of the breakdown of his relationship with his longtime girlfriend, Ashley Baker, in the days immediately preceding his suicide, the coroner found.
“Her account of the decline of their relationship makes clear the corrosive effect of Kyle’s gambling,” Lawrie said.
The coroner, at times becoming emotional, was scathing of an “extraordinary” submission made by Sportsbet, with whom 85% of Hudson’s gambling had occurred.
Sportsbet had argued that the court had not seen sufficient evidence to conclude Hudson had been suffering from gambling harm.
“It is chilling that this is Sportsbet’s view,” Lawrie said.

Hudson made bets on 110 of the 187 days in the last six months of his life, averaging 9.2 bets for each betting day. Over the four years he gambled with Sportsbet, Hudson had triggered behavioural alerts within the company’s systems on 37 occasions – once every six weeks on average, with the first occurring within two months of his 18th birthday.

The betting companies told the inquest they believed at the time that Hudson was “betting within limits” and that he never met their highest risk threshold, though representatives from Entain and Bet365 acknowledged in evidence that, with all the facts in view, Hudson appeared to have been suffering from gambling harm.
“Sportsbet maintains that Kyle was not suffering from problem gambling,” Lawrie said.
“I do not accept this proposition. The analysis of Kyle’s betting activity detailed above presents a startling picture of a young man whose life after age 18 was dominated by online gambling.”
Hudson had engaged in problem gambling throughout much of the four years, and “as a consequence, he suffered significant gambling harm, which increased as time progressed”, the coroner found.
after newsletter promotion
“The impact went far beyond the money Kyle lost. Online gambling had taken over so much of his life. This is made crystal clear in the astonishing measurements of his betting activity,” he said.

Hudson sustained an overall net loss of more than $47,000 through gambling, a forensic accounting analysis had shown, but the coroner found it would have been difficult for Hudson to have known precisely how high his tally of losses was. The coroner recommended the federal government change the consumer framework to require online betting companies to prominently display customers’ net financial position over time in their accounts.

Hudson redeemed 489 inducements over the four years he was gambling. There could be “little doubt” that the promotions and inducements Hudson received over the years “catalysed Kyle’s betting behaviour” and had a “contrary and corrosive impact” on the effect of any of the gambling companies’ safer gambling efforts, the coroner said.

Gambling companies provided the details of their advertising budgets to the court confidentially, under a claim of commercial sensitivity. Lawrie did not reveal those figures, but on Tuesday described them as “a level of expenditure on gambling advertising in Australia that is arresting”.
“It is close to impossible to move through the modern world without being exposed to [gambling] advertising,” Lawrie said.

“Kyle did not decide out of nowhere to open his first betting account on his 18th birthday … There can be little doubt that Kyle began his online gambling as soon as he could because he was primed by the phenomenon that was swirling about him before he turned 18.”

He recommended the Australian government consider further restrictions, including prohibitions on advertising for online gambling, and establish a national online gambling regulator to oversee licensing, safety, gambling harm interventions and data collection.

He also recommended the government establish and fund an independent “data vault”, which he said had been introduced in various European countries, and allowed for better regulation of online gambling companies. This vault would hold standardised gambling data, which gambling companies would be compelled to provide, and mechanisms to allow for thorough independent research on gambling harm and gambling safety.

There were “critical and obvious deficiencies” in the current system of monitoring and intervention for online gambling harm, which lay mainly with companies themselves, and relied on partial data and, sometimes, verbal assurances from a customer that they were betting safely, the coroner said.
Hudson’s case “should be a clear signal that we cannot leave monitoring and intervention solely in the hands of the betting companies”, Lawrie said.
“The status quo cannot be justified.”

articles.title: NBI findings on Duterte properties came too late for trial
articles.summary: The NBI says it found major discrepancies involving properties allegedly linked to Sara Duterte, including land it says has a mansion, pools and a helipad.

blocks.text: October 20, 2026 | 2:28pm

MANILA, Philippines — House prosecutors are leaving it up to the Ombudsman and the Department of Justice to act on the National Bureau of Investigation's findings on multi-million properties allegedly linked to Vice President Sara Duterte, saying the findings came too late for the trial as they've already rested their case.

Lead prosecutor Rep. Jinky Luistro (Batangas, 2nd District) said the panel remained interested in the NBI’s investigation, including one lofty Davao City property the bureau claims has a mansion and a helipad. But the prosecution has already wrapped up evidence on the unexplained wealth charge, the only article of impeachment left against Duterte.
“We lament that we are in the process of filing already our formal offer of documents, which signifies the prosecution’s resting its case,” Luistro confirmed at a briefing on Tuesday, October 20.

“We just want to express our interest on the ongoing investigation of the NBI because these properties are of course supposed to be part of the unexplained wealth in our articles of impeachment, except that we have concluded already the presentation of our evidence,” she said in mixed English and Filipino.
The findings however can still be pursued by agencies "like the Department of Justice and the Office of the Ombudsman,” she added.

NBI Director Melvin Matibag first publicly shared findings of the alleged mismatch of the properties' worth on Duterte's wealth declarations on October 12. That was the same day the prosecution’s final witness, forensic analyst Alexander Cabrera, finished his testimony, and the panel formally rested its case the next day.
Duterte's properties nevertheless came up in the impeachment court when Sen. Erwin Tulfo raised them during his interjection.
The NBI has since identified three more properties that it claims involve discrepancies in the declarations of Duterte and her husband.

Luistro’s remarks narrow earlier statements by her co-prosecutors who said senator-judges should also "consider" the NBI's findings. Rep. Terry Ridon has said the prosecution panel was studying whether it could use the NBI’s findings that the properties are worth more than what Duterte declared in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).

The NBI said one property in Barangay Catigan, Davao City, was declared in Duterte’s SALN as agricultural land worth about P890,000. The bureau said independent appraisals and site inspections valued it at P14 million to P61 million, and that it has a mansion, swimming pools and a helipad.

The NBI began looking into the properties after dismissed policeman Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. alleged that he had delivered cash to the vice president, her brother Rep. Paolo Duterte and former president Rodrigo Duterte on the instructions of former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco.
Duterte and Velasco’s camp have both denied the claims.

Duterte has denied owning the properties and called the NBI’s move to link them to her a form of “public deception.” She has also said that such conduct was why the NBI was "dropped" from the prosecution’s witness list.
‘Not simple living’
At Tuesday’s briefing, House prosecutor Rep. Joel Chua (Manila, 3rd District) said the Duterte camp owed the public a full explanation for the property.

“They need to give a stronger explanation for the property they declared as worth P800,000. When the NBI presented this, turned out to be a big mansion with two swimming pools and a helipad,” Chua said in Filipino.
“If you put a helipad on a property, it means you have a helicopter. So the next question is, does this family own a helicopter? Why does their property and mansion have a helipad?” he said.
Luistro said the findings were at odds with how the Dutertes had presented themselves to the public.

“They tried to give us the impression that they are just a simple family with a simple life. But how can we characterize them as simple people if they have a mansion?” she said. Citing the NBI, she said the property had “his and hers” swimming pools.
The prosecution’s final witness Cabrera estimated that Duterte and her husband had accumulated P817.87 million in unexplained and undeclared assets.
Duterte has accused the prosecution of fabricating evidence.

articles.title: Brendan Nugent’s family say Helen Haines has been their friend for more than 20 years
articles.summary:
Father of 43-year-old Tarrawingee man who allegedly attacked the independent MP say incident is ‘devastating and unfathomable’

  • Follow our

blocks.text: The father of a 43-year-old man accused of allegedly attacking Helen Haines has pledged to work with police and described the incident as “shocking and horrific”.

The independent MP remained in a critical condition on Tuesday after being airlifted from Wangaratta in northern Victoria to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital for emergency surgery on Monday night. She has lost one leg, with surgeons working to save the other.
Police confirmed a 43-year-old Tarrawingee man alleged to have driven the Toyota LandCruiser was arrested at the scene.
In a statement, Brendan Nugent’s father, Rod Nugent, and Rod’s partner, Christine Cunningham, said Haines had been their friend for more than 20 years.
“What happened to her yesterday is devastating and unfathomable,” they said.

“We would like to sincerely thank members of the local community and police who came to Helen’s aid yesterday after the shocking and horrific crime. We will be assisting Victoria Police in any way we can.
“Helen Haines is a deeply respected, valued and much loved member of our local community.”
Guardian Australia has spoken to local residents who have been concerned about Nugent’s behaviour for several years, including multiple allegations of abuse and threats from him.
They reported erratic behaviour, shouting and music playing loudly until the early hours of the morning. They also raised concerns about his mental health.
Nugent is a long-term forestry campaigner in the state’s north-east. Environment campaigners who worked with Nugent several years ago have expressed shock at his arrest.

Nugent has a master’s of forest ecosystems science from the University of Melbourne and spent years researching the forestry industry in Victoria. He has also been a registered business owner in Wangaratta.
Nugent was a committee member for the Save our Strathbogie Forest group, which campaigns against logging in the region. He became inactive around 2019-20.
His arrest has shocked the group’s chair, Bertrant Lobert, who said he initially appeared to be “a reasonable and thoughtful person but then he drifted away”.
“He was engaging, he was thoughtful and to hear what has happened now, if it all turns out to be true, is just completely shocking,” Lobert said.
“This is quite personal as a lot of people in our group knew Helen personally and were friends.
“This is more than just a tragedy about the targeting of public figures, it’s about our community and the people we know.”
Helen McKernan, the president of the Strathbogie Ranges Conservation Management Network Inc, also worked with Nugent as an activist before 2020.
She says Nugent lost contact with her network of forestry campaigners around this date.
“He was a committed activist,” McKernan said. “He would sleep out if necessary and help behind the scenes. We could always rely on him to turn up and contribute.”
after newsletter promotion
“It’s just a shock.”

When the then-Victorian minister for environment, Lily D’Ambrosio, visited the Strathbogie forest in November 2019 to announce a ban on native forest logging, Nugent was among a group of about a dozen environmentalists who posed for photos.
Also among the group was Rebecca Swift, a friend of Dezi Freeman who owned the property where he was living when two police officers were killed and a third injured in a shooting last year.
Swift and Freeman shared conspiratorial beliefs about government and the Covid-19 pandemic, but it is unclear whether Nugent also embraced those views.
“Lily I was so pleased to be in the Strathbogie forest to hear your announcement today,” Swift commented on D’Ambrosio’s Facebook post announcing the logging ban.

“You gave us heart and hope that we are heard, and that our beloved wild landscapes are valued for so much more than merely dollars. Forest and wildlife defenders welcome a future where we can assist genuine governments to care for our national parks.”
Swift was contacted for comment.
The Victorian Nationals MP Tim McCurdy said Nugent was known to his Wangaratta office and regularly came in to raise different issues.
“He’s been at our office,” McCurdy said. “We get plenty of people come in, half a dozen a day come for various things. So yes, he’s been into our office, [to raise] various issues.
“Our office didn’t feel threatened by him, if they had they would ring the police. I want to wish Helen all the best.”
In October 2019, when Nugent was still actively campaigning on forestry issues, he praised Haines for her stance on climate change.
When Haines posted on X about an ABC Q+A episode, Nugent wrote “Would’ve been nice to include a politician who takes climate change seriously, such as yourself”.
– with AAP

blocks.text: Canada's Alberta province has overwhelmingly rejected a plan to begin the process of seeking independence from Canada.

Canadian public broadcaster CBC projects a decisive victory for the federalist side, with official results showing more than 76% support for remaining in Canada after roughly a third of the votes had been counted.
The nonbinding referendum asked residents whether they wanted to stay in Canada or start the legal steps needed for a future binding vote on separation.
The vote marks the first separation referendum held outside Quebec, where past independence movements have been driven by language and cultural differences.

In Alberta, the campaign was largely fueled by economic grievances. The vast oil-rich state is almost double the size of Germany in terms of land mass, but is much more sparsely populated, with around 5 million residents. Almost half of them live in its two main cities, Edmonton and Calgary.

The result is a significant setback for separatist groups and their supporters but a much-needed win for Prime ​Minister Mark Carney as ​he ‌attempts to keep the country unified amid an ongoing trade war with ‌the US.

articles.title: Indoor bouldering 101: Sending your first climb
articles.summary: Chalk, shoes, technique, and everything in between

blocks.text: Being a first-time climber can be intimidating, whether you’re afraid of heights, unsure if you’re fit enough, or even feel pressured by the gym. But don’t worry, it is easier than it looks, even for beginners.

Indoor bouldering is a sport where you climb short walls following a set of the same colored holds. More than a physical sport, it also involves strategic thinking, as you have to consider where you will place your hands and feet as you get to the top. Hence, climbers use the term “projects” to refer to what climb they are trying to do, as each route is a small physical and mental problem that you get to solve.

It might seem difficult, but don’t worry, as you don’t need to know the perfect way up before you start. Trying a move, adjusting, and trying again is part of the climb. To send your first climb, here are some tips that helped me enjoy and keep climbing.
Before climbing, it is a must to gear up and prepare; this not only applies to your shoes and chalk, but also to preparing your mind and body.

To get started, wear clothes that you can move comfortably in, and give yourself a few minutes to warm up from head to toe before climbing. This will help you avoid muscle strains and prepare your body for physical activity.

Climbing shoes and chalk are also a must. If you don’t have any of these, every climbing gym will have them in stock. Compared to regular shoes, climbing shoes have a firm sole and allow a tighter fit, helping you to step on small holds better, giving your feet the proper traction. Meanwhile, chalk gives you the proper grip and avoids abrasions or wounds on your hands. For your first climb, focus less on having the perfect gear and more on getting comfortable trying a climb.

Ready to get climbing shoes? Looking at the curvature of the soles and their comfort level are the two most important factors to consider so you can get the best pair for your experience level. Here are some climber-recommended options to help you get started.
If you’re looking for an all-day shoe while still giving you a good fit and performance, ClimbX Rave is a strong pick.

At an affordable price, ClimbX Rave is more of a comfort-oriented shoe with a slight downturn on the soles. So, if you are starting out with climbing, this is a good option for you to find the proper footing and confidence on the wall.
Get ClimbX Rave here. (Also available at Bhive Circuit Makati)
For more performance-based shoes, Scarpa Vapor V along with La Sportiva Solutions are two options worth considering.

One main difference between the two is their downturn curve. Solutions gives an aggressive downturn shape and a stiff sole, making it ideal for steep routes. Their shape gives precision and power on small footholds, as it is designed for demanding projects.
Meanwhile, Vapor V is a moderately downturned shoe, prioritizing support and comfort while still giving you good grip and precision.
Get Scarpa Vapor V here.
Get La Sportiva Solutions here.

If you just want the top of the line, this shoe is a one-stop shop. Despite its aggressive curve, climbers often find it comfortable due to its soft build aimed at sensitivity. This allows you to feel and hold on to smears, small, and complex holds.
If you’re ready to invest in your climbing journey, this could be a splurge worth considering.
Get Scarpa Dragon LV here.

It is normal to feel nervous about falling, not being strong enough, or simply climbing in front of other people. I felt those same worries, too when I started. But bouldering gave me the chance to face them one climb at a time. And after realizing that it wasn’t as difficult as I made it to be, bouldering became much more enjoyable.

As an example of facing my fear of heights, a pre-briefing for beginners on proper falling technique taught me how to confidently fall from heights that seemed too high. Furthermore, there are also easy-to-grab holds across all walls that are mainly for assisting me as I climb down; hence, even when jumping off feels scary, climbing down gives me the peace of mind that I can reach a safe height. You do not have to conquer your fear before you start climbing, but starting small can help you build that confidence.

You do not need to be super strong before trying bouldering. Climbing gyms use “tags” to show how difficult each bouldering project is, helping climbers choose a level that suits them best, from V0-V1 being the easiest and beginner-friendly, to V8 being the hardest (some gyms go beyond V8). These are usually color-coded in climbing gyms, so make sure to check, as they vary per gym.

When I started climbing, I depended on my strength to pull me up. This was one “not to do” lesson I learned that led to early fatigue. To guide you on the right path, here are a few basic techniques that can help you rely less on strength and more on technique:

items: Push with your legs instead of relying only on your arms.
Keep your arms straight when you can so you are not holding yourself up with bent arms the whole time.
Turn your hips toward the wall to help shift your weight from one hold to another.
Use the tip of your climbing shoes to place your feet more precisely, allowing you to pivot.
Pay attention to which direction the holds point and grab it in that direction.

blocks.text: Remember: Climbing is not about rushing to a higher grade. It is about finding new ways to move and enjoying the climbs along the way.

All the technicalities aside, what matters most is whether you enjoy climbing. For me, more than a sport, bouldering taught me how to appreciate doing hard things, facing my fears, having courage, and constantly trying even after experiencing setbacks.
Bouldering might not be the sport for everyone, but it is definitely a sport everyone can do. So if you feel a connection with bouldering, try to send your first project! – Rappler.com

articles.title: Adamson’s strong start surprises Nash Racela, adds to La Salle’s woes
articles.summary: ‘I apologize to my players because they really surprised me, the whole team,’ says Adamson coach Nash Racela as his Falcons cap the UAAP first round strong with an upset of defending champion La Salle

blocks.text: LEADER. Mathew Montebon in action during Adamson's first-round duel against La Salle in the UAAP.
UAAP

‘I apologize to my players because they really surprised me, the whole team,’ says Adamson coach Nash Racela as his Falcons cap the UAAP first round strong with an upset of defending champion La Salle

items: Adamson has surprised many by achieving a 4-3 record in the UAAP Season 89 men's basketball tournament, including a notable win against defending champions La Salle.
Head coach Nash Racela acknowledged the team's unexpected success and emphasized their strong defensive performance, allowing the fewest points per game in the league.
Despite their strong start, Racela cautioned that the team must remain focused and continue to learn as they have seven more games in the second round.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Adamson has exceeded expectations, and even head coach Nash Racela is surprised by the heights the Soaring Falcons have reached.

The Falcons secured the third-best record at 4-3 by the end of the first round of the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament, capping it with a 70-68 stunner over defending champion La Salle Green Archers.
As the Falcons soared, La Salle slipped to 3-4, joining Ateneo in a tie for sixth place.
Few expected Adamson to find itself among the league’s top teams after seven games, with Racela admitting that while he believed in his team’s potential, he did not anticipate such a strong start.
“We should be happy with where we are at right now,” Racela said. “To be honest, as a coach, I knew what we could do as a group. I could see our potential.”
“I apologize to my players because they really surprised me, the whole team. I wasn’t expecting to be at this point after the first round,” he added.
Adamson’s only losses in the opening round came against league-leading NU, Ateneo, and the UP Fighting Maroons.
Against UP, the Falcons controlled much of the game before the Maroons caught fire from beyond the arc in the final six minutes to steal the win.

Adamson nearly suffered the same fate against La Salle, but this time, it held its ground down the stretch. Matty Erolon delivered the decisive blow with a clutch three-pointer to help seal the two-point victory.
The result further complicated the title defense of the Green Archers, who are still leaning on last season’s championship core led by Jacob Cortez, but this time, minus Mike Phillips.

In keeping with its identity, Adamson has built its early success on the defensive end. The Falcons have allowed a league-best 65.86 points per game, making them the toughest defensive team to score against through the first seven games.

Graduating guard Mathew Montebon has also emerged as one of the UAAP’s most productive floor generals after averaging 12.14 points, 2.71 rebounds, 3.71 assists, and 2.14 steals per game in the first round, while shooting 36% from three-point range on more than six attempts per game.

Erolon has provided another scoring option, averaging 10.57 points per contest, while foreign student-athlete Precious Jonah has made his presence felt on both ends of the floor with 10.43 points, 7.71 rebounds, 1.00 steal, and 2.57 blocks per game.
Ray Allen Torres, Mat Edding and Earl Medina have also delivered valuable offensive contributions while helping maintain the team’s defensive intensity.
For Racela, the progress goes beyond the numbers as he has seen his players grow more comfortable in his system and develop greater trust in one another.
“At this point, my players should know that I trust them so well. And I see slowly that they’re building trust in me,” Racela said.
Despite Adamson’s strong finish to the first round, Racela is not letting the team get carried away.
With seven games still to come in the second round, he knows the Falcons have yet to accomplish anything significant.
“Seven games are done, but it does not really mean anything,” Racela said. “Experiential learning. We have to go through fire to learn.”
La Salle will open the second round against the winless UE Red Warriors on Wednesday, October 21, while Adamson takes on the FEU Tamaraws next on Saturday, October 24. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Alberta voters reject plan for referendum to leave Canada, CBC projects
articles.summary:
Projection delivers a victory for prime minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity

Voters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin a process toward…

blocks.text: Voters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin a process toward independence, the national broadcaster CBC has projected, delivering a victory for prime minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity.

With more than 1 million votes counted early Tuesday, about 76% supported remaining in Canada, compared with 23% who backed beginning a process that could lead to separation. About a third of ballots had been counted.

Even though the vote was not explicitly about independence – a point that frustrated separatists – the ballot question nonetheless exposed divisions in Alberta’s politics and raised questions about the durability of national unity.

Delays at roughly 100 of the 1,400 at polling stations across the province pushed results back by more than two hours – but shortly after polls closed on Monday evening, the results suggested a decisive win for those looking to remain in Canada.

The separation question – whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could lead to a second vote – was one of 10 put to Albertans on Monday. The others covered issues including immigration, healthcare, education and the province’s constitutional powers. Elections Alberta said the remaining results could take days to count.
In the days leading up to the vote, provincial leaders and federal politicians crisscrossed the province to make the case for a unified country.
Prime minister Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, warned against a vote from residents of the oil-rich province simply looking to “send a message” to the federal government.
“A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he told an energetic crowd last week.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, whose parliamentary seat is in the province, told a crowd of supporters that Albertans were not “quitters”.

“To those people who are thinking about taking out their frustration on the current government by voting for separation in the referendum, I say this: Canada is more than a government,” he said. “It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”

Data from Elections Alberta indicated roughly 43% of eligible voters – or 1.3 million Albertans – had already cast ballots before Monday’s vote through advance voting and mail-in ballots. That figure pointed to a potentially higher turnout than the province’s last referendum in 2021.
The Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, has said publicly that she will vote to remain in Canada, but that she will not require elected members of her party to do the same.

Her tenure as leader of the United Conservative party is due in large part to separatists within the party who ousted her predecessor, Jason Kenney. In recent months, Smith has tried to placate both the separatists and federalists in the party, in a province where a majority is not interested in secession.

The referendum has also become a political liability for Smith’s party, which has seen popular support tumble in recent months, including the loss of a one-time conservative stronghold during a byelection.
Still, members of the separatist movement told the Guardian they would continue their push for independence.

In an interview before the results, the Calgary mayor, Jeromy Farkas, a staunch opponent of the independence movement, told the Guardian the city’s “best future is here, as a Canadian city” amid fears that uncertainty could lead to capital flight.
“I am Canadian because I’m Canadian, not in a transactional way and regardless of the flavour of prime minister,” said Farkas.

“And I’m going to continue to make the case for how our future is strongest together because no result will permanently put this to bed,” he added, “The separatist movement sees this as a long-term project.”

articles.title: Tuesday briefing: Can Andy Burnham beat Britain’s headphone dodgers?
articles.summary:
In today’s newsletter: The prime minister’s campaign against noisy passengers has struck a chord with commuters. Whether anyone hears him remains to be seen.

Good morning.

Me again,…

blocks.text: Good morning.

Me again, back from the October school holiday (a week in glorious Wales, thanks for asking) and ready to hear your commuter woes. For our prime minister, it’s “one of the most annoying things on public transport”: maybe you’re trying to work, or read, or you’ve finally got your kid to sleep, when someone starts blasting sound from their phone at full volume.

As I sign off this First Edition en route from Glasgow to London (the things I’ve heard on this commute, against my will, I’ll save for another newsletter), I’m hoping everyone has been paying attention.

I’m struck by how few voices there have been suggesting Burnham should be concentrating on more important matters. It seems to me that other people’s noise, and other inconsiderate behaviour on public transport, has become shorthand for wider concerns about social cohesion, generational conflict and political fragmentation. Put simply, we are all making much more noise, and have become much worse at listening to what anyone else is actually saying. For today’s newsletter, I spoke to a bus driver, a transport expert and a cultural critic to find out more. That’s after the headlines.
Five big stories

items: France | The prime minister has said he has asked regional authorities to impose partial curfews in some cities after the government admitted police had “lost control” in several places during violent weekend protests around the country.
UK politics | Andy Burnham has told officials to rip up their plans for how to fix Thames Water and present him with more radical options for what to do with the stricken company.

Yemen | At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government forces in the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.
Israel | Israeli police have detained 10 people in a rare raid against settlers, after a weekend of extreme violence in the occupied West Bank including an attack on US photojournalist Heidi Levine.
Reform | Nigel Farage undermined his own claims that a £5m gift was for security when he referred to the money as a reward for Brexit, according to one of his closest aides.

blocks.text: In depth: Can a campaign against ‘loudcasting’ make public transport quieter?

blocks.caption: Andy Burnham said: ‘It’s a simple thing, but one that will make journeys that little bit better for all of us.’ Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: When Andy Burnham launched his crusade against unnecessary noise and antisocial behaviour on public transport with a chatty Instagram post recorded on a morning train into Manchester Piccadilly, my first thought was: “I bet he didn’t upload that on the dodgy onboard wifi.”

The prime minister’s sights were set on the phenomenon described as “loudcasting” or “headphone dodging” – but you don’t need a specialist term, because you know it when you hear the passenger next to you blasting Facebook slop on loudspeaker.

Alongside a nationwide campaign encouraging people to plug in their headphones and “share the carriage, not the noise,” Burnham announced new guidance to help local transport authorities introduce fines of up to £100 for nuisance behaviour like vaping, littering and playing loud music or videos on buses. Train operating companies already have powers to impose fines of up to £1,000 for antisocial behaviour.
If you’re grinding your molars at the thought, you’re not alone. A hefty majority of Britons, about 88% according to recent polling, consider it unacceptable to play music out loud on a train.
Who will actually enforce the rules?

It’s still unclear how these new rules would be enforced. Government officials have reassured bus drivers that they won’t be expected to police passengers themselves. That job will fall on transport safety officers or police officers.

Mark, a bus driver in central London, tells me he and his colleagues simply don’t have the capacity to help. He spends his working life in the glass cabinet at the front of the vehicle. He can’t hear every noise or spot every puff of vape smoke on the top deck, and, as well as navigating the city traffic, he already has other things to focus on, such as fare-dodging.

Mark’s route has become noisier in recent years, though he’s keen not to point out “it’s an all-ages” issue, and not to lay the blame solely with younger passengers. He doubts whether Burnham can isolate the problem to public transport. “It’s a whole society thing: being kinder and more aware of their environment.”
“It’s not workable without resources,” he says. “I don’t really see how it would be enforceable: you can’t have someone on every bus and train.”
Here lies the difficulty: fines for nuisance noise on trains are already vanishingly rare, with offenders able to shut up or leave the carriage before enforcement arrives.

The number of British Transport Police (BTP) officers has fallen by more than 10% over the past two years. The people left to challenge the noisy doom-scroller are, therefore, you and me. Transport for London, for example, has done some great work on bystander intervention, suggesting straightforward ways to interrupt bad behaviour without putting yourself in danger, but many of us would think twice about confronting a stranger in the confines of a moving vehicle.
Is this a crackdown on bad behaviour, or a distraction from worse problems?

Not everyone is impressed by the scale of the response. Sharon Graham, general secretary of Unite – a woman resolutely resistant to hoping, again – described the new policy as “well-meaning but wholly inadequate” to tackle the “avalanche of escalating abuse” faced by the transport workers she represents.

“There has been a massive escalation in reported assaults on public transport across the country,” says our transport correspondent Gwyn Topham, who reported earlier this month on the growing number of verbal and physical assaults faced by transport workers and passengers. In my previous incarnation as Scotland correspondent, I wrote about bus driver Keith Rollinson, who died at Elgin bus station after a violent assault by a teenage passenger.

Thoughtlessly broadcasting your TikTok scrolling is at the other end of the spectrum, but there’s an argument that antisocial behaviour exists on a continuum, and that a “nip it in the bud” approach might prevent more serious problems from escalating. Zero tolerance policing of course has a mixed record – and if you detect Tony Blair vibes here, so do I. Dropping a grand for loudcasting your tunes has more than a whiff of New Labour’s respect agenda and the classist asbo culture it ushered in, which singularly failed to tackle antisocial behaviour at its roots.

Still, there’s much to be said for elevating the issue from shared eye-rolls to official tannoy announcements. This is a policy that is going to appeal hugely to commuters, Gywn predicts, and when we are speaking he points out that the article about the campaign launch has been most-read across the Guardian website throughout the morning. “What he’s done well is to acknowledge an everyday irritation, that doesn’t cost a lot of money to fix, but can hopefully alter public behaviour.”
Can telling people to behave better work?

Gentle nudges towards more respectful behaviour, rather than sledgehammer fines, have made a difference historically, writer Dan Hancox tells me. His latest book, Multitudes, is about crowd behaviour, and recalls “a real moral panic” in the early 2010s over teenagers playing tinny MP3s aloud from basic mobile phones.

Dan could see why people found this irritating, but defended it at the time: “It was a rare example of sharing of music as a social adhesive, at a moment when David Cameron was introducing austerity and the spaces in which young people could gather together were being shut down.”
Crucially, within a couple of years the behaviour had died down again, as often happens after the initial buzz around new technology and the social pressure points they create.

But this phenomenon of people playing video out loud on their phones has got noticeably worse in the last couple of years, he believes, and, as I match Dan’s anecdotal experience with my own, it’s not all about the young ones this time. Indeed, younger travellers seem more likely to rely on noise-cancelling headphones – which some audiologists have raised concerns over potential links to auditory processing problems.

So why are otherwise apparently mature adults broadcasting their content and calls on the bus? The notion that people have “forgotten how to behave” since the Covid lockdown is one that Dan refutes. “It feels like an easy answer for something that is much more complex,” he says. “But it didn’t go on for that long, and the really remarkable thing about human beings is how quickly and elastically they bounce back to their previous sets of behaviours.”
The more boring answer, he suggests from his own research, is that as 5G makes watching videos easier to do wherever we are – people are simply seizing that opportunity.

But crowd psychology tells us that other people’s propensity to broadcast noise has a minimal effect on our own behaviour. “People’s pre-existing values and social mores are incredibly robust and are unlikely to change based on the behaviour of a complete stranger,” says Dan. And this makes it much more susceptible to the kind of nudge messaging over the train tannoy that Burnham is proposing.

In my own experience of antisocial behaviour on public transport, it seems that two things can be true at once: there’s a growing anxiety that this indicates an unravelling of the social contract, and in the main our interactions with fellow passengers often reassure us this is not, in fact, the case.

It’s possible that anxiety about strangers and the malign influence of the crowd arises at moments of wider pressures, says Dan. “When people are worried about paying the rent or feeding their families, as wars in the wider world rock our sense of stability and faith in human beings, our suspicion of the random person on the bus grows.

“But my day-to-day experience of life in a big and supposedly alienating city like London tells me people want this kind of spontaneous connection more than ever, and it’s a joy when it happens. Even if it’s just a few warm words exchanged with a stranger at the bus stop, on the train or in the shops – this is what it means to live in a society.”

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

blocks.caption: Two adult sandwich terns with a chick. Photograph: David Kinchin Smith/RSPB

blocks.text: In 2022, bird flu wiped out the colony of sandwich terns nesting at Pagham harbour, West Sussex. But their numbers have since bounced back to 756 breeding pairs – and populations of other birds such as ringed plovers and oystercatchers have also increased along the same coastline.

The turnaround is thanks to conservation efforts by RSPB staff and volunteers, which have included removing certain vegetation to make space for shorebirds to nest, and erecting special fencing to keep out predators such as foxes.

The RSPB’s Wez Smith said: “It’s taken several years of dedicated conservation action, but the situation began to ‘tern’ around last year, and the site is now thriving with record breaking populations using it.”

articles.title: Myanmar’s ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi seen in rare photos after receiving gift from King Charles
articles.summary:
Critics said images of detained former leader were a stunt by the military to end country’s diplomatic isolation

Myanmar has delivered presents from Britain’s ​King Charles to

blocks.text: Myanmar has delivered presents from Britain’s ​King Charles to Aung San Suu Kyi, releasing rare photos of the imprisoned former leader in what critics said was a stunt by the country’s military to end diplomatic isolation.

A presidential spokesperson said on social media that home ministry officials handed over two gardening books on soil, “along with one sealed envelope and a sealed diplomatic pouch”, from King Charles, who is known to have an interest in planting and the environment.
Photos showed the Nobel Peace laureate smiling in a wood-panelled room, a paper calendar on the wall behind her.

Suu Kyi, 81, the daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San, has spent much of her life in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements. She is now serving multiple sentences under house arrest at an undisclosed location in Naypyidaw, the capital.

Over her lifetime, the country’s military rulers have been cautious about locking Suu Kyi away in prison due to her beloved domestic status and international prominence, particularly in Britain, where she lived and married an Oxford academic. Most other political prisoners languish in jail.

Despite winning a 2015 election, she was deposed in a military coup in 2021, triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to the independent conflict monitor ACLED. Since then, Suu Kyi’s whereabouts and health have been difficult to determine until an International Committee of the Red Cross visit in August.

Coup leader and former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely condemned as a sham, and has been making efforts to rebuild regional and international diplomatic ties.
Kim Aris, Suu Kyi’s son who lives in London, said in a statement that he welcomed Charles’s gifts but warned their delivery should not be exploited by the regime.

“We must not allow the military regime to use such selective disclosures to create an illusion of normality or gain international legitimacy,” he said. “My mother’s fundamental human rights continue to be violated.”
Min Aung Hlaing remains under US sanctions for human rights abuses, including the 2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims that Washington considers a genocide.

The former commander-in-chief has recently conducted several regional visits to rebuild bilateral ties with neighbours, after the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) regional bloc barred him from its summits for not following an Asean-brokered ‌peace plan.
During his most recent trip to Malaysia this month, the leader was given an official welcome and honour guard. Min Aung Hlaing earlier visited Laos, Thailand, Vietnam and Cambodia.

blocks.caption: Aung San Suu Kyi pictured delivering a speech in 2020.  Photograph: Aung Shine Oo/AP

blocks.text: Phil Robertson, director at the Asia Human Rights and Labour Advocates (AHRLA) group, said the Suu Kyi book photo op was part of Myanmar’s “quest for global legitimacy”.

“The bottom line is Asean has grown tired of arguing with Min Aung Hlaing and Myanmar’s intransigent military leaders and having nothing to show for it, and they desperately want to move the bloc on to other, more cheery issues,” he said.

“So as the Asean dominoes fall to the Myanmar charm offensive, they just want to make their regional capitulation look good – and that requires Myanmar to play its part by trotting out Suu Kyi at occasional intervals to receive their latest beneficence.”
Min Aung Hlaing has also made efforts to reach out to Donald Trump’s administration, saying in a September interview with Time magazine that “it would be ideal if the US could cooperate with us”.

Weeks later, Reuters reported that the US and Myanmar officials had held talks in Naypyidaw and Tokyo, in part to shut down scam centres that target Americans, but which could be broadened to exploitation of Myanmar’s mineral deposits.

The US state department has said it is re-examining “the range of tools the United States has historically leveraged to promote core interests in the country”. China has become Myanmar’s key global partner.

Myanmar has always denied the accusations of genocide, and Suu Kyi, who held the role of state counsellor at the time of the atrocities, defended the country at the international court of justice, disappointing many in her global support base.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed to this report

articles.title: Signal No. 1 up in 5 Luzon areas as Super Typhoon Rosal enters PAR
articles.summary: Tropical Cyclone Wind Signal No. 1 was raised over five areas in Luzon after Super Typhoon Champi entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) and was given the local name Rosal, the state…

blocks.text: October 20, 2026 | 1:06pm

MANILA, Philippines — Tropical Cyclone Wind Signal No. 1 was raised over five areas in Luzon after Super Typhoon Champi entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) and was given the local name Rosal, the state weather bureau PAGASA said Tuesday.
Rosal entered PAR at 10:40 a.m. on Tuesday, October 20.
In its 11 a.m. bulletin, PAGASA said Rosal was packing maximum sustained winds of 185 kilometers per hour near the center and gusts of up to 230 kph.
The super typhoon was last spotted 1,385 kilometers east of Central Luzon, with strong to typhoon-force winds extending up to 720 kilometers from its center.
Rosal is moving west-northwestward at 25 kph.
Warning signal
The state weather bureau hoisted the following tropical cyclone wind signal:
Signal No. 1
Luzon

items: Batanes
Eastern portion of Babuyan Islands (Babuyan Island, Camiguin Island, Didicas Island)
Eastern portion of mainland Cagayan (Santa Ana, Gonzaga, Lal-Lo, Santa Teresita, Camalaniugan, Aparri, Buguey, Gattaran, Baggao, Peñablanca)
Northeastern portion of Isabela (Maconacon, Divilacan, Palanan, San Pablo, Cabagan, Santa Maria, Tumauini, Ilagan City)
Northeastern portion of Catanduanes (Pandan, Bagamanoc, Panganiban, Viga, Gigmoto)

blocks.text: Residents in these areas may experience strong winds ranging from 39 to 61 kph within the next 36 hours, which could pose minimal to minor threats to life and property.
PAGASA said the highest wind signal that may be raised during Rosal's passage is Signal No. 2 or 3.
The northeast monsoon and Rosal's outer circulation will also bring strong to gale-force gusts over parts of Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao.
Sea conditions
Very rough seas, with waves reaching up to 4.5 meters, are expected along the northern and eastern seaboards of Catanduanes.

Rough seas, with waves reaching up to 4 meters, may affect the seaboard of Isabela, the eastern seaboards of Batanes, Babuyan Islands and mainland Cagayan, as well as the northern seaboards of Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur, Northern Samar and Eastern Samar.

PAGASA advised mariners to remain in port or seek shelter in a safe harbor in areas where very rough seas are expected. Operators of small vessels, including motorbancas, were also advised against venturing out to sea under rough conditions.
The weather bureau said a gale warning may be issued Tuesday afternoon or evening over the northern and eastern seaboards of Northern Luzon and the eastern seaboards of Southern Luzon.
Track, intensity
Rosal is expected to move west-northwestward until Wednesday, October 21, before moving generally northwestward until Friday morning.
On Friday afternoon, the super typhoon is forecast to turn north-northwestward to northward before exiting PAR by Friday evening or early Saturday, October 24.
PAGASA said Rosal is forecast to maintain its super typhoon strength and may further intensify while moving over the Philippine Sea.

It is expected to weaken into a typhoon on Thursday, October 22, and may further weaken into a severe tropical storm by Saturday evening or Sunday morning while outside PAR due to an unfavorable environment.

articles.title: How is the US economy really doing under President Trump?
articles.summary: Ahead of the midterms Trump has boasted about the performance of the US economy. BBC Verify looks at inflation, jobs and economic growth in the country.

blocks.text: ByBen Chu
Policy and analysis correspondent
President Donald Trump has been boasting about the performance of the US economy ahead of the midterm congressional elections, claiming he has boosted incomes, reduced inflation and created jobs.
Trump has repeatedly said: "We have the hottest country anywhere in the world."

While the overall US economy is faring better than many expected after Trump launched his sweeping "Liberation Day" tariffs in 2025, there's evidence those import taxes and the impact of the US-Israel war with Iran have pushed up inflation, with the harmful effects felt by most American households.
The US economy is also being helped by an AI investment boom, and could falter if that spending were to dry up.
So how does all this feel for the average American? BBC Verify has looked at whether the evidence supports the president's claims.
1. US economy growing
The overall US economy is growing at a respectable clip by the country's recent historic standards.
The latest data shows US GDP, external - which is how economists measure the size of the US economy - currently expanding at an annualised rate of 2.2%.
And it has increased by around 3.2% overall since the end of 2024, just before Trump took office for his second term.
That is more growth than any other member of the G7 group of leading economies over that period.

The US growth rate has been faster than was forecast by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), external in the immediate wake of Trump's announcement of a swathe of new tariffs on goods coming into the US on 2 April 2025.
It downgraded its forecasts at the time, citing the negative impact of Trump's import duties on investment and consumer spending.
Though it is important to note that Trump eased the tariffs considerably in the months that followed, reducing the impact that had initially been expected on the economy.
The US economy has also been heavily supported in recent years by American technology companies making massive investments in AI, including by constructing data centres around the country.
Spending on building data centres, external (excluding the IT hardware to go in them) by US businesses in August 2026 was $5bn, almost double the monthly rate when Trump returned to office.
2. Inflation picked up
Many American voters wanted to punish Joe Biden in the 2024 presidential election, holding him responsible for the pain caused by a significant spike in prices in the wake of the pandemic.
The current rate of US inflation, external is 3.7%.
That's still well down on the recent peak rate of 9% under Biden in 2022, but higher than the 3% rate that Donald Trump inherited in January 2025.
Economists estimate, external US inflation would have been lower without the new tariffs imposed by Trump since he returned to office.
While the impact of the Iran war on global energy prices, with the significant disruption to oil and fuel supplies from the Middle East, has also helped push up US domestic inflation.
3. Household income growth held back
Average US household incomes are still rising under Trump.
The median income - after adjusting for inflation - rose 2.6% in 2025 to $87,460, the highest on record, external.
However, the Institute on Taxation and Economic Policy (ITEP) think tank has estimated the combined effects of the following, external on US households:
- Trump's tax cuts
- The expiry of extra government subsidies that had made health insurance cheaper for millions of Americans
- Higher-than-expected price rises during Trump's second term, including those linked to tariffs and the Iran war
ITEP's conclusion is that the middle fifth of households are, on average, around $1,700 worse off in 2026 than they would have been, while the poorest fifth are around $750 worse off.
The richest 1%, by contrast, are estimated to be an average of $12,560 better off than they woud have been, primarily because of Trump's tax cuts.
ITEP's estimates about the impact of tariffs on American households of different income levels are broadly similar to those of the Tax Foundation think tank, external.
4. Job creation slowed down
Trump predicted his tariffs would result in America being "flooded with jobs", external as manufacturing firms set up new factories on US soil to avoid their products being taxed at the border.
Since he returned to the White House, an average of 34,000 jobs have been added to the economy each month.
​​But that is significantly down on the 122,000 jobs added each month in the final year of Biden's presidency, external.
5. Borrowing costs rising
The growing deficit is also one of the reasons the US government gets charged more to borrow money in financial markets.
The 10-year US government bond yield has risen sharply since Trump returned to office in January 2025 and is now above 5%, the highest rate since the global financial crisis in 2007.
That increase in the market cost of US government borrowing also puts upward pressure on the interest rates on mortgages available to American households.
The interest rate on a new 30-year US mortgage has risen to 7.4%, external per year, up from 6.9% when Trump returned to the White House.

That's added to problems in the US housing market, making homes less affordable for new buyers. It has left many existing owners reluctant to move because doing so would mean giving up their cheaper mortgages, which they took out at lower rates, external and cannot take with them to a new property.
Data graphics by Erwan Rivault.

articles.title: Senate panel approves proposed 2027 OVP budget in under 20 minutes
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte skipped the budget hearing to represent her father at the inurnment of a Davao City official, OVP chief of staff Zuleika Lopez tells the Senate finance sub-committee A

blocks.text: Vice President Sara Duterte talks to supporters as she prepares to leave the Quezon City Regional Trial Court after the postponement of the arraignment for her grave threats case, on October 9, 2026.
Noel Celis/Reuters
Vice President Sara Duterte skipped the budget hearing to represent her father at the inurnment of a Davao City official, OVP chief of staff Zuleika Lopez tells the Senate finance sub-committee A

MANILA, Philippines – The proposed P785.2-million of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) for 2027 hurled the deliberations of a Senate Finance sub-panel on Tuesday, October 20, in under 20 minutes.
Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito arrived in the upper chamber at around 10:16 am to open the deliberations of Senate finance sub-committee A on the OVP’s proposed budget.
Ejercito proposed the budget’s approval for plenary consideration at around 10:31 am, extending inter-parliamentary courtesy to the OVP.

“This representation acknowledges the tradition of inter-parliamentary courtesy in respect to the OVP while also assuring to the public that the fiscal year 2027 proposed expenditure program is taken up wth due diligence,” the lawmaker said.
OVP chief of staff Zuleika Lopez represented the agency at the hearing.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian asked Lopez about the absence of Vice President Sara Duterte at the budget hearing. He noted that last year, Duterte took time out of her busy schedule to lead her agency in defending their budget.

blocks.caption: Senate panel approves proposed 2027 OVP budget in under 20 minutes

blocks.text: Lopez answered, “The Vice President is actually representing former president Rodrigo Duterte in the inurnment of our long serving city planner in Davao City. The schedule for the inurnment is today, October 20. So she’s the representative of the former president.”
Gatchalian, who was Senate finance committee chair during the budget deliberations in the previous year, expressed hope that Duterte would defend the OVP budget at the plenary.
The OVP is proposing a P785.2-million budget for next year — 11% lower than its P889 million budget for 2026. Among their projects are socioeconomic programs targeted to extend aid.
The Senate is on a break in the impeachment trial of Duterte to focus on the proposed 2027 budget. – Rappler.com

articles.title: In ruby-red Kansas, Trump contemplates the possibility of a Democratic win in the state
articles.summary:
The president came out in support of Senator Roger Marshall, who is facing and unexpectedly strong challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton

The fact that Donald Trump was here at all said more…
articles.byline: David Smith in Park City, Kansas

blocks.text: The fact that Donald Trump was here at all said more about a looming electoral disaster facing his Republican party next month than anything contained in his dark and discursive 98-minute stump speech.

On Monday, amid raucous chants of “USA! USA!”, the president held his first campaign rally in Kansas for eight years. No Democrat has won a US Senate seat in this ruby-red state since 1932, the year Herbert Hoover was president, Amelia Earhart was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic and the Nazis became the biggest party in the German Reichstag.

Since then Republicans in the state have built one of the longest winning streaks in Senate history, but such is the collapse in public esteem of the president that the midterms on 3 November could be the night that a blue wave engulfs the heart of Trump country.

“You’re really sort of – I hate to say it – you’re sort of tending toward the purple,” the president told about 5,000 supporters in a multipurpose arena outside Wichita, acknowledging that Kansas already has a Democratic governor in Laura Kelly. “That’s why I have to be sure that we get this guy.”

The “guy” concerned was Roger Marshall, a first-term Republican senator facing an unexpectedly strong challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton, a Methodist megachurch pastor. Opinion polls show them running neck and neck. In the third quarter, Hamilton reportedly raised $11m while Marshall managed just $800,000.

blocks.caption: Attenders cheer as Donald Trump arrives to speak during the rally in Park City, Kansas. Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Marshall, 66, is an obstetrician-gynaecologist and ex-congressman who has proved a staunch Trump ally, including by embracing his debunked claim that the 2020 presidential election was stolen. Hamilton, 62, founded the 24,000-member Church of the Resurrection, the biggest United Methodist congregation in the country. He opposes Trump’s tariff agenda and what he calls the president’s “erratic leadership”.

Despite Hamilton’s background as a pastor and former Republican, Marshall insisted on Monday that Hamilton was “too woke for Kansas”. Accompanied by Chuck Berry’s Johnny B Goode as he walked on stage, Marshall said: “This is a guy that participates in protests against police. He supports drag shows. He tells us to apologise for the colour of our skin. And in a state with more cattle than people, he tells you to stop eating beef.” The crowd jeered each time.

Trump, 80, is barnstorming the country in what some have called a “desperation tour” aimed at rescuing Republicans from the hole he has dug for them. Critics suggest he might actually be making life harder by nationalising races that candidates would prefer to keep focused on local issues.

blocks.caption: Trump shakes hands with Senator Roger Marshall at the Kansas rally.  Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

blocks.text: By imposing himself in Kansas, at a rally that was disrupted by several protesters, Trump underlined the election as a referendum on his presidency, with the potential to cost Republicans control of both the Senate and House of Representatives just two years after they swept into power.

Farmers in Kansas, a heavily agricultural state, have been hit hard by the consequences of the Iran war: a gallon of diesel costs nearly $6. The president upset cattle ranchers with a plan to reduce import tariffs to lower the price of beef and with aggressive immigration raids that prompted some agricultural workers to stay at home. On Monday Trump announced a new program to provide farmers with $8bn in support to offset diesel costs during the harvest season.

The election will test whether the old playbooks that fuelled his presidential campaigns – hurling insults, stirring bigotry and telling lies – can still work among an electorate weary of the cost of living, foreign wars and government corruption.

blocks.caption: Trump dancing at the campaign rally. Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP

blocks.text: Trump launched a tirade against Hamilton, dismissing him as a “radical left lunatic” and a “phoney who’s pretending to be a moderate”. Trump claimed the Democrat supports flooding Kansas with refugees who “go around killing people”, that he used church money to fund “transgender crap”, that he “openly mocks Jesus” and that he believes America is systemically racist.
“He wants you to repent for being born white,” Trump said.

The president also sought to weaponise the recent upheaval in France, pushing the baseless nativist claim that the violence is being led by immigrants. “We’re not going to let that happen to this country,” he said. “When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what the radical Dumocrats want to ​do to America.”

Trump unleashed bitter attacks on three Muslim politicians: Abdul El-Sayed, Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib. When Tlaib’s name was mentioned, members of the crowd yelled: “Deport her!” Trump falsely claimed that both El-Sayed and his sister are members of the Muslim Brotherhood, an Islamist opposition group in Egypt. He mockingly warned that, should El-Sayed be elected and sit on the Senate intelligence committee, he would leak information to the enemy.

Supporters roared their approved, thrilled by what they saw as Trump’s transgressive daring. The president, who won Kansas by 16 percentage points against Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, showed he can still draw a crowd in one of the most surprising battleground states in the country.

Earlier, in warm sunshine, a long line of people snaked through fields outside the 5,000-seat multi-purpose arena in Park City, Kansas. There were sights that have become familiar over more than a decade: giant Trump flags, tables full of “Make America great again” caps, spangly “DJT” and “Trump the golden age” jackets, “Alligator Alcatraz” merchandise, “We are all Charlie Kirk now” sweaters and T-shirts that said “Stand for the flag, kneel for the cross”.

blocks.caption: Trump eyes the crowd during the rally in Park City. Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: One woman wore a sweater that said: “0% liberal.” One man wore a T-shirt that declared: “I love Trump because he pisses off all the people I can’t stand.”

For these supporters, Trump rallies are galvanising and still the best way to get out the Republican vote. Cybersecurity worker Justin Nelsen, 44, said: “It fires us up, it gets us all excited for the cause and allows us to put out there what we want here as the state of Kansas. That’s why I’m here.”

Attendees were aware of the danger posed by Hamilton. Brittany Jones, a 33-year-old lawyer wearing a Stars and Stripes sweater, said: “If you know Adam Hamilton at all you know that he’s a problem and a chameleon and good at saying what he thinks people want to hear, even if he doesn’t believe it. He has shown himself to be not only a turncoat to things that matter to Christians, he has wholly given himself to the local agenda. Even though he claims to be a moderate, there’s nothing moderate about him.”

A Democratic victory here would represent a political earthquake, Jones acknowledged. “It’s seismic. It would be sad for most Kansans when they realise what happened, and some people just aren’t thinking through the consequences, but he has a built-in audience of people who are highly motivated.”

blocks.caption: A protester is removed as Trump speaks at during the rally. Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/Reuters

blocks.text: Jones, who had her friend’s three-month-old baby, Hannah, tucked under one arm, said she mostly welcomed Trump’s second term. “Overall I care about the social issues and he’s done a lot to protect girls’ sports, he’s done a lot to protect kids from being put through harmful gender transition procedures. Those things matter to me, they matter to the future of girls all across Kansas and America, and so I’m excited about those things.”
Construction worker Thad Snider, 42, who attended wearing a red “Make America Great Again” T-shirt alongside his mother, said he was not overly worried about the Senate seat falling to the Democrats.

“I don’t think Adam’s as strong a candidate as what the media is trying to sell him as,” he said, pointing to Hamilton’s past political donations to Democrats including Hillary Clinton. “I don’t think it’s going to happen but, if it did happen, it would be very shocking.”

Snider argues that voters faced a stark choice between political parties, describing the Republicans as the “least bad” option because “at least they’re not socialists or communists”. He added that he disagreed with foreign wars and wished Trump had done more on election integrity, but remained loyal to the president. “Any time you turn around a battleship, it takes time.”

That sentiment was echoed by Darrell Claphan, 72, a retired sales worker, who said of Trump: “He’s doing fantastic. He’ll go down in history being the number one president at what he’s done for the country in my lifetime.”
Claphan dismissed opinion polls showing a close race, stating: “Polls have been wrong ever since I’ve been alive.”
Asked how he would react to a Democratic Senate victory in Kansas, Claphan said: “I’d be shocked. But I don’t think it’s going to happen.”

articles.title: Filipinos split on Marcos admin’s handling of China dispute — survey
articles.summary: Filipinos are split on the Marcos administration’s handling of the West Philippine Sea dispute with China, but nearly three in four want the government to prioritize diplomacy.

blocks.text: October 20, 2026 | 12:01pm

In this handout photo from the Philippines' Presidential Communications Office taken and released on July 21, 2026, shows Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr (2nd R) holding talks with Chinese ambassador to Manila Jing Quan (2nd L) in Manila, after the diplomat was summoned to Malacanang presidential palace over a clash between the Chinese Coast Guard and the Philippine Navy on disputed South China Sea waters on July 20, which left two Filipino troops injured.
Presidential Communications Office

MANILA, Philippines — Filipinos are split on the Marcos administration’s handling of the West Philippine Sea dispute with China, but nearly three in four want the government to prioritize diplomacy, a Momentum Research survey showed.
The August 2026 survey found that 45.2% of respondents thought the administration was handling the dispute effectively, while 45% said it was not. The rest were undecided or declined to answer.
On dealing with China’s actions in the West Philippine Sea, 73.3% favored diplomacy. Some 19.1% disagreed, while 7.5% were unsure or declined to answer.
Metro Manila had the highest support for diplomacy at 86.9%, followed by Generation Z at 79% and opposition-aligned respondents at 76.6%.
In Mindanao, more respondents said the administration was handling the dispute poorly than well, at 46.4% and 35.8%, respectively. Another 17.7% were unsure or declined to answer.

Among Marcos supporters, 65.5% said the administration was handling the dispute effectively. A majority of Duterte-aligned respondents (52.3%) and opposition-aligned adults (56.7%) disagreed. Among independents, 48.4% said the administration was doing well, while 44.5% said otherwise.
Majority say Philippines relies too much on other countries
More than half of respondents (56.8%) said the Philippines relies too much on other countries for protection against China. About a third (33.7%) disagreed.
The view was most common among opposition-aligned respondents at 71.2%, followed by those in Metro Manila at 64.3% and Gen Z at 63.4%.
Half say West Philippine Sea info is sufficient

Half of respondents said they had enough information about developments in the West Philippine Sea. Meanwhile, 39.2% said the information available was insufficient, while 10.7% were unsure or declined to answer.
Millennials were more divided, with 49.6% saying they had enough information and 43.9% saying they did not.
Among Baby Boomers, 42.8% said the information was sufficient, while 25.3% were unsure. Respondents in Mindanao and those who identified as independents also had mixed views.

The Philippines and China have long disputed parts of the South China Sea, including the West Philippine Sea. Beijing has rejected the 2016 arbitral ruling that affirmed the Philippines’ sovereign rights in its exclusive economic zone.
The Philippine Coast Guard has repeatedly reported Chinese vessels entering Philippine waters. Filipino vessels have also faced water cannon attacks, ramming and blocking by Chinese vessels.

The Department of Foreign Affairs recently summoned Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan over his remarks that Beijing could “easily win” a confrontation with the Philippines and comments directed at Filipino officials who criticized him.
Some lawmakers have called for the envoy to be declared persona non grata. Malacañang has said President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has no intention of expelling him.

The survey was conducted through face-to-face interviews with 1,487 Filipino adults nationwide from August 18 to 23. It has a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 percentage points at a 95% confidence level.
