articles.title: Christiane Amanpour to leave CNN after 43 years
articles.summary: Christiane Amanpour's announcement comes after Paramount Skydance's controversial merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, CNN's parent company.

image.caption: Christiane Amanpour rose to prominence for her on-the-ground reporting from war zones in the 1990sImage: David Cruz Sanz/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Veteran journalist Christiane Amanpour on Monday said she was leaving her role at CNN after 43 years at the network.
"After thinking carefully for several months and experiencing a few sleepless nights, as you can imagine, I've decided to separate from CNN," Amanpour, 68, said in a statement.

"This daily show on CNN and PBS will come to an end at the end of this year. But CNN and I have worked out a smooth transition where we continue doing Amanpour once a week through to June," she said in a video message posted on social media.
Amanpour, who became famous for her on-the-ground reporting from major war zones, did not give a reason for her departure.
That said, her move to resign comes weeks after CNN's parent company, Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), was formally taken over by Paramount Skydance.
After a yearlong process, Paramount closed its merger with WBD on October 6, uniting two giants in TV news — CBS and CNN — under one roof.
The merger has drawn concerns over the independence of the newsroom at CNN as the merged company's owners, the Ellison family, are close allies of US President Donald Trump.
Trump bans media outlets from White House

"You know I've always been fiercely independent, and I will continue to be that for you as long as I am here and beyond. That's especially important today as we face unprecedented pressures from all sides, political, financial, and also from the rising dangers in the field," she said, without directly referring to the deal.
What to know about Amanpour's career

Amanpour, who was born in London to an Iranian father and British mother, joined CNN in 1983 as an assistant. In the next few years, she went on to cover major wars in the 1990s, including the Gulf War and the Bosnian War.
Amanpour has interviewed many world's leaders, reported from conflict sites and interviewed newsmakers from hotspots such as Iraq, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Somalia, Rwanda and the Balkans.

blocks.caption: Amanpour is one of the most recognized international correspondents [PHOTO: 2004]Image: Chris Helgren/REUTERS

blocks.text: She said she "looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral."
In a memo, CNN Chief Executive Mark Thompson praised Amanpur for "43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship."
"Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I'm very sorry to see her go, but I've come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally," Thompson said.

articles.title: Senate panel clears OVP budget in under 20 minutes as Duterte skips hearing
articles.summary: The Senate finance committee endorsed on Tuesday, October 20, the proposed P785.2-million budget of the Office of the Vice President for 2027 after a hearing that ran less than 20 minutes, with Vice…

blocks.text: October 20, 2026 | 11:21am

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate finance committee endorsed on Tuesday, October 20, the proposed P785.2-million budget of the Office of the Vice President for 2027 after a hearing that ran less than 20 minutes, with Vice President Sara Duterte absent.
Senate finance panel chair Sen. JV Ejercito declared the budget submitted for plenary consideration after Sen. Imee Marcos moved for its endorsement and Sen. Bong Go seconded. No senator objected.

Before suspending the session, Ejercito apologized that it had not been a shorter hearing. "Gusto ko sana, fifteen minutes eh. Kaso tumagal lang konti. So pasensya na po," he quipped. (I wanted it to be 15 minutes, but it took a little longer. So my apologies.)

The Senate committee's swift endorsement of the OVP's spending plan comes after the House of Representatives in September had also quickly dispensed and approved the OVP's proposed budget without debate.

For 2027, the OVP stands to get P785.2 million. This is P104 million, or 11.7%, lower than its P889.2-million budget for this year. It is also only slightly higher than the record-low 2025 budget of P733.198 million.
Of the total, P561.7 million is allotted to maintenance and other operating expenses, including P193.1 million for goods and livelihood grants and other aid.
Duterte's office contains no confidential funds in its proposed budget for a third straight year.
Congress has long extended "parliamentary courtesy" to the offices of the president and the vice president, typically clearing their budgets at committee level with few or no questions.

The same Senate committee approved the Office of the President's P10.15-billion budget in roughly the same amount of time on September 30, with Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian moving for approval before Executive Secretary Ralph Recto had presented it.

But the courtesy has not always held for the OVP. In 2024, the House cut the office's proposed P2.037-billion budget for 2025 to P733 million after Duterte declined to directly answer questions on her use of confidential funds. Senators in turn kept the same amount for the OVP and reasoned that the office failed to submit documents the finance panel requested.

On Tuesday, Gatchalian asked where the vice president was. "Traditionally, when budget deliberations are held, the head of office comes here to defend their budget," he said, noting that Duterte had attended last year.
OVP chief-of-staff Zuleika Lopez said Duterte was in Davao City representing her father, former President Rodrigo Duterte, at the inurnment of a former city government official.
Gatchalian said he hoped the vice president would defend the budget in person at the plenary stage.
The Senate president also said the lower budget showed the OVP was spending "as efficiently, as wisely as possible."

No senator asked about the OVP's spending record or how its aid funds would be distributed. Gatchalian said in August that issues before the impeachment court could not be raised in the OVP's budget deliberations, as they form part of the case.

articles.title: Canadian tourist found guilty of animal cruelty after stealing Las Vegas flamingo from enclosure
articles.summary: The man testified that he snatched Peachy from its enclosure at the Flamingo hotel and casino after drinking 30 to 40 beers, but did not mean any harm.

blocks.text: A Canadian man has been found guilty of animal cruelty after he took a flamingo from its enclosure in Las Vegas and brought it back to his hotel room during an alcohol-fuelled bender.
Mitchell Fairbarn, who was visiting the US city, took the Chilean flamingo named Peachy from the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino in March.

Videos shown at his trial showed a smiling Fairbarn carrying the bird by the neck as he took a lift to his room. He testified that he had drunk 30 to 40 beers before the incident and said he never meant to harm the animal. He faces nearly five years in prison.
Animal experts testified the flamingo had feathers torn out and suffered blood loss due to Fairbarn's actions.
A lawyer for Fairbarn said his actions were intended as a harmless prank, and blamed alcohol for his "bad decisions".
"He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn't have touched a bird, shouldn't have taken Peachy inside," said his lawyer Josh Tomsheck, external.
"The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions."
His lawyer added he had received death threats since his arrest.
Testifying in his defence, Fairbarn, 34, said he thought it would be "funny" to take the bird.
He said he had been up drinking all night and had just gotten off a call with a colleague when he made the decision to abscond with the bird.

The Flamingo Las Vegas, located along the famous Las Vegas strip, features a wildlife habitat inside its hotel and casino that is free to walk through. It features a flock of Chilean flamingos, other birds, fish and turtles.
During the trial, the jury heard from 14 witnesses and reviewed more than 112 pieces of evidence, according to CBS, the BBC's US partner.
It took a jury around five hours to convict him on felony and misdemeanour animal abuse charges.
Fairbarn has been unable to leave the US since his arrest. He remains on house arrest in Las Vegas, with a sentencing hearing due to take place in December.
A veterinarian for the state said that Peachy has largely recovered since the event but has a now has a more anxious demeanour around humans.

articles.title: Seventh day of violent clashes between Albanian protesters and police
articles.summary: Almost 300 people have been injured, more than half of them police, as violent anti-government demonstrations show no sign of easing.

blocks.text: Protesters in Albania have fought with riot police on the seventh consecutive day of violent clashes.

The protesters, many of them high school and university students, are trying to oust embattled Prime Minister Edi Rama. Official figures said 295 people have been injured, 186 of whom are police officers, before Monday's violence.
"The moment the state negotiates with this," Rama told grim-faced police chiefs, brandishing a rock hurled at police on Sunday, "the state has fallen".

A police station and government buildings in Tirana have been attacked during the protests, which are being driven by demands for better university conditions, anger over corruption and calls for Rama's resignation.
The protesters included "young men and women who have been radicalised by dark forces in Europe and the US", Rama said. "Albania has become one of the targets of a well co-ordinated attack."

In brilliant October sunshine in Rinia Park, also known as Youth Park, I watched people prising loose cobble stones - like that brandished by the prime minister - as ammunition for later battles with police. They did not have long to wait.
A convoy of police vehicles advanced down a broad boulevard, led by an armoured truck firing water cannon and tear gas canisters among the fleeing protesters.
Squads of riot police chased the predominantly student crowd through the park. Protesters took refuge in a cafe where even the eyes of the waiters streamed from the teargas.

Under trees, volunteers in yellow reflector jackets stood their ground helping those overcome by the fumes. I watched a young man remonstrating with a policeman, who then fired pepper spray in his face at point-blank range.
"The police actions are often chaotic and stupid," human rights lawyer Gentian Sejrani told the BBC. He provides legal support to more than 100 people who have been arrested.
"In court, the police rarely present evidence," he said. His clients include a man arrested on his way to a bus stop – completely unrelated to the protests, he said.
"Those who are actually throwing stuff at the police rarely get caught, because they run the fastest," Serjani said.
Police appear as incensed by the violence against their colleagues as the protesters are by the strong-arm tactics of the police. The result is mayhem.

Outside the cafe in the park, when the gas has cleared, 27-year-old activist Sidorela Vatnikaj, a masters student, describes her typical day. In a movement without leaders she is one of the more experienced, with eight years in the forefront of anti-government protests behind her.

"In the morning, you try to co-ordinate with all the groups - where they are, and where the protest is taking place. If any lawyers are needed, if any first aid kit or any kind of equipment is needed. And you also have to make sure all your friends, your family members in the protest are OK."
The day is spent going from protest to protest, much of it running from police, she said.
She is uncomfortable with the violence towards the authorities from her fellow protesters, but blames the police for starting and fuelling it.
"When I see people throwing stones at the police, I understand their anger. I don't judge them. I'm not happy, but they have no other way to be listened to," Vatnikaj said.

"They come from families whose family members had no other choice than to leave the country - a million in the past decade. They have not only been robbed, they have been bullied, ignored and now they they have also been beaten up."
At the weekend, the prime minister asked rhetorically what would happen if he stepped down.

"We need a technocratic government for one year, to prepare the country for real, democratic elections," Vatnikaj replies. She has accused Rama of rigging previous elections, and of being hand in glove with rich foreign investors and organised crime groups.
Young people in Albania feel encouraged by their fellow Gen Z protesters around the world, Vatnikaj said.
"I have seen my mother and father's generation, working all their lives and dreaming of having a democratic society where they could live with dignity. That never happened," she said.

Rama has been in power for 13 years, and has been a dominant figure in Albanian politics since the turn of the century. He has promised EU membership by 2030, and said he is the only one who can deliver it.

articles.title: Zelenskyy accuses US of delaying Patriot missile shipment
articles.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused the United States of delaying deliveries of air defense missiles already paid for by European allies, as relations between Washington and Kyiv…

image.caption: Zelenskyy has accused Washington of deliberately stalling arms deliveriesImage: Henry Nicholls/PA Wire/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused the US administration of delaying the delivery of crucial missiles needed by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks.
He told US senators on Monday that "the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles" even though they had already been paid for by Ukraine's European allies.
The accusations come as Ukraine-US relations are strained. US President Donald Trump has eased sanctions on Russia and directly criticized Zelenskyy, calling for someone else to take his place.
What did Zelenskyy say?

The Ukrainian president said that the US was holding back interceptor missiles, with one shipment only waiting for the signature of US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth before it could be sent to Ukraine.
He also said that Ukraine's European allies had agreed to transfer some of their own Patriot missiles but that this too was pending the green light from the US .
"The missiles are ready, and they could already be in Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "But unfortunately, there is still no approval."

blocks.caption: Ukraine urgently needs more air defence missiles like the Patriot systemImage: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

blocks.text: Earlier on Monday, he said Ukraine had again not received any early warnings about incoming Russian missile strikes. The country is dependent on the ability of US intelligence to spot fast-moving ballistic missiles fired by Russia.

There are also growing concerns over restrictions affecting Starshield, a military satellite communications network developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX. Ukrainian military communications and drone operations depend on using Starshield data.
The US government controls access to Starshield, but Trump has denied ordering any restrictions.
US says it's not withholding intelligence

The accusations come as Ukraine faces renewed Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure. In the night between Sunday and Monday, several Russian ballistic missiles struck the Ukrainian capital and its surroundings, cutting off electricity to more than half a million households.
"Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners," Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram about the attack.
The US, though, dismissed claims it was withholding information, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio insisting that Washington had not paused its intelligence sharing with Kyiv.
Regarding the easing of sanctions and the diesel deal between Washington and Moscow, Donald Trump strongly criticized Zelenskyy for calling out the deal.
"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said on Monday. "To be honest, I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."

articles.title: Car allegedly did U-turn and struck Helen Haines twice, in what some believe was targeted attack against MP
articles.summary:
Independent MP is in critical yet stable condition, as police interview alleged attacker in Wangaratta incident

  • Follow our

blocks.text: The man accused of attacking Helen Haines allegedly made a U-turn before ramming the independent MP twice in what some believed may be a targeted attack near her electorate office, according to eyewitnesses.
The independent MP remains in a critical condition after being airlifted from Wangaratta in northern Victoria to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital for emergency surgery on Monday night.

A 43-year-old Tarrawingee man alleged to have driven the Toyota Land Cruiser was arrested at the scene. The alleged attacker has been named as Tarrawingee man Brendan Nugent, Guardian Australia has confirmed.
Police were expected to interview the suspect in the attack on Tuesday, Acting Supt Ashley Mason said.
The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said witnesses alleged the driver completed a U-turn before the incident.
“What witnesses have described is the driver doing a U-turn to get into the car park and to ram Helen against a vehicle, then to reverse and do it a second time,” he told ABC radio.
“A bystander ran towards the scene, got the driver out of the vehicle and held the driver until police arrived.”
Ricky Jefferies, whose barbershop is next door to Haines’ office, ran from his shop to help after hearing the crash.
“I had no choice but to take him out of the car because it was the right and safest thing to do,” he told reporters on Tuesday morning.

blocks.caption: Barber Ricky Jefferies speaks to media outside his Wangaratta barbershop, next door to Helen Haines’ constituency office. Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Jefferies, who returned to work on Tuesday morning, alleged the driver had a knife on him. “He didn’t pull it out,” he said. “Basically just … took it out of his pocket and threw it away.”
Burke said: “I think every Australian is grateful for those moments when a hero like this runs towards the most dangerous place.”
The home affairs minister said the nation’s security agencies and police will be working through what more could have been done to prevent the alleged attack and to help keep others safe.
On Monday Burke reported that there had been 1,067 reports of harassment or threats against high office holders in Australia in the last financial year, an increase from 951 the year before.
“We we already knew that we needed to do more to be able to keep people in public office safe and we have been,” he said.
“While we don’t make public the dollar figures and the and the exact provision of security for obvious reasons … we had a very significant uplift in the budget.
after newsletter promotion
“There is a direct line between the temperature of debate and things willing people will say, and then when people are willing to take action.”

blocks.caption: A woman places flowers outside the office of federal independent MP Helen Haines in the Victorian regional city of Wangaratta. Photograph: William West/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has been joined by leaders and parliamentarians from across the country in calling for a calming of political discourse.
The mayor of Wangaratta, Irene Grant, expressed gratitude to Jeffries for stepping in to stop the man.
“I spoke to the barber this morning and he just shrugged his shoulders. He seemed to just take it in his stride. This was something that he had to do and he did it,” she said.
“He was extraordinarily modest about the very brave action that he took yesterday … he did an amazing job.”

blocks.caption: Haines was airlifted to Alfred hospital in Melbourne for treatment for critical injuries. Photograph: Martin Keep/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Wangaratta, the rural city in which the incident occurred, is a tight-knit community in north-east Victoria. At the last census it had a population of about 20,000 people, while the broader LGA had just under 30,000.

Haines was elected to federal parliament in 2019 and has been key to the establishment of the National Anti-Corruption Commission, as well as campaigning for rural health services, telecommunications access and pushing back on misuse of taxpayer funds, or pork barrelling.

articles.title: DILG chief Remulla says he regrets not arresting Bato dela Rosa
articles.summary: Remulla said he regretted a past decision to honor a "gentleman's agreement" between him and Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano that prevented Dela Rosa's arrest on Senate premises, admitting that trusting the…

blocks.text: October 20, 2026 | 8:41am
Senator Ronald Dela Rosa reacts as he talks to the media before the start of a plenary session at the Senate of the Philippines in Pasay, Metro Manila on May 12, 2026.
AFP / Jam Sta Rosa
MANILA, Philippines — Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said he regrets not arresting fugitive Sen. Bato dela Rosa when he had the chance in May this year.

In an ANC interview on Monday, October 19, Remulla said he regretted a past decision to honor a "gentleman's agreement" between him and Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano that prevented Dela Rosa's arrest on Senate premises, admitting that trusting the arrangement was a mistake.
“I dropped the ball. I should have arrested him in the Senate. Except there was an agreement right back then,” Remulla said.
During the arrest of suspended Sen. Jinggoy Estrada on June 1, Remulla personally arrested the lawmaker over plunder charges.
Remulla recounted telling Cayetano that they had lost the privilege of law enforcement authorities not arresting a lawmaker while in Senate custody when they allowed Dela Rosa to escape.
The International Criminal Court publicly revealed the arrest warrant against Dela Rosa on May 11, amid his public appearance before the Senate after hiding for almost six months.

However, he escaped in the early morning of May 14, hours after the May 13 shooting incident in the Senate between personnel of the Office of the Senate Sergeant at Arms and the National Bureau of Investigation.
Dela Rosa escaped by riding in the van of Sen. Robin Padilla, who faces complaints of obstruction of justice before the Department of Justice for helping Dela Rosa escape the Senate premises.
When asked about Dela Rosa’s current whereabouts, Remulla said he was in Mindanao, being protected by a “powerful group” with which the government is currently negotiating for his turnover.
While Remulla maintained that the government can arrest the senator, launching a hard tactical operation is off the table due to the risk of casualties.
“We do not want a civil war to start because of our arrest of one man. We want to do it properly and we want to do it judiciously, and we want to do it cleanly,” Remulla said.
Dela Rosa is wanted by the ICC for alleged crimes against humanity of murder during former President Rodrigo Duterte's drug war.
According to the ICC, Dela Rosa is accused of involvement in the killing of at least 32 people, allegedly committed between July 2016 and April 2018.
RELATED: Anyone who helped Bato dela Rosa may face charges — DOJ

articles.title: At least four dead after flooding in eastern Spain
articles.summary: At least four people have died in Spain as torrential rain has battered the country's eastern Mediterranean coast. The severe flooding had left more than 450 people stranded on rooftops, in buildings…

image.caption: The rain and flooding has devastated several communities along Spain's eastern coastImage: Jose Jordan/AFP

blocks.text: At least four people have died after heavy rain and severe flooding across eastern Spain, forcing hundreds of people to flee. The worst-affected areas are in the Valencia and Alicante regions, on Spain's eastern Mediterranean coast.
In the town of Oliva, two bodies were recovered on Monday. One victim was a 79-year-old woman found at her home, while another was a man who died from a heart attack at a campsite.
In Sagunto, a man drowned while swimming at the beach, while in Catalonia, a woman died after falling into a rain-swollen stream in Catalonia.

Emergency services have rescued more than 450 people who were stranded by the rising water. Some had to be airlifted from rooftops, flooded buildings and vehicles, while others were brought to safety by boat.

blocks.caption: Roads were underwater on MondayImage: Rober Solsona/EUROPA PRESS/dpa/picture alliance
Residents use buckets to drain water from their homes in DaimuzImage: Ana Beltran/REUTERS
Pile of furniture on a muddy streetImage: Rober Solsona/EUROPA PRESS/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Emergency restrictions
Authorities imposed emergency restrictions across several municipalities, asking people to stay indoors. Most restrictions have since been lifted.
The Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean, including Mallorca and Ibiza, were also affected, with schools closed, and some flights cancelled or delayed.
Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said military emergency teams were assisting with the rescue efforts and pledged full government support.
The latest flooding comes almost two years after the Valencia region suffered a devastating flood disaster that killed more than 220 people.

articles.title: Canadian who stole a Las Vegas flamingo after drinking '30 to 40' beers convicted of animal cruelty
articles.summary: A Las Vegas court convicted Ontario man Mitchell Fairbarn of animal cruelty charges Monday for snatching a flamingo named Peachy from its habitat at the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino last March…

image.caption: Mitchell Fairbarn breaks down while testifying during his trial at the Regional Justice Center in Las Vegas on Friday, Oct. 16. Fairbarn was convicted of animal cruelty Monday after stealing a flamingo named Peachy from its habitat at a the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino last March. (Benjamin H

blocks.text: Canada

A Las Vegas court convicted Ontario man Mitchell Fairbarn of animal cruelty charges Monday for snatching a flamingo named Peachy from its habitat at the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino last March in what prosecutors called a drunken and malicious act.
Mitchell Fairbarn of Ontario told court he meant no harm to Peachy, bird he took from Flamingo Hotel in March
What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas. Unless you drink "30 to 40 beers" and steal a flamingo — because that will make international news.

A Las Vegas court convicted an Ontario man of animal cruelty charges Monday for snatching a flamingo named Peachy from its habitat at an iconic Las Vegas hotel in what prosecutors called a drunken and malicious act.

Mitchell Fairbarn was accused of "willfully, unlawfully, maliciously and feloniously" injuring the flamingo in the early morning hours on March 3, according to the indictment viewed by CBC News. He pled not guilty and his trial started last week.

After jurors returned convictions on felony and misdemeanor animal cruelty counts, Fairbarn remained in custody pending a Dec. 1 sentencing hearing. He faces up to four years in prison for the felony conviction, plus six months of jail time for the misdemeanor conviction.
"I thought it was something that we could joke about for the rest of our lives," Fairbarn, described by various Las Vegas media outlets as a contractor from rural Ontario, said in court Friday.
The façade of the Flamingo hotel in Las Vegas is seen at night on Las Vegas Boulevard in this file photo. (Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images)

Fairbarn told the court that on the day of the incident, he drank "30 to 40" beers over the course of 24 hours while he was in Las Vegas for a construction expo, he said in video footage of the trial posted by multiple media outlets.

Fairbarn entered the flamingo habitat at the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino around 5 a.m. on March 3, according to the Las Vegas Review-Journal, and took the bird because he thought it would be a "silly joke" with his friends.
"I thought it would be, at the time, funny," Fairbarn said.

The Flamingo's wildlife habitat, which the hotel says spans four acres and is certified by the National Wildlife Federation, is home to the resort's namesake Chilean flamingos, among other birds, turtles and fish.
Peachy was shaking, bleeding: witness

Video played at the trial showed Fairbarn holding the flamingo by the neck in an elevator and carrying it down a hotel hallway. He spent about 15 minutes with the bird, and two-to-three minutes with it in his room, reported 8NewsNow, citing police evidence heard in court.

Two of Fairbarn's friends testified earlier this week that they had been out drinking, then woke up in their hotel room to find the flamingo there before moving it to the hallway, notes Fox 5 Las Vegas.
A hotel facilities engineer searching for Peachy eventually corralled the bird into a corner with a towel, and told the court Peachy was shaking and bleeding.

items: Canadians are still boycotting Las Vegas. The Sin City slump is now a major election issue
Italian wine thieves nab $8M of vino in heist. Here's why wine is a 'great target'

blocks.text: The flamingo was injured during the incident, suffering seven to eight missing feathers, broken feather shafts and blood loss consistent with trauma, the bird's treating veterinarian testified in court, according to Fox5 Las Vegas.
Peachy, who is 27 years old, needed antibiotics, anti-inflammatories and weeks of pain medication, the news outlet reported.

CBC News has reached out to the Las Vegas Justice Court for access to court filings and has not yet received them. But multiple local media outlets present in court have aired footage from court where Fairbarn doesn't deny his actions — just his intent.

His lawyer Joshua Tomsheck said Monday it was a drunken act and no harm was intended. When Tomsheck asked Fairbairn Friday if he had any malicious intent "in your mind or your heart when you picked up that bird," Fairbarn shook his head and answered, "no."
CBC News has reached out to Tomsheck, but has not yet received a response.

Fairbarn testifies during his trial at the Regional Justice Center on Friday in Las Vegas. He says he didn't intend to hurt the flamingo he took up to his hotel room in March. (Benjamin Hager/Las Vegas Review-Journal/The Associated Press)
Justice delivered: animal rights advocate

Prosecutors said Fairbarn willfully caused the bird physical pain, noting feathers were found on the hotel floor and video showed the bird squawking while Fairbarn handled it. But Tomsheck said his client regrets his actions while intoxicated and never meant to harm the bird, a key element in the felony charge.
"He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn't have touched a bird, shouldn't have taken Peachy inside," Tomsheck said in court Monday.
"The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions."

Fairbarn told the court Friday that he has remained under house arrest in Nevada since the incident. Court records viewed by CBC News show he had to surrender his passport as one of his bail conditions.
Jurors began deliberations after both sides presented closing arguments Monday morning.
Nevada animal rights advocate John Waudby, who recently helped strengthen the state's animal cruelty laws, told The Associated Press he believes justice was delivered on Peachy's behalf.
"I hope this sends a message to anybody else that wants to mess with our animals, that you're not going to do it in Nevada," he said outside the courtroom after Monday's verdict.
The Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino is home to the resort's namesake Chilean flamingos, which reside at the hotel's wildlife habitat. (Ceasars Entertainment)
Peachy has since recovered, according to Fox 5 Las Vegas. But the flamingo is just one of several recent cases involving animal cruelty at Las Vegas casinos, reports the Las Vegas Review-Journal.

In June, a woman was charged after allegedly jumping into the fountain at The Venetian and grabbing a duckling named Daffy. In May, a teen girl was arrested and accused of stabbing three horses the the South Point Arena & Equestrian Center so they couldn't compete in a barrel race.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news. She's worked as a journalist since 2009, with stints at the Globe and Mail and Postmedia News, among others. Before joining CBC News, she was the parents editor at HuffPost Canada, where she won a silver Canadian Online Publishing Award for her work on pregnancy loss. You can reach her at natalie.stechyson@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Super Typhoon Champi maintains strength near Philippines
articles.summary: In its weather forecast on Tuesday, October 20, PAGASA said Champi is estimated to be 1,605 kilometers east of Central Luzon, with maximum sustained winds of 195 kilometers per hour (kph) and gusts…

blocks.text: October 20, 2026 | 7:48am
Satellite image from state weather bureau PAGASA showing Super Typhoon "Champi" as of 2 a.m. on Oct. 20, 2026.
PAGASA / Released
MANILA, Philippines — Super Typhoon Champi has maintained its strength as it moves closer to the country, the state weather bureau PAGASA said.

In its weather forecast on Tuesday, October 20, PAGASA said Champi was estimated to be 1,605 kilometers east of Central Luzon, with maximum sustained winds of 195 kilometers per hour (kph) and gusts of up to 240 kph.
Champi is moving west-northwestward at 20 kph.
According to PAGASA, Champi's trough may bring cloudy skies, scattered rains, and thunderstorms to Catanduanes, Northern Samar and Eastern Samar.
PAGASA warned residents of these areas of possible flash floods or landslides due to moderate to, at times, heavy rains.
Palawan may expect cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms due to the Intertropical Convergence Zone.
The easterlies may also bring partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rain showers or thunderstorms in Batanes and Babuyan Islands.
Meanwhile, Metro Manila and the rest of the country may expect partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rain showers or thunderstorms due to localized thunderstorms.

articles.title: Morocco's first female prime minister caught between the king, clerics, and feminists
articles.summary: Will Fatima El Mansouri advance women’s rights amid religious and political barriers?

blocks.text: The Islamic saying "a people who entrust their affairs to a woman will never succeed" has resurfaced in Morocco since King Mohammed VI named Fatima Zahra El Mansouri as the country's first female prime minister.

Mustafa Ramid, a former justice minister in an Islamist-led government, cited the saying earlier this month, in a lengthy Facebook post questioning whether a woman should hold the country's highest political office.

He argued that Morocco, a Muslim majority country, had found a balance between equality and the responsibilities of state leadership, as the highest office - that of the king - continued to be reserved for men.
Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy. Yet executive power remains in the hands of the 63-year-old monarch.

El Mansouri's Authenticity and Modernity Party (Pam) won the most seats in September's parliamentary election and has since announced a coalition with three other parties. Together, they hold 207 of the 395 seats in parliament.
El Mansouri's royal appointment was historic but it exposed persistent reservations about women in positions of power.
The day after her appointment, local broadcaster Chouf TV took to the streets to ask Moroccan men "what they thought" of a woman heading the government.
Several men, mostly middle-aged or older, hesitated before answering. Some said they accepted the decision because it was the king's choice.
One grey-haired man, who did not give his name or age, said: "It feels strange to have a woman as head of government. I'm not sure if it sits well with me."
Criticism of the monarchy carries legal risks in Morocco. The penal code criminalises certain forms of offence or insult against the king, the royal family and the monarchy.
Online, the appointment became fodder for political satire.
A video showing two women pulling each other's hair was widely shared, with captions suggesting that this is what parliamentary disagreements between El Mansouri and her colleagues might look like.
However many younger Moroccans, especially women, welcomed her appointment.
While attitudes are changing in Morocco, conservative, religious views still hold great weight.
Some of the country's most contentious debates over gender equality centre on family law, including inheritance, marriage and divorce.
Under existing inheritance rules, a daughter typically receives half the share of a son in comparable circumstances.
The Higher Council of Ulemas, the country's body of religious scholars, has resisted calls for equal inheritance, citing Islamic jurisprudence.
It has also rejected proposals to abolish taasib, a rule that can require female orphans without brothers to share their inheritance with male relatives, including distant ones.
In a 2022 report, Morocco's National Human Rights Council said unequal inheritance rules contributed to poverty among women.

Polygamy is also legal under certain conditions. Proposed changes to the family code have included allowing women to stipulate in their marriage contracts that their husbands cannot take another wife.
But exceptions remain, including provisions relating to a first wife's infertility or illness, which women's rights groups have criticised on grounds of privacy and medical confidentiality.
These issues are at the heart of proposals to reform the Moudawana, Morocco's family code, which governs marriage, divorce and child custody.
A package of changes was announced in 2024, but the reforms have yet to become law.
As well as family law, some young women hope the new prime minister will try to improve education for girls.

Morocco's High Commission for Planning, the country's official national statistics agency, found in 2025 that just 55% of girls aged 15–17 were going to school in rural areas, where poverty, early marriage and dropping out of school remain key barriers. In urban areas, it was 100%.

"Many girls in rural Morocco drop out of school early because schools are far away, transport is unsafe or unavailable, and families with limited means often keep their daughters at home," Chifae Laazouzi, a young Moroccan woman, tells the BBC.
She says one reason is that many girls in poor and rural areas cannot afford menstrual sanitary products.
"Menstrual health is still treated as a taboo... I would like to see free menstrual products in schools," Laazouzi says.
El Mansouri is no newcomer to politics. Over more than two decades in public life, she has served as mayor of Marrakech, held government posts and sat in parliament.
For the past five years, she served as minister for national territory planning, urban planning, housing and city policy under the previous Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.
After her appointment, El Mansouri presented the moment as a milestone for Moroccan women.
"Being the first female head of government is not just a source of pride for me, but for all the women of the kingdom," she said.
Since her appointment, she has not indicated whether she plans to try and push through the reforms to the family code.
In her political career so far, she has not made any prominent public statements about women's rights, even while changes to inheritance rules, polygamy and the family code were being widely debated.
Dr Irene Fernandez-Molina, an expert on the Global South at the University of Exeter in the UK, sees the appointment in the context of the monarchy's broader political interests.

"Two headlines have dominated coverage of [September's] parliamentary election in Morocco: a two-decade low turnout and King Mohammed VI's appointment of a woman as prime minister for the first time in this country's history," she tells the BBC.
"The latter cannot be understood without the former."
Official figures put turnout at just 38% of registered voters, while the proportion of all eligible voters who cast a ballot was even lower.

Fernandez-Molina describes the appointment as an example of "authoritarian state feminism, a top-down, selective instrumentalisation of the struggle for women's rights for regime legitimation purposes".

She argues that promoting a woman to the highest government office might be intended to project an image of modernisation and progress, even when the political system and the pace of social reform remain largely unchanged.
For Moroccan women's rights advocate Yasmina Benslimane, the appointment breaks a longstanding barrier, but says El Mansouri's background is also important.
"It does challenge stereotypes, because it finally breaks a ceiling that was never broken," she says. "But it matters how she got there."

El Mansouri's late father was a pasha, a senior local official, and a diplomat. Benslimane argues that her privileged background and access to political networks distinguish her from many Moroccan women who have fewer opportunities to enter public life.
For Benslimane, like many women's rights groups in the country, reform of the Moudawana remains a key test of the new government.
However, El Mansouri's room for manoeuvre is shaped by the country's political system.
The king retains extensive powers over key areas, including defence and foreign affairs, while the head of government operates within a system where authority is shared.
When it comes to Moudawana reform, she would have to face the country's religious scholars, who are mostly men.
While some Moroccan women welcome her appointment, they say it is what she does as prime minister that really counts.

"I don't think El Mansouri should be judged by the fact that she is a woman. Being a woman in power doesn't automatically make someone a champion of women's rights," Sara Zouiten, a young Moroccan woman, tells the BBC.
"Her party presents itself as a modernising political force, so I want to see whether that translates into actual change."

articles.title: Five ways El Niño is affecting the weather around the world
articles.summary: As the strongest El Niño on record continues to intensify, what impacts on weather patterns are already being felt across the globe? Sarah Keith-Lucas looks at the evidence.

blocks.text: In the eastern Pacific, where El Niño tends to strengthen hurricane activity, it has been a very active season so far.
There have been 22 named storms and 12 hurricanes, including 10 major hurricanes.
This is already above the number that would typically develop in the whole of an average season, with two months left to go until its end.
Here, El Niño provides the ingredients of higher ocean temperatures and weaker winds high in the atmosphere, making it easier for storms to gain strength.
Hurricane Polo is one such example of this.
The hurricane experienced rapid intensification, producing wind gusts of 180 mph (285 kmh), fueled by the very warm waters produced by El Niño.
Polo was also one of three hurricanes churning away in the same basin at the same time, along with Odalys and Nolo.
Moreover, it has happened twice now in the space of a month.
Earlier in September, the energy produced by exceptional ocean heat resulted in three simultaneous hurricanes in the central and eastern Pacific: Lowell, Karina and Marie.
Until this year, the last time there had been three Pacific hurricanes at the same time was 2015.
In contrast, the Atlantic Ocean has remained eerily quiet.
El Nino has a tendency to increase wind shear in the north Atlantic, a factor which tears apart storms and limits formation.
There has only been one hurricane - Isaias - which made landfall in the Florida Panhandle and Alabama.
This was the latest forming hurricane on record in the satellite era (1960s onward).
Before this year, the record was 11 September, set in 2002 and 2013.
In an average season, there would have been 10 named storms, five hurricanes and two major hurricanes by this point.
This year, however, there have only been eight tropical storms: Arthur, Bertha, Cristobal, Dolly, Edouard, Fay, Gonzalo and Hanna.

articles.title: 'Not out of the woods': Family rallies around soldier badly burned in CFB Wainwright fire
articles.summary: Before he was airlifted to hospital and intubated, Sean Hiatt managed to call his mom and tell her he'd been injured in a training accident at CFB Wainwright. He was coherent at the time, according…

image.caption: Sean Hiatt, 24, is intubated in hospital after suffering burns to about 50 per cent of his body in a grass fire incident on base during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright. (Kelly Patterson)

blocks.text: Calgary

Before he was airlifted to hospital and intubated, Sean Hiatt managed to call his mom and tell her he'd been injured in a training accident at CFB Wainwright. He was coherent at the time, according to his sister, and it gave the family hope. Now they're focused on his immediate care, and taking things 12 hours at a time.
Sean Hiatt is in an Edmonton hospital with burns to half of his body

Before he was airlifted to hospital and intubated, Cpl. Sean Hiatt — the second-youngest in a family of 12 — managed to call his mom and tell her he'd been injured in a training accident at CFB Wainwright.
The 24-year-old was coherent at the time, according to his sister, and it gave the family hope.
Now they're focused on his immediate care, and taking things 12 hours at a time.

On Saturday afternoon, Hiatt suffered burns to about half of his body when wind gusts of up to 90 km/h pushed a grass fire one kilometre in less than a minute and onto a group of soldiers doing live-fire training.
Four soldiers were killed and 39 were injured. Hospitals across the province took in the wounded, including University of Alberta Hospital in Edmonton where Hiatt’s medevac landed.

“He was, and still is, sedated and intubated, he was completely wrapped up, they didn’t know the degree at that point because they had to get him stable,” Hiatt’s sister Kelly Patterson said in an interview with CBC News.
“It is really rough…. It was a shock to see him like that.”

items: 4 dead, at least 19 in critical condition after deadly fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta

blocks.text: Of the injured, 19 are in critical condition, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said at a news conference on Sunday.
One of those is Hiatt, from Edson, Alta., about 200 kilometres west of Edmonton.
One by one, family members began showing up at Hiatt’s bedside — brothers, a nephew, sisters and parents — to be with the guy they describe as “happy going”and “cheerful.”
'He's a fighter'
Patterson says her brother “perked up” with every visit, breathing a little bit better and “looking a little brighter."
The road ahead is going to be long and Patterson says Hiatt is “not out of the woods.”
Doctors are still concerned about lung damage and have yet to begin skin grafts. He faces weeks in the ICU and months longer in hospital.
The family is leaning on prayer and the knowledge that Hiatt is "a fighter.”
“He got out of there so he’s going to make it,” said Patterson.
'The whole community is feeling this'
Meanwhile, 200 kilometres from Hiatt’s hospital bed, he and the other injured and fallen soldiers are on the minds of folks in Wainwright, a town deeply connected to its base.
“Everyone’s really connected, everyone really cares for each other,” said Grade 12 student Rylan Pow. “It really was heartbreaking honestly.”
Grade 12 students showed up Monday morning with bouquets of flowers to pay their respects to those who were injured and killed in Saturday's fire at CFB Wainwright. (Gilbert Rowan/CBC)
On Monday morning, with their principal’s blessing, Pow and his entire class from Blessed Sacrament School showed up with their teacher to lay flowers at the town’s memorial clock cenotaph.
Teacher Janae Wildboer said she was in a panic when she learned of the fatal fire and wondered what she could do to help.
“Our school just wanted to do something to honour those who have lost their lives,” said Wildboer. “The whole community is feeling this; it's heavy and we're just now supporting where we can.”
'Still kind of in shock'
Down the street, outside of the Royal Canadian Legion Branch 29, which was set up Monday as a referendum polling station, David Campbell finished voting and then turned his mind back to the tragedy.
"Everyone's still kind of in shock,” said Campbell, who has lived in the area for more than 40 years.
“The base is very important, a lot of people work here. We’re farmers and we have cattle in the community pasture, we work with the military all the time, they live in town here, a lot of them.
“They’re part of the community, we know so many of them. Their kids are in hockey, my grandkids are playing hockey with a lot of the kids. It's very devastating.”
Smoke in the air
As the winds changed direction Sunday night and into Monday, the smell of smoke drifted in and out of the community. Fire Chief Aime Smyl warned that could continue in the days ahead.
The fire is still burning but considered contained, said Smyl in his social media post Monday afternoon. It’s not expected to breach the fire guard.
Local MP and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre attended the Wainwright cenotaph with flowers Monday morning. (Josh McLean/CBC News)
Smyl also thanked the seven other fire services that stepped up to help with Saturday’s grassfire response.
“I am also humbled by the number of departments that reached out to help,” he wrote.

By Monday morning, some of Smyl’s firefighters had been awake for three days, according to Local MP and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, who showed up at the cenotaph with flowers after a meeting with the fire chief.
Poilievre thanked the first responders, “who ran towards and not away from the fire” to help.
“It has been a phenomenal show of the best of Canada here in Wainwright.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Meghan Grant is a justice affairs reporter. She has been covering courts, crime and stories of police accountability in southern Alberta for more than 15 years. Send Meghan a story tip at meghan.grant@cbc.ca.

articles.title: In pictures: Dussehra celebrated across India as triumph of good over evil
articles.summary: The festival, which commemorates the triumph of good over evil, is celebrated with different rituals across India.

blocks.text: Image source, AP
The festival includes a variety of celebrations involving actors playing deities - pictured here an actor portraying Lord Ram prepares ahead of a procession in Prayagraj, Uttar Pradesh
ByRachita Prasad
BBC News, Mumbai

Millions of people across India are marking Dussehra, one of the country's most widely celebrated Hindu festivals, with processions, prayers and the ceremonial burning of giant effigies to symbolise the triumph of good over evil.
The festival is observed with different rituals and traditions across different parts of the country but with grand celebrations everywhere.
It commonly marks the deity Lord Ram's victory over the mythological 10-headed king Ravan.
The festival coincides with Vijayadashami, celebrated in eastern, southern and other parts of India, to honour goddess Durga slaying the buffalo demon Mahishasura.

Hindus follow a lunar calendar, and Dussehra falls on the 10th day after Navratri, a nine-night festival of worship and celebrations.

In the days leading up to Dussehra in northern India, performers wear elaborate costumes and make-up to stage Ramlila, the dramatic retelling of the ancient Hindu epic Ramayana. They recount Lord Ram's exile and his wife Sita's abduction by Ravan, culminating in the battle that symbolises the victory of good over evil. The final act is followed by the ritualistic burning of the effigies of Ravan, his brother, Kumbhkaran, and son Meghnath.
The vibrant stage is usually accompanied by a carnival-like atmosphere with food stalls, rides and smaller performances.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Ramlila performances often coincide with wider family-friendly events including stalls and rides, as pictured here in Noida

blocks.text: Ramlila performances often coincide with wider family-friendly events including stalls and rides, as pictured here in Noida
In the east and some other parts, as well as among Hindus in Bangladesh, the festival sees devotees worshipping the divine feminine power with Durga Puja celebrations.

Temporary tents housing idols of Goddess Durga and other deities are set up across cities and towns. People visit these structures, known as pandals, where Durga is often depicted slaying the buffalo demon Mahishasura.
Current affairs often make their way into the traditional celebrations, like theme-based decoration of tents in Kolkata city, which is famous for its Durga Puja celebrations.
