articles.title: 7 Filipinos hurt in attacks on Saudi Arabia; 3 in critical condition
articles.summary: Seven Filipino workers have been wounded in a string of attacks on Saudi Arabia, three of them critically, the Department of Foreign Affair said on Monday, October 19. Manila called on “all…

blocks.text: October 20, 2026 | 7:00am

This screen grab taken from CCTV footage played on a screen during a press conference by the Saudi-led coalition in Riyadh on October 15, 2026, and made available via AFPTV, shows what the coalition says was a Houthi attack on Abha International Airport on October 7, 2026.
AFPTV

MANILA, Philippines — Seven Filipino workers have been wounded in a string of attacks on Saudi Arabia, three of them critically, the Department of Foreign Affairs said on Monday, October 19. Manila called on “all parties to cease hostilities.”

The DFA said it was working with the Department of Migrant Workers and Saudi authorities to get medical care and other help to the injured. In a short statement, it offered condolences to the families of those killed, called the attacks “a grave threat to regional peace and stability,” and urged a settlement “through dialogue and diplomacy.”
Yemen’s Houthis have claimed responsibility for missile and drone strikes on Saudi targets, including a missile attack that hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.
That strike, on October 10, killed 12 people and injured 309, according to Saudi authorities. Reports described it as the deadliest attack in the kingdom in more than a decade.
The Houthis have hit Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers since a truce in Yemen’s long-running war broke down in July.
The fighting is part of a broader regional conflict that stems from the war that broke out on February 28 when the United States and Israel attacked Iran.
Nearly one million Filipinos live in Saudi Arabia, according to the DFA. More than 2.4 million live across the Middle East.
Saudi Arabia is the third-largest source of remittances from overseas Filipino workers (OFWs), behind the United States and Singapore.

articles.title: Trump borrows from far right to blame unrest in France on immigration
articles.summary: President ignores school conditions and cost of living and says he warned Macron ‘the whole world was coming in’

blocks.text: Donald Trump and JD Vance deployed a familiar US playbook on Europe, claiming that immigrants were responsible for rioting in France that began as student protests against crumbling schools and the high cost of living.

The nationwide protests on Saturday were called over rising fuel prices and falling purchasing power, and in several cities they escalated into clashes with police that left a historic town hall torched and led to 1,800 arrests. On Monday, overnight curfews were issued for a number of French cities, including parts of Paris.
“France is burning!” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Sunday, blaming “the immigration of people from an entirely different world” for the violence and looting.
He urged Paris to “Close your Borders and take control”.

Vance, a day earlier, argued that the unrest was the result of what he called a liberal failure. “Western liberals imported the third world into France,” he wrote on X, adding that the country had “ignored fundamental questions about assimilation and compatibility”.

The rhetoric echoes France’s far-right National Rally, whose president, Jordan Bardella, described the violence as a convergence of ultra-left extremism and delinquent populations from the suburbs. Trump and Vance have both publicly backed Marine Le Pen, and the unrest has added pressure on Emmanuel Macron six months before an April election to choose his successor.

The demonstrations in France began weeks ago, when high school students began marching for teacher shortages, crumbling classrooms and an opaque university admissions system. The CGT, one of France’s largest unions, has backed the movement and called for lower prices, higher pensions and better wages. The anger has since widened to fuel prices, which have climbed since US strikes effectively shut the strait of Hormuz, and other economic grievances.
As Trump set off for a campaign rally in Kansas on Monday, the US president told reporters at the White House that he had warned Macron he was “making a big mistake”.
“The whole world was coming in, and as you know, Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn’t the deal,” he said, adding: “We closed our borders. He didn’t.”

Not all protests have drawn the same attention from Washington, as young people have taken to the streets across Europe, in Spain, Portugal and Italy, over underfunded schools, housing costs and a wider squeeze on living standards.

Neither have the US president and vice-president commented on protests in Albania, where demonstrators have targeted both the government and a luxury tourism development backed by an investment firm founded by Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

Before Trump arrived on stage in Park City, Kansas, giant TV screens played about 10 minutes’ of Fox News coverage of the unrest that has gripped Paris and other cities, which included commentary blaming the trouble on the French government’s immigration policies.

Earlier in the day, the official White House X account posted: “If you import the third world, you become the third world.” An array of Republican politicians have lined up to make a similar argument, seeking to leverage the unrest in France against Congressional Democrats ahead of the 3 November midterms, in which their party faces significant headwinds.

House Speaker Mike Johnson posted: “France is descending into chaos because they wanted OPEN BORDERS — just like the socialist Democrats in America. What we are witnessing is a chilling warning for all Americans of what happens if the radical Marxist insurgent left gets their way.” Senator Eric Schmitt added: “The anti-civilization Left is devouring France. It will devour America if we let it.”
The vice president said he hoped Americans were paying attention as they cast their ballots.
“This is the future congressional Democrats seek for your country,” he concluded.
David Smith contributed reporting from Park City, Kansas

articles.title: US grants deportation reprieve to migrants from Ukraine and Sudan
articles.summary: DHS says migrants ‘retain protections’ after temporary protected status was set to expire on Monday

blocks.text: More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire on Monday.

Temporary protected status was set to end on Monday for about 101,000 Ukrainians and 1,800 Sudanese. But the DHS said an announcement “will be made at the appropriate time”. Until then, the department said in a written statement, Ukrainians and Sudanese in the US covered by those temporary measures “retain protection”. The department did not indicate how long they could stay or when a final announcement would be made on their status.
The DHS did not respond to a question about whether they can keep their work permits, but TPS generally allows people to work while their protections remain in effect.

The decision marks another incident where the Trump administration, which has previously sought to end these temporary protections from deportation and send people back to their home countries, has allowed people covered by the temporary status to stay in the country but without giving any guidance as to how long.

Yuriy Boyechko, CEO of Hope For Ukraine, a non-profit that provides humanitarian aid in Ukraine and helps resettle newcomers in the US, described the government’s announcement as “last-minute patches”.

It is a “bandage that has been placed on a wound that does not solve the real issue,” he said. “It’s time for US to come up with some normal path to permanent residency for all these people,” Boyechko noted. He emphasized that they cannot safely return to Ukraine.

Andrew Arthur, a national-security and immigration expert at the Center for Immigration Studies, a Washington thinktank that favors lower immigration, said the government will eventually decide but faces no deadline. Until then, nothing changes, he said.

“It’s simply going to be an extension until it is a termination,” he said. “It’s beyond cavil that both Sudan and Ukraine are experiencing ongoing armed conflict, and therefore the secretary is well within his authority to continue TPS for each of them.”
The Trump administration has already terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria.

But in a change in practice roughly a month ago, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorians whose TPS was set to expire on 9 September. In that case they also said that they were going to make a decision at the appropriate time and that in the meantime, people from El Salvador could continue to work and live in the US.

Activists and a bipartisan group of lawmakers have been raising the alarm over the upcoming deadline for TPS to expire for Ukrainians, arguing that conditions remain unsafe for them to return home amid the war with Russia.

Ukraine was first designated for TPS in April 2022, following Russia’s full-scale invasion two months earlier. The Biden administration subsequently extended the designation, most recently in January 2025, when the DHS authorized an additional 18 months of protection through October 2026.

The TPS program for Sudan was established in 1997, and since then, successive US administrations have extended it due to the armed conflict and political instability that have plagued the African nation.
Monday’s decision comes two weeks before the midterm elections, when Trump’s hard line immigration policies will face a test at the ballot box.

articles.title: New AI tool can predict cancer survival by a single patient selfie, study suggests
articles.summary:
System can estimate a person’s biological age and predict chances of cancer survival from a single photograph

Doctors have developed an artificial intelligence tool that can predict a cancer…

blocks.text: Doctors have developed an artificial intelligence tool that can predict a cancer patient’s chances of survival from a single photograph of their face.

The AI system was custom-built by experts at Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit, integrated academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, to estimate biological age and directly predict survival outcomes in patients diagnosed with cancer.

It is one of the most comprehensive demonstrations to date of how AI analysis of a selfie could help assess a patient’s health and potentially guide their medical care, and was trained on data from more than 40 million facial photographs across a range of ethnicities and ages.
Details of the breakthrough were published in the Lancet Digital Health journal.

The system can estimate a person’s biological age – the age a person looks, rather than their actual, chronological age – and predict the chances of survival for cancer patients from an ordinary photograph of their face, according to the results of a study that examined the model.

Doctors used the technology to develop two complementary tools. FAHR-FaceAge estimates a patient’s biological age, and predicts cancer survival. FAHR-FaceSurvival predicts survival from a facial photograph directly, rather than inferring survival through biological age.
Although FAHR-FaceAge and FAHR-FaceSurvival were derived from the same model, they captured different and complementary information about a patient’s health.

Each algorithm also relied on distinct parts of the face to make respective predictions of age and mortality risk. FAHR-FaceAge focuses on the creases that run from the sides of the nose down to the corners of the mouth, the forehead area just above the eye sockets, and the temples. FAHR-FaceSurvival, meanwhile, evaluates the region below the eyes and around the nasal bridge.

“FAHR-FaceSurvival advances the field of facial health recognition AI a step further by learning survival risk directly from facial photographs of patients with cancer,” said Hugo Aerts, a co-senior author of the study. “To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that an AI model can directly predict cancer survival from a simple photograph.”

Among cancer patients treated with radiotherapy in the US, the people who, according to FAHR-FaceAge, looked five or more years older than their actual age had a 21% higher risk of dying during the average four-year follow-up than the rest of the group. The patients who looked five or more years younger had a 17% lower risk.

“The key technical advance is that FAHR-Face learns a general representation of the face from more than 40 million images, which can then be adapted to distinct health outcomes such as biological age and survival,” said Aerts. “This foundation-model approach gives us a scalable way to develop multiple facial health biomarkers rather than training each model from scratch.”
The results of the study suggest people’s biological age estimates are closely linked to their physical health, which could reflect their ability to survive certain treatments.
The breakthrough could pave the way for AI facial analysis to assist doctors in making difficult decisions about the best way forward in terms of treatment for their patients.
The tool could help better predict the risk of death or complications after major surgery or other treatments for cancer.

Dr Raymond Mak, a radiation oncologist at Mass General Brigham, said: “As the population ages, physicians need better ways to estimate physical reserve and frailty before recommending intensive treatments such as radiation, surgery or systemic therapy.
“Our goal is to make face photograph-based health assessment more quantitative, consistent and scalable so it can support personalised treatment decisions rather than replace physician judgment.”

Researchers found lifestyle factors were associated with facial ageing. For example, heavy alcohol use, drug use and smoking were linked to looking biologically older in AI analysis of facial photographs.

“Another surprising finding was how consistent FAHR-FaceAge was across common real-world photo variations, including pose, lighting, facial expression and makeup,” said Mak. “It was also stable across most tested plastic surgery procedures, with only a small shift observed after rhinoplasty.”
Doctors cautioned that while single facial photographs could offer an easy, low-cost way to support personalised treatment decisions, more research was needed before the tool could be widely used.

articles.title: Man who lost legs to MS warming heads and hearts by knitting tuques on custom-made cot
articles.summary: Leonard Foidart built a cot so he can knit comfortably while lying down. The 84-year-old from Notre-Dame-de-Lourdes, Man., lost his legs decades ago and finds it difficult to sit but loves to knit,…

image.caption: Leonard Foidart built a cot so he can knit comfortably while lying down. The 84-year-old from Notre-Dame-de-Lourdes, Man., lost his legs decades ago and finds it difficult to sit but loves to knit, donating more than 1,000 tuques in the last five years. (Michele McDougall/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba

Leonard Foidart built a cot so he can knit comfortably while lying down. The 84-year-old from Notre-Dame-de-Lourdes, Man., lost his legs decades ago and finds it difficult to sit but loves to knit, donating more than 1,000 tuques in the last five years.
'You're here to help people, and that's my goal,' says 84-year-old Leonard Foidart
Before Leonard Foidart starts knitting, he lies face down on his custom-made cot, reaches down to adjust the light, grabs two knitting needles and selects the wool he feels will be just right.
Foidart, 84, loves to knit but is unable to sit for more than a few hours at a time. He lost his legs in the early 1990s due to complications from multiple sclerosis.
"The bones don't like me sitting on them too much," Foidart said from his home in Notre-Dame-de-Lourdes, Man., about 110 kilometres southwest of Winnipeg.

He said he has knitted and donated more than 1,000 tuques to numerous charities in the last five years, including Winnipeg's Siloam Mission and Central Plains Cancer Services in Portage la Prairie. Much of the wool is donated.
Foidart was diagnosed with bone and prostate cancer a few years ago. His wife, Tharsile, died last year after suffering a stroke.
"She taught me how to knit. So, every time I knit a tuque, she is right here beside me. In the 20 years, we never had a single argument. We had a good life," he said as his voice broke with emotion.

That's why, Foidart said, he refuses to give up knitting. After his cancer diagnosis, Foidart decided to build a cot. It sits on four wheels and has a comfortable body cushion, and a leather headband so he can rest his head.
Foidart shows off one of many baskets of donated wool. (Michele McDougall/CBC)

"I was a letter carrier for 19 years, and in my spare time I did carpentry work. And because I've been in this chair for 35 years, whenever a problem came along, this guy solved it," Foidart said as he tapped the side of his head.
He keeps meticulous records of each donation, with photos of labelled bags showing the date and number of tuques.

items: More stories from Southwest Manitoba

blocks.text: "You're here to help people, and that's my goal, to do the best I can to help people wherever they are and whatever shape they can be in," Foidart said.
His most recent donation of 200 tuques was to the Portage la Prairie Community Revitalization Corporation last week. The corporation supports and advocates for vulnerable people in the community.
Kimberly Sharp, left, and Tawnee Kowerchuk from the Portage la Prairie Community Revitalization Corporation hold some of the 200 tuques Foidart delivered last week. (Michele McDougall/CBC)
Co-ordinator Tawnee Kowerchuk said they got an email from Foidart's niece preparing them for delivery but she was shocked when he delivered the tuques himself.
"It was really special. When he showed up and we saw exactly what we were dealing with and how many, we were totally beside ourselves. It was just amazing," Kowerchuk said.
"And he was adamant they go to people who are in need. And they will."
Foidart is already working on the next batch of tuques. He said he doesn't set a goal of how many he wants to make in a month or a year but never strays from his schedule.
"I do the best that I can do today, and maybe tomorrow, even better. And mistakes now are very rare. After 1,200 tuques, they better be rare," he said as he laughed.
Manitoba senior with knack for knitting uses custom-made cot
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Michele McDougall is a news reporter at CBC Manitoba based in Brandon. She previously worked at the Brandon Sun covering health stories in western Manitoba.

articles.title: Curling controversy: Unusual finish generates boos, ruffles feathers at Slam event
articles.summary: The Grand Slam of Curling's competition committee plans to meet this week to discuss an unusual finish at the Co-op Invitational that sent two Canadian teams into the playoffs and led to pointed…

image.caption: Boos were heard throughout Victoria's Save-On-Foods Memorial Centre when teams skipped by Matt Dunstone and Brendan Bottcher, pictured, were not aggressive in the final end of their round-robin finale Friday night. (Paul Daly/Canadian Press/File)

blocks.text: The Grand Slam of Curling's competition committee plans to meet this week to discuss an unusual finish at the Co-op Invitational that sent two Canadian teams into the playoffs and led to pointed words from an American rink left outside the cutline.
Stones thrown deliberately through house 'not a good look,' says American Ben Richardson
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 19, 2026 6:03 PM EDT | Last Updated: 4 hours ago

Boos were heard throughout Victoria's Save-On-Foods Memorial Centre when teams skipped by Matt Dunstone and Brendan Bottcher were not aggressive in the final end of their round-robin finale Friday night.

Both teams deliberately threw stones through the house early in the end before Bottcher scored one for a tie that forced a shootout. That gave both sides enough points to advance and eliminated Danny Casper's rink from playoff contention.

"They're on ESPN in the U.S. and [Sportsnet] in Canada, thousands of people are watching it, I'm sure, and it looks horrible," Team Casper second Ben Richardson said from Victoria over the weekend. "It definitely leaves a bitter taste in my mouth.
"I can't speak [for] all the people that watched it, but it's definitely not a good look for our sport.”

Normally, a one-point game would lead to a tense eighth and final end. But with the stakes clear — reach the shootout and you're guaranteed a playoff spot — both rinks chose a passive style down the stretch.
When it became obvious both teams were comfortable with a tied score, many spectators voiced their displeasure that any late-game excitement had been scuttled.
"Don't be upset with the players, be upset with the format," said Dunstone, who earned two points for the 6-5 shootout victory.

items: Einarson wins 7th Grand Slam of Curling title, 1st since 2024

blocks.text: Bottcher picked up one point for the shootout loss, giving him seven points overall and the final berth. Casper, who would have played a tiebreaker if the game was decided in regulation, missed the cut with six points.
"I understand why both of them would want a shootout," Richardson said. "I don't understand why both of them would not try to win in the last end. I completely disagree with that."
At issue for many were the early shots in the eighth end.
World No. 1 Schwaller beats Norway's Ramsfjell in Co-op Invitational men's final
Walker miss raised eyebrows
Team Dunstone lead Ryan Harnden drew the button, and Team Bottcher lead Geoff Walker flashed his first rock. The Walker miss raised the eyebrows of Team Casper third Luc Violette.
"You would always see a team throw a corner guard in that situation if they were trying to maximize their odds of winning the game outright," he said.
Harnden's second shot stopped at the top of the four-foot ring. Walker then made a double-takeout and his shooter rolled out.
Violette said the flash improved Dunstone's chances to steal. He would have expected Harnden to follow with a tight centre guard in that situation.
"Instead, they lobbed one right on top of it to leave an easy double," he said.
For second stones, Team Dunstone's Mark Nichols deliberately threw his first rock through the house, and Team Bottcher's Tanner Horgan did the same thing.

items: Curling's PointsBet Invitational quietly dropped from competition calendar this season

blocks.text: That sparked boos and jeers throughout the venue. Some spectators shouted "Borrrrr-ing!" while others yelled out "Shame! Shame!"
The broadcast team also sensed what was happening.

"Both of these teams, if this game goes to a shootout, will get into the playoffs," said on-air host John Cullen. "This looks like maybe a bit of a handshake agreement that both teams are saying, 'Let's do it."'
"I doubt that there's any agreement," analyst Brent Laing replied. "I think they're both just smart enough to know there's no need [to] take on any risk, and the other guy thinks the same thing."
After exchanging hits, Dunstone's final rock settled on the 12-foot ring and Bottcher drew the button for one point. Both skips said there was no agreement in place to play for the draw.
That Curling Show returns with a weekend recap of GSOC Victoria
'How the scoreboard played out'
"In eight, they threw a rock in the house and Geoff's first rock picked," Bottcher said in a text message. "That said, our team knew we needed a point to qualify given the format."
Dunstone, reached on the phone from Victoria, said: "there was no conversation whatsoever."
"It was just how the scoreboard played out," he said.
Nic Sulsky, CEO of GSOC owner The Curling Group, said while he likes the 3-2-1-0 scoring system that's in its second season of use on the circuit, he wasn't impressed with what transpired.
"It was a little too obvious, it was a little too raw," he said. "And I feel for the Casper boys. But at the end of the day, fans are in the stands watching rocks being thrown through the house.

items: More curling coverage

blocks.text: "I'm not a supporter of [that] in a situation like [Friday] night."
The seven-member competition committee was expected to meet Thursday or Friday, Sulsky said.
Dunstone went on to lose his quarterfinal to eventual champion Yannick Schwaller of Switzerland while Bottcher dropped his playoff opener to Canada's Brad Jacobs.

"This isn't why we didn't win this weekend," said Violette. "But at the same time, if this were another sport, I do think there would be some sort of sanction or something that happens as a result of a scenario like we saw play out."
"I feel like this was, I guess, a step back in us feeling confident in the integrity among teams at our highest level," he added.
The next stop on the circuit is the Nov. 3-8 GSOC Masters in Medicine Hat, Alta.

articles.title: Colorado wildlife overpass cut vehicle-animal collisions by 91%, report finds
articles.summary:
Elk, bear, frogs and other animals have used the overpass, which connects 39,000 acres of habitat, since its completion

Colorado officials have tracked herds of elk, bears, pronghorn and…

blocks.text: Colorado officials have tracked herds of elk, bears, pronghorn and even northern leopard frogs ambling across its new wildlife overpass. According to a newly released report, the overpass, which acts as a bridge over a busy stretch of interstate, has cut wildlife-vehicle collisions by 91% since its completion 10 months ago.

“One of the most heartwarming moments for me was when [Colorado department of transportation] sent me a picture of an elk mama taking her calf under [Interstate-25],” Brandon Marette, a wildlife biologist for Colorado parks and wildlife, told CBS News. “All came to fruition in that one moment. That elk with her calf was just standing there in safety.”
The Colorado department of transportation said prior to the overpass being built, there was an average of one wildlife-vehicle crash a day in this corridor.

Such wildlife crossings are popping up across the country as a way to protect wildlife habitat and reduce collisions, which can result in injuries and deaths in humans and animals. Research has shown that overpasses are successful in “nearly eliminating” these accidents and that such infrastructure buildouts often “pay for themselves” by preventing costly crashes.

Nearly 20 wildlife crossings are underway in the US, with the structure in Colorado currently the biggest. The overpass, which sits between the state’s two biggest cities, Denver and Colorado Springs, spans six lanes of traffic and connects 39,000 acres of habitat on both sides of the interstate. The bridge is covered in grass and measures 200-ft-wide and 209-ft-long with gradually sloped entrances to ease crossings for animals.

This region of Colorado is known for high movement of large game. State officials say that wildlife underpasses and tunnels often don’t work for big animals, such as elk, because they restrict mobility and don’t accommodate their antlers.

“Elk and pronghorn like these big open structures where they can see for miles in each direction,” Chuck Attardo, the environmental manager for Colorado department of transportation, told CBS News. “For decades, pronghorn going from Trinidad to Greenland were looking for a place to cross on I-25. And when we open this up, we have pronghorn on video using the overpass, and for the first time in decades they’re coming over here to the west side.”

While large game animals have been taking advantage of the crossing, officials have also tracked smaller wildlife using the corridor, including mule deer, coyotes, rabbits, frogs and the threatened Preble’s meadow jumping mouse.

The project received $22m in federal funding and $8m from the state, but officials say they were able to complete it for just $15m. Now, the Colorado department of transportation says it’s hoping to build other wildlife crossings across the state.

articles.title: California to recieve $6m settlement after 23andMe data breach
articles.summary:
The 2023 breach exposed millions of customers’ genetic and personal information, including more than 855,000 Californians

California attorney general Rob Bonta on Monday announced the state…

blocks.text: California attorney general Rob Bonta on Monday announced the state will receive a $6m settlement payment in 23andMe’s bankruptcy, resolving California’s legal claims related to a 2023 data breach that exposed 6.9 million customers’ ⁠genetic and other ⁠personal information.

California had ​unsuccessfully tried to block the $305m sale of 23andMe assets to TTAM Research Institute, a nonprofit controlled by 23andMe ⁠co-founder Anne Wojcicki. The state had argued that the bankruptcy sale violated California’s Genetic Information Privacy Act, and it had said ⁠consumers did not give express consent to the sale.
Once a trailblazer in DNA testing ​kits, 23andMe filed for bankruptcy in ‌March 2025, seeking to ‌sell its business at auction after a decline in demand and legal ‌fallout from the data breach.

A US bankruptcy judge ruled against California’s objections to the sale, and later ruled that the state could not sue to recover money from the bankrupt company’s successor. California lost an appeal over the sale in federal district court, and it agreed to drop further appeals as ‌part of the $6m settlement, according to court documents filed on Monday.

Customers of 23andMe retained the option to delete their data during ​the bankruptcy sale process, but California had argued that the court should have disallowed the transfer of any data unless 23andMe customers first gave express consent to the sale.

“I am proud to fight for the privacy rights of Californians and to ⁠deliver this settlement for consumers who put their trust in 23andMe,” ​Bonta, a Democrat, ​said in a statement on ​Monday. “I want to remind Californians that customers of 23andMe ​can delete their private, ‌genetic data – no ​matter who owns ​it.”
The data breach exposed the genetic information of more than 855,000 Californians, according to the attorney general’s office.
23andMe agreed to pay $46.75m to victims of the 2023 data breach as part of its bankruptcy.

articles.title: US Church on frontline of battle against drug known as 'tranq'
articles.summary: Synthetic opioids like fentanyl are more powerful and in plentiful supply, and they have transformed the drugs landscape.

blocks.text: America has been fighting the War on Drugs for decades, but the drug cartels, the suppliers and the dealers appear to be always one step ahead of the authorities.
President Trump has declared the cartels, "terrorists" and labelled fentanyl, the powerful synthetic opioid, a "weapon of mass destruction".
But the drug supply is changing, with other deadly synthetics being added to the mix, including strong animal tranquillisers, known on the streets as "tranq".

While overdose deaths are falling, the potency of the new drugs has recovery workers worried. For some the answer might lie in reducing demand, giving users support and helping them end their addiction.
BBC international correspondent Quentin Sommerville and camera journalist Darren Conway travelled to Columbus, Ohio to find out more.

articles.title: Tennis star Svitolina says emotional toll of Ukraine war led to Monfils separation
articles.summary: The two top tennis pros married in 2021 and have one child together.

blocks.text: Ukrainian tennis star Elina Svitolina has announced the end of her marriage with French former tennis player Gaël Monfils, citing the emotional impact of the war in her country.
The 32-year-old, who is ranked number six in the world, wrote in a heartfelt post on Instagram about the effect the conflict and "what the war has done to me inside".
"This is the most difficult thing I have ever had to share," she wrote, saying "I need to find my way back to myself". Svitolina said she felt she could not do that within her marriage.
She said her husband Monfils, 40, "listened" and "respected what I need with a strength and grace I will never forget".
"Some battles happen deep inside you, and no amount of love from someone else can win them for you," the four-time Grand Slam semi-finalist wrote.
It was "the hardest thing I have ever had to tell the person I love", Svitolina said.
"Everyone knows how much Ukraine means to me," Svitolina, who grew up in Odesa, said.
Ukraine's Black Sea port city has been heavily bombed by Russia throughout the war.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
"What you didn't see were the sleepless nights, the doubts, and the feeling of slowly losing myself."
The tennis power couple married in 2021 and have one child together - a four-year-old daughter called Skai.
Svitolina said her daughter "will always come first", adding "our marriage is ending, but our family is not".
Monfils, a former world number six, was expected to play the final tournament of his career at next month's Paris Masters in an emotional farewell.
However, the two-time Grand Slam semi-finalist's retirement was effectively confirmed last week when he appeared on the International Tennis Integrity Authority's list of retired players.
Once a player removes themselves from anti-doping protocols, they are not eligible to compete in professional tournaments.
Monfils, who won 13 titles on the ATP Tour, is preparing to start a new career in finance after joining a Swiss wealth management firm.

articles.title: Cop killer Curtis Dagenais returns to Saskatoon courtroom to argue about fate of his truck
articles.summary: Curtis Dagenais returned on Monday to the same Saskatoon courtroom where, 17 years ago, a jury convicted him of murder.

image.caption: Curtis Dagenais arrives at court in Saskatoon in March 2009, during his trial for the murders of two RCMP constables and attempted murder of a third. He was convicted on all three counts and is serving three life sentences. (Geoff Howe/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan·New
Curtis Dagenais returned on Monday to the same Saskatoon courtroom where, 17 years ago, a jury convicted him of murder.
Judge to give decision on Crown's application for forfeiture on Dec. 4
It's been more than 17 years since a jury sat in courtroom No. 1 at Saskatoon Court of King's Bench for Curtis Dagenais's murder trial.
Since then, the courthouse has been expanded and renovated. Its name changed too, after the death of Queen Elizabeth II.

The third-floor courtroom itself looks a little different — the jury's seats were relocated to the other side of the room and the windows no longer have an exterior view — but it was there, in March 2009, that a jury convicted Dagenais of two counts of first-degree murder and one count of attempted murder, for killing RCMP constables Robin Cameron and Marc Bourdages and wounding Const. Michelle Knopp.
He shot the officers on July 6, 2006, after Cameron and Bourdages chased him down rural roads before ramming his truck and dying in the shootout that followed. Knopp arrived moments later.
Dagenais appealed his convictions to the Saskatchewan Court of Appeal, which dismissed his appeal in a ruling issued in 2012.

items: Curtis Dagenais's truck is still in RCMP cold storage. The Crown says it's time to destroy it

blocks.text: For the last 20 years, the 1986 blue GMC 1500 truck that Dagenais was driving has been sitting in storage. Through an oversight, the Crown didn't apply to have it forfeited until years later.

For prior hearings on the application, Dagenais appeared via video link from the Saskatchewan Penitentiary, where he is serving his three life sentences. He opposes the Crown's application, saying the truck holds evidence that proves his innocence, which he still maintains, and that its parts have some monetary value.
A photo from Curtis Dagenais's trial shows the RCMP vehicle that hit the side of his blue truck. (Geoff Howe/The Canadian Press)
On Monday, Dagenais was transported to the courthouse to appear in person, representing himself after he did not get a lawyer.

At first, the deputy sheriff seated the 61-year-old in the prisoner's box, but when Justice Daryl Labach arrived and opened court, he asked Dagenais to come forward to the long tables where the lawyers sit, and for his leg shackles to be removed.
He then patiently explained the law to Dagenais and repeatedly asked him if there are any reasons why his truck shouldn't be forfeited.

items: Fate of convicted cop killer Curtis Dagenais's truck still undecided after judge grants adjournment

blocks.text: Dagenais gave a variety of answers, ranging from comments about ballistics and evidence, to comments about the rarity of parts for that make of truck.
He characterized the actions of the Crown as "kicking me in the shins" and taking away "another few dollars" that he can't use to defend himself.

Crown prosecutor Scott Bartlett, one of the two Crown lawyers who prosecuted Dagenais at the 2009 murder trial, repeated the arguments he has made previously, that the truck is offence-related property and should be forfeited.
Labach is scheduled to give his decision on Dec. 4.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Hannah Spray works as a reporter and copy editor. She began her journalism career in newspapers, first in her hometown of Meadow Lake, Sask., moving on to Fort St. John, B.C., and then to the Saskatoon StarPhoenix. She joined CBC in 2022. Send story tips confidentially via Signal to HannahSpray.10

articles.title: Mission blasts off for Mars to grab a piece of its moon
articles.summary: A spacecraft is set to launch on an ambitious mission to bring 10g of Martian moon dust back to Earth.
articles.byline: Rebecca Morelle, Alison Francis, Kevin Church

blocks.text: Mission blasts off for Mars to grab a piece of its moon
Watch: Spacecraft heading to Mars' moon Phobos lifts off from Japan
ByRebecca MorelleAlison Francis and Kevin ChurchBBC News Science
A spacecraft has launched from Japan headed for Mars' moon Phobos, where it will attempt to grab some moondust and bring it back to Earth.
If it is successful, this will become the first time a sample has been returned from Mars or its moons to be analysed in laboratories here on Earth.
The spacecraft is scheduled to arrive at Phobos in August 2027.
It is hoped that the Mars Moons Exploration (MMX) mission, which is led by the Japanese Space Agency, will solve the mystery of how Mars's moons formed.

Prof Sara Russell, from the Natural History Museum, who is the MMX mission's deputy for sample analysis, said: "There hasn't yet been a successful mission to go to Phobos and bring a bit back to Earth.
"I think this is an incredibly ambitious and fun mission," she said.

blocks.caption: This is an infographic that shows the MMX spacecraft travelling from Earth to Mars' moon Phobos. There are four numbered stages. Stage 1: The spacecraft leaves Earth. Stage 2: Spacecraft enters orbit around Phobos and lands a rover. Stage 3: Spacecraft lands to collect a sample of moon rock. Stag…

blocks.text: There are only three moons in the inner Solar System: our own Moon, and two around Mars, which are called Phobos and Deimos.
Both of these are tiny - Phobos is about 20km (12 miles) across and Deimos is about 10km (six miles) across. They are also irregularly shaped, looking a bit like space potatoes.
The MMX spacecraft will study Deimos as it arrives in the Mars neighbourhood, and then will focus on Phobos.
It plans to set down a small rover to explore the terrain, though this will be no easy feat.
Sara Russell says no one has ever landed a rover on such a small moon.
"The moon itself doesn't have very much of its own gravity," she explained.
"But it's next to an enormous planet that's got a much higher gravity, and that makes it much harder to get a rover onto the surface."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mars got its moons about 4.5bn years ago - but no one knows how they formed

blocks.text: Image source, NASA
Mars got its moons about 4.5bn years ago - but no one knows how they formed
The rover will scout out a landing site so that the MMX spacecraft itself can later touch down on Phobos.
Once on the surface, it will deploy a robotic arm and two samplers to grab some moon dust.
This material will be packed into a small capsule that will return to Earth in 2031, landing in the Woomera desert of South Australia.
The amount of material that will come back is tiny - just 10g.
"It's a very small [amount] actually," said Dr Chrysa Avdellidou, from Leicester University, who is working with the Japanese mission.
"However we can do several studies even on individual grains… You don't need to have kilos back from a surface in order to do science. So it's worth every gram," she said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The spacecraft will collect 10g of moon dust from the surface of Phobos

blocks.text: Image source, JAXA
The spacecraft will collect 10g of moon dust from the surface of Phobos
Scientists believe the sample will finally shed light on the puzzle of where Mars's moons came from.
There are two competing ideas.
Either a space rock smashed into Mars early in its history, and Phobos and Deimos were created from the debris.
Or the moons are two wandering asteroids from the outer Solar System, which were grabbed by the Red Planet's gravity.
"When we get the sample back, we'll be able to look in detail at its chemistry and its mineral composition - and the two hypotheses will produce very distinct results," said Sara Russell.
"It should be pretty much immediately obvious.. whether it's the product of this dramatic impact or whether it's a captured asteroid. So we'll find that out really quickly."
The team is also hoping there might be an extra bonus coming back to their labs.

"One of the really exciting things is that Phobos is so close to the Mars surface that whenever there's an impact into the Mars surface, little grains might actually become implanted into Phobos itself," said Russell.
"And that means that the sample we get back may actually contain grains of Mars as well. So it can give us really direct information about the composition and history of Mars."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Martian meteorites are rare - this one is on display at the Natural History Museum

blocks.text: Image source, Kevin Church/BBC News
Martian meteorites are rare - this one is on display at the Natural History Museum
Bringing material from Mars back to Earth has long been an ambition of space scientists.
The Nasa Perseverance rover, which has been exploring Mars since 2021, has been carefully collecting samples on Mars and storing them in canisters.
But a second Nasa/ESA mission, called Mars Sample Return, that would have picked up and returned these canisters, has been effectively cancelled, after its funding was halted by the US Congress.
China is planning its own sampling mission to Mars, set to launch in 2028. It will attempt to return Martian material to Earth in 2031.
We do already have some fragments of the Red Planet here on Earth in the form of Martian meteorites.
These are pieces of Mars that were blasted off the surface by asteroid strikes, and ended up being hurled towards the Earth.
Martian meteorites are extremely rare, but like all space rocks that fall to our planet, they become contaminated as soon as they get here, mixing with the air, dust, soil and water.
Scientists are so desperate to get their gloved hands on a direct sample from Mars and its moons because it would be pristine.

articles.title: Helen Haines: independent MP in critical condition in Melbourne’s Alfred hospital after being struck by car in Wangaratta – follow updates
articles.summary: A joint counter-terrorism taskforce is investigating the incident, which Anthony Albanese alleged ‘wasn’t an accident’

That’s a really important part of our democracy. But we continue to take advice.
He added: “I think we can have disagreements without questioning people’s motives or their patriotism.”
Anthony Albanese says Australians need to turn down the temperature of political and public debate.

double quotation markAll of us are responsible for that. Whether we’re politicians, whether we’re the media, whether we’re citizens, in just being able to discuss things in a civil way. We can have disagreements in a democracy.

A man remains in police custody.
Anthony Albanese: 'This is a tragic situation'
The prime minister is speaking on Channel Seven’s Sunrise program this morning.
He says he will be briefed by police on the investigation into the alleged attack on Helen Haines later this morning, alongside the Victorian premier, Ben Carroll.
double quotation markAt this stage its not clear what that motivation was.

But he alleged: “It is clear that this wasn’t just an accident – this was an attempt to harm Helen Haines outside Wangaratta at her electorate office. Helen was getting things from the boot of her car when this incident occurred.”
He said:

blocks.text: What we know so far
First of all let’s set out what we know so far about what happened in Wangaratta yesterday.

items: Helen Haines has been critically injured in an alleged attack involving a car outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, regional Victoria, at about 3.35pm on Monday.
The independent MP was taken to Melbourne’s Alfred hospital and underwent surgery overnight. She remains in a critical condition.

A 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee is in custody, and the alleged attack is being investigated by the Australian federal police, Asio and the joint counter-terror taskforce. The motive is not yet known. A knife was allegedly found in his car after he was detained by a passerby when he got out of his vehicle.

Anthony Albanese, Angus Taylor, the Greens leader, David Shoebridge, the One Nation leader, Pauline Hanson, and politicians across the parliament have sent their thoughts and well wishes to Haines and her family.
In a press conference on Monday evening, Albanese described Haines, who has represented Indi since 2019, as a “thoroughly decent human being, full of integrity and respected right across parliament”.

Addressing the media in Wangaratta on Monday evening, acting supt Ashley Mason said police were still investigating whether the incident was targeted. He said there was no ongoing threat to the community and nothing to indicate the parties were known to each other.
