articles.title: Calgary Opera replaces performer who unfurled Palestinian flag during Tosca bow
articles.summary: On Friday, the bass singer Gabriel Sanchez-Ortega held up the flag at the end of Giacomo Puccini's drama about love and betrayal during political upheaval in Napoleonic Rome.

image.caption: Gabriel Sanchez-Ortega, right, holds up a Palestinian flag during the curtain call of the political opera Tosca on Oct. 16, 2026. Sanchez-Ortega, who had been playing an escaped political prisoner, was removed from the production by Calgary Opera, which said individual political protest was a violat

blocks.text: Calgary
On Friday, the bass singer Gabriel Sanchez-Ortega held up the flag at the end of Giacomo Puccini's drama about love and betrayal during political upheaval in Napoleonic Rome.
Actor playing escaped political prisoner says he has 'no regrets'
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 19, 2026 3:39 PM EDT | Last Updated: 27 minutes ago
The Calgary Opera has replaced a performer who unfurled a Palestinian flag during the curtain call of the political opera Tosca.
In a statement issued Sunday, the Calgary Opera called the action "unexpected and unauthorized," adding that individual political protest violated company policy.
The institution apologized for the "discomfort and distress" some may have felt and said Sanchez-Ortega's role will be performed by another artist for the remainder of the shows.
Sanchez-Ortega played a character named Cesare Angelotti, an escaped political prisoner.
In a post to Instagram, Sanchez-Ortega wrote that he had "no regrets" and that "this is the state of cultural institutions in Canada."
The Calgary Opera and Sanchez-Ortega did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

In its statement about the Oct. 16 performance, the Opera said individual political protest contravenes its "responsibility to create a more connected, caring and civil society through shared artistic experiences."
Sanchez-Ortega said he holds no resentment.
"After the theatre, [political or otherwise] we all have to go home, and look at ourselves in the mirror," Sanchez-Ortega continued in his statement.
"It was my honour to play the role of Angelotti, an escaped political prisoner."

articles.title: 'You Can See Everything' sells out theatres, and people can't stop talking about it
articles.summary: 'You Can See Everything' is the movie everyone wants to talk about but no one wants spoiled. It's drawing big numbers at the box office.

image.caption: Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes appears in a still from the documentary You Can See Everything. (A24)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
'You Can See Everything' is the movie everyone wants to talk about but no one wants spoiled. It's drawing big numbers at the box office.
'An absolutely phenomenal crazy fever dream'
You Can See Everything is the movie everyone wants to talk about but no one wants spoiled.
Maybe that's why so many people rushed to theatres on opening weekend to see the nearly three-hour documentary about Theranos founder and convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes.

Whatever the reason, the film made more than $15 million US in ticket sales during its debut weekend — the second-largest opening weekend for a non-musical documentary in domestic box office history, behind only 2004's Fahrenheit 9/11.
It's a considerable achievement, considering You Can See Everything had a limited release at just 855 theatres in Canada and the U.S.

The reviews following its debut were overwhelmingly positive: rated 99 per cent fresh on Rotten Tomatoes, and scoring a 4.8 on Letterboxd, making it the highest-rated movie in the site's history. (Both those ratings have come down since then, but only slightly.)
As the five-star reviews started pouring in online, so too did the comments: "My mouth was agape for basically the entire last two hours," from Letterboxd user James (Schaffrillas).
"Just an absolutely phenomenal crazy fever dream of a documentary," said user vgoodatkissing.
You can read everything — no spoilers here

The documentary's premise is straightforward. A film crew, including dual director-producers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, briefly move in with Holmes, her partner Billy Evans and their children, and document their lives, 34 days before she is due to start serving an extended prison sentence for fraud.
Toronto film critic Teri Hart says watching You Can See Everything in theatres was a visceral experience.
"People were actually physically leaning into the screen," she told CBC News. "There were gasps at times; people applauded at the end of the movie, lots of laughter."

"You leave this movie and you don't know if you want to talk about Nathan Fielder, if you want to talk about Elizabeth Holmes, if you want to talk about Billy or if you want to talk 'where did they put the camera.'"

items: Nathan Fielder's You Can See Everything gazes into the abyss of Elizabeth Holmes

blocks.text: The trailer gives audiences a glimpse into Fielder and Holmes's unusual dynamic.

"Nathan Fielder is not afraid of awkward. Nathan Fielder is not afraid of asking questions in a way that is unlike anybody else," said Hart. "He has a level of provocateur, I think, that is so fascinating to watch.
Boundary-pushing directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim documented Elizabeth Holmes's life during the 34 days before she was sent to prison for defrauding investors. (A24)
"Place him with Elizabeth Holmes, who also has a unique way of communicating, and you have magic."

Indeed, the documentary delivers on the intense and deliberately uncomfortable interviews that Fielder, a Canadian who was born in Vancouver, became known for on shows like Nathan for You, as well as his paradigm-shifting approach to the truth.
Hart calls the documentary a theatrical experience few people will have ever had — one that may lead audiences to question what we think of as the truth.
Another win for A24

You Can See Everything was distributed and partly produced by A24, the same company behind some of this year's most talked-about films, including Olivia Wilde's The Invite, the Anthony Bourdain biopic Tony and the record-breaking horror Backrooms.

"A24 is a distributor that has a brand. And that brand is — to my mind — working with auteurs, working with writer-directors or even just directors that really have a specific vision and have a strong, strong artistry associated with them," said Hart.
Nathan Fielder searches for truth in You Can See Everything

items: Tony director says making biopic was like being in 'a conspiracy with Anthony Bourdain

blocks.text: She said that's helped A24 make a splash, as the company pushes back against the general consensus that Hollywood has no new ideas.
As a movie lover, Hart said she is grateful for anything that gets people back in the theatres and talking about what they've seen. She says You Can See Everything is a great example of that.

"They're, like, shocked and surprised or walking out of the theater with all kinds of thoughts and ideas and questions. Because let's be clear, this movie does not tie anything up with a nice pretty bow. It does not. So people have questions.
"And I think that that is a really thrilling experience for people to share with strangers. "
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Helen Surgenor is a producer for CBC News based in Toronto, currently working for the entertainment unit. She spent years waking up before dawn to make the daily news podcast World Report. She has reported in Alberta, Iqaluit and Barbados. You can reach her at helen.surgenor@cbc.ca.

articles.title: DFO searching for injured whale struck by B.C. Ferries vessel in Howe Sound
articles.summary: Marine conservation officers are searching for an injured humpback whale that passengers aboard a B.C. Ferries vessel say they felt being struck on Sunday.

image.caption: DFO says it is investigating after a humpback whale was reportedly struck after surfacing in front of a B.C. Ferries vessel in Howe Sound on Sunday. (Aspen Wing)

blocks.text: British Columbia
Marine conservation officers are searching for an injured humpback whale that passengers aboard a B.C. Ferries vessel say they felt being struck on Sunday.
People travelling on the ferry say they felt the strike and saw the whale in distress
Marine conservation officers are searching for an injured humpback whale that was struck by a B.C. Ferries vessel in Howe Sound on Sunday.
The Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) said the collision involving the Queen of Surrey vessel happened between Grace Point and Keats Island.
It said two humpbacks were observed in close proximity to the ferry at the time and one was struck.
Passengers aboard the ferry, which was sailing from Langdale on the Sunshine Coast to Horseshoe Bay, said they felt the whale being struck and watched it in distress behind the vessel.
B.C. Ferries said it takes incidents like the whale strike on Sunday very seriously. (Alanna Kelly/CBC)
Aspen Wing was travelling with her son when she said they felt the collision at 1:33 p.m. PT.
She said a group of girls shouted that a whale had been nearby, and her son spotted the injured humpback off the stern of the vessel.
"A lot of people on the ferry were really distraught and upset by what they were witnessing," Wing said.
She recorded a video of the whale splashing in the water and said she watched the whale blow blood into the air.
Aspen Wing says she saw the whale blowing blood into the air after it was struck. (Aspen Wing)
"To watch that animal in obvious distress was really disheartening and upsetting for a lot of us, I'm still kind of sick to my stomach about seeing it," Wing said.
Crews searching for humpback whale
B.C. Ferries said in a statement that it is deeply concerned about the incident and potential impact on the whale.
"Based on initial reports, the whale surfaced directly in front of the vessel, leaving the crew with very little time to react," said spokesperson Kit Billings.

items: Calf with deep gash identified as humpback struck by ferry off Vancouver
Video captures grey whale being struck by Sea-Doo in Vancouver

blocks.text: Billings said the immediate focus has been on "responding to the incident, notifying the appropriate authorities and gathering accurate information about what happened, including the potential impact on the whale."
DFO said in a statement that B.C. Ferries is cooperating.
What is B.C. Ferries doing to prevent whale strikes?
Canada's Marine Mammal Regulations state that any vessel operator that’s involved in contact with a whale must immediately notify DFO.
"DFO is reviewing the situation and will work to identify the whale and assess its condition," DFO said.
A crew from DFO is in Howe Sound on Monday trying to locate the whale.
Fatal whale strikes
Almost one year ago, on Oct. 23, 2025, a humpback whale was struck by a whale-watching company off Keats Island in Howe Sound, near Sunday's incident.
A few days later, a four-year-old humpback whale washed up dead in the same area.
A humpback whale was found dead and floating in the water off Keats Island on Oct. 26, 2025. (Alex Cole)
DFO identified the dead humpback whale found at Keats Island as BCY1464, also known as Wisp, and said there was an active investigation.
Whales have been hit in other coastal areas recently, too.

A humpback whale was struck by a Hullo Ferries vessel off Vancouver, a person driving a Sea-Doo struck a grey whale near English Bay, and a humpback whale was found dead after being reported hit by a B.C. Ferries vessel in Wright Sound.
"It's a busy wildlife corridor, and especially at this time of year, there have been times I've been on that ferry, and I've seen 11 humpbacks like on that one sailing," Wing said.
She feels the communication on Sunday could have been handled better.
"There was no announcement made on the ferry. There was no attempt to like … it didn't feel like there was a slowdown," Wing said. "It was disturbing."
Push for slower vessel speeds
Jackie Hildering with the Marine Education and Research Society said Howe Sound, where the strike happened Sunday, is well-known to be frequented by humpbacks from October to December.
"This has to be about prevention," Hindering said. "We want very much, [for] these tragedies to lead to positive change."
The society is pushing for vessels to be limited to slower speeds in whale habitats.
In June, the Northern Expedition route, where a humpback whale was fatally struck in Wright Sound, adopted a travel speed of 10 knots, down from the previous 18 knots.
Hildering said that speed could still cause a fatality, but is far less likely to.

The Queen of Surrey was travelling at 16 knots at the time of the strike Sunday, B.C. Ferries spokesperson Lilian Kim said in an email, and typically travels at between 19 to 19.5 knots in that area, depending on conditions.
Hildering said she's working to determine which whale was struck.
"It is extraordinarily unlikely that a humpback would have survived that," she said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Alanna Kelly is a CBC News journalist based in Squamish, B.C., covering the Sea-to-Sky region, including Whistler, Pemberton and the Sunshine Coast. You can email story ideas to alanna.kelly@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Bulgaria seeks suspects in Germany after Starlink sabotage
articles.summary: A Bulgarian court has issued arrest warrants for two young German nationals suspected of setting fire to Starlink antennae. The case is reminiscent of another in Poland, which Warsaw says was…

image.caption: Separate sabotage attempts took aim at Starlink facilities in Poland and Bulgaria within a matter of weeksImage: Rafapress/Depositphotos/IMAGO

blocks.text: Bulgaria on Monday issued European arrest warrants against two 19-year-old German nationals, saying it suspected their involvement in the sabotage of a series of Starlink antennae near the capital Sofia.

"The evidence gathered makes it possible to conclude that there are reasonable grounds to suspect the involvement of the two defendants," the court in Sofia rules, granting a request from prosecutors.
Ukraine's military uses Starlink's military-grade satellite internet service Starshield for battlefield communications amid Russia's invasion.

Bulgaria does not directly border Ukraine, but it is on the Black Sea, one of the flashpoints of the conflict. A similar case in Poland, which does directly border Ukraine, led to a total of four arrests last week, also in Germany.
What do we know about the incident in Bulgaria?
The two teenage suspects are accused of deliberately setting fire to the antennae on the evening of October 9.
Of 18 in a mountainous region south of Sofia, three were destroyed entirely, two were partially burned and three more were damaged, according to prosecutors.
Prosecutors say the suspects entered from Serbia in a car with German license plates, claiming to be tourists, staying just a few hours around the time of the alleged crime.

Plamen Tonchev, the head of Bulgaria's domestic intelligence agency DANS, said he was working on the assumption that it was deliberate sabotage and said other such acts could not be ruled out in future.
What is the potential tie-in to a Polish sabotage case?
News of the arrests follow just a week after a total of four people were arrested in Germany, accused of sabotaging a Starlink satellite communications station in central Poland in late September.
German police detained three resident men and a woman, two of them Turkish nationals, early last week.
Polish officials said they believed that Russia was behind the sabotage attempt, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk calling it an act of "hybrid warfare."
The domestic intelligence agency also claimed that Russia had cooperated with organized crime elements in Germany on the alleged operation.
Meanwhile, in the Baltic, Lithuania's prime minister on Sunday said that Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites.

articles.title: Ukrainians dying because US restricting intelligence sharing, Zelensky adviser tells BBC
articles.summary: Serhii Beskrestnov says there has not been enough time to warn people about incoming missile attacks.

blocks.text: Ukrainians have died because Kyiv is still not receiving reliable US warnings of incoming Russian attacks, according to a key adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky.

Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov told the BBC that lives had been lost because there had not been time to warn citizens about ballistic missile strikes, saying: "It's dangerous... I think it's really very bad... People [have] already died."
The adviser also said restrictions to Ukraine's use of the Starlink internet network were ongoing.
The White House said there had been no changes to intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
Ukraine first reported an interruption to US intelligence sharing last week, as a row with the Trump administrations over its controversial deal to import Russian oil sent relations to new lows.
Despite the denials from Washington, many in Kyiv suspect the Starlink issues are not a coincidence.
On Monday morning, Zelensky wrote on social media: "Overnight two ballistic missile attacks were reported on the capital, one without warning, the second with only minimal time to take shelter."
Hours earlier, an interview the president did with NBC was published, in which he said intelligence sharing had been restored after a three-day pause.
"We are very thankful for this," he said. "Only [the] United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles."
But Beskrestnov told the BBC that American intelligence continued to be incomplete and inconsistent, and that the US had failed to provide a clear explanation for the issue.
"This looks very strange," he said. "Sometimes we receive this information before the attack, another time we [do] not."
He continued: "And for example, last night we received it, but... one minute before the attack."
However, he said other collaboration with US continues, adding: "Intelligence data keeps flowing, and the issue is solely with the air raid alert component."

Beskrestnov also said the US had given no clarity about who was responsible for the ongoing restrictions to the Starlink internet network and its military service Starshield, which Kyiv uses to provide connectivity for drones, helicopters and military communications.
Last week, Starshield restricted the speed at which mobile units could move while staying connected to the network to 100mph (160km/h).
This has limited Ukraine's ability to shoot down incoming drones or to launch mid-range drone attacks into Russian-occupied areas.

Starlink owner Elon Musk said last week that the US government ultimately controls access to Starshield, which was designed for the Pentagon, suggesting it may therefore be behind the restrictions. Trump has denied involvement.
Beskrestnov said he thought both issues occurring at the same time was "probably" a deliberate move to put pressure on Ukraine.
He told BBC News: "It's probably the United States trying to say [to] us, 'let's have the conversation, negotiation with Russia, you should find the compromise'."
Beskrestnov also said Ukraine had its own radar data to provide some limited warning of incoming attacks, but was urgently looking into using alternative communication systems.
He added: "Now we understand that something begins to happen with Starlink, and we're not sure what will be the next step.

"We understand that we should be prepared for some problems in future. And now we're thinking about an alternative for Starlink, not only for air defence, for communication between our forces, between our staff, for civilians also, because we don't know what we should expect in future regarding Starlink."
Earlier on Monday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there had not been a "pause" to intelligence sharing.
"I don't know where [Zelensky is] getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press," he told reporters on Monday.
Rubio said he could not comment on the incident, adding: "I know a few nights ago there was a software problem involving their early warning system."
The BBC has contacted Starlink for a response.
A White House official said there were no changes to intelligence sharing operations between the US and Ukraine.
The official spoke on background to discuss intelligence matters. Trump is focused on ending the war, the official said, and added that the US has provided more aid to Ukraine than any other country.

articles.title: Israeli police detain 10 people in rare raid against West Bank settlers
articles.summary:
Move comes after US photojournalist and group of European diplomats and Palestinians were assaulted in separate attacks

Israeli police have detained 10 people in a rare raid against…

blocks.text: Israeli police have detained 10 people in a rare raid against settlers, after a weekend of extreme violence in the occupied West Bank including an attack on US photojournalist Heidi Levine, which she described as an “attempted lynching”.

She was knocked down, kicked and beaten by a group of masked Israeli men as she covered the olive harvest in a Palestinian village on Friday. The militants broke four vertebrae and a rip, ripped open her finger so it required surgery and left her with lacerations across her body.
“I was practically, basically lynched by a gang of Jewish settlers in the area of Ramallah,” Levine said, in an interview with the BBC from her hospital bed on Monday.

The day after that assault, Israeli militants armed with sticks and iron bars attacked a group of European diplomats and Palestinians harvesting olives outside the town of Taybeh, assaulting a visiting French mayor, smashing the window of an official car, and causing severe injuries to a young Palestinian man.
The Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, questioned the accounts of Israeli militant violence, ignoring extensive video and witness evidence.
He referenced an “alleged attack” on Levine, whose severe injuries were visible in interviews from her hospital bed, and “unproven allegations” the diplomats had been targeted by militants.

The attacks and his response drew a furious international reaction, including from the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee – generally considered a staunch ally of the current Israeli government – European nations and the editor of the Washington Post, Matt Murray.
On Monday morning Israeli police released footage of a rare raid on settlers, and said they had detained 10 people connected with the attacks on foreigners and construction of an illegal outpost.
Hours later a court extended the detention of six men connected with the attacks on foreigners, to between three and four days.
There has been little response to extreme violence against Palestinians across the West Bank, and Levine said the global focus on her attack highlighted extreme double standards.
“People are dealing with this, undergoing attacks, losing property, losing family members, being injured all across the West Bank and nothing is being done,” she said.
Israelis target Palestinians with near total impunity in the occupied West Bank, where arrests are unusual, indictments rare and convictions even more unusual.

Israeli human rights group Yesh Din has documented 561 incidents of settler and soldier violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank over three weeks since 27 September. That is an average of more than 26 each day.

“It is telling that it took attacks on foreign nationals to prompt a significant response from Israeli authorities,” said the group’s executive director, Ziv Stahl. “Palestinians have endured years of systematic settler violence, with 94% of investigations into cases of settler violence against Palestinians closed without indictments.

Levine said her body armour and helmet had prevented even more serious injuries, and she considered herself “lucky” given the ferocity of the attack. Netanyahu’s attempt to cast doubt on the attack felt like a “a big slap on my face”, she added.

Netanyahu’s statements, apparently undermined by security forces arrests days later, were widely seen as an attempt to court far-right voters inside Israel, as the country heads into the final days of an election campaign.

His coalition partners include extremist settlers, who support the campaign of violence that has driven thousands of Palestinians from their homes and land in the occupied West Bank over the last three years.

Haaretz reported on Monday that political pressure was preventing the army from confronting “Jewish terrorism” in the West Bank, even when the targets were foreigners including diplomats and journalists.
Commanders are reluctant to challenge settler leaders, or take action against Israeli civilians and soldiers who attack Palestinians, Israeli defence officials told the paper.
Formal investigations and disciplinary procedures are limited and undermined by unofficial but clear messages of support from top commanders, the report said.

It cited the response to an attack on a CNN crew in March. Central Command chief Maj Gen Avi Bluth suspended the battalion responsible from operational duty and announced disciplinary action against soldiers involved.
Later that night, the brigade commander came to a base where the soldiers were staying to express his support and join them in prayer, Haaretz said.

articles.title: Quebec's reserves of maple syrup almost depleted, says new report
articles.summary: The head of Quebec's maple syrup producers' association says the province's strategic syrup reserve has run dry amid high demand for the product.

image.caption: Cans of maple syrup wait to be processed at Érablière Côté et Fils in Roxton Pond, Que., on Monday, March 9. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Montreal·New
The head of Quebec's maple syrup producers' association says the province's strategic syrup reserve has run dry amid high demand for the product.
Province's producers ask government for financial support, help finding new markets abroad
· The Canadian Press
· Posted: Oct 19, 2026 1:41 PM EDT | Last Updated: 16 minutes ago
Québec Maple Syrup Producers president Luc Goulet says government support will be needed to ensure the industry doesn't miss out on opportunities to grow the sector.
Maple syrup yields depend on weather conditions. As a result, the producers' association has established a strategic reserve to ensure prices and supply remain relatively stable.
Last year, U.S. commercial customers stocked up, fearing that U.S. President Donald Trump would carry out his threat to impose tariffs.

items: Fake maple syrup class action now targeting major grocery store chains

blocks.text: Goulet says the buffer has been exhausted as sales continue to rise.
"Our strategic reserve has been reduced to zero," Goulet said in an interview at the release of a report on the industry's economic benefits.
That means the industry could lose customers if weather conditions are less favourable for maple sap flow, he said.
Goulet cites the stock shortages in 2007 and 2008 as an example.

"We lost some markets because the product wasn’t available," Goulet said. "Then, consumers very quickly turn to another sweet product. And once that happens, those consumption habits are established."

items: Canada is unlocking its maple syrup vault. Here's what it looks like

blocks.text: Quebec maple syrup is gaining market share abroad, according to the president of the Maple Industry Council, which represents authorized buyers.

Louis Turenne notes that exports increased by 9.34 per cent in 2024 compared to the previous year. The pace accelerated in 2025 with a 15.8 per cent increase as the threat of new tariffs loomed over the industry.
In 2026, exports rose at a slower rate — 2.48 per cent from January through August compared to the same period the previous year.
"It's always hard to beat an exceptional year," Turenne said.
Currently, nearly 65 per cent of maple syrup exports go to the United States. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)
Goulet acknowledges that satisfying the demand of eager consumers is a nice problem to have.
However, he believes the industry can still grow. "There is still a great deal of untapped potential in Quebec’s maple groves," he said.
Investments from Quebec City "are too low for our liking," says Goulet, who hopes to have the ear of the newly elected Parti Québécois government.
"When we’re told that we have an industry that's thriving, that we’re growing, and that we don’t need support — well, I no longer accept that line of reasoning at the government level," he said.
For his part, Turenne believes that Quebec could encourage increased production by providing financial support to producers, and helping processors in their search for new markets abroad.
Currently, nearly 65 per cent of maple syrup exports go to the United States.
"We’ve made significant progress in diversifying our markets in recent years. Twenty years ago, that figure was 80 per cent," Turenne said.
“But we need to accelerate the opening and development of European, Australian, and Asian markets to become less dependent on the U.S. market,” he said.
Industry concentrated in Quebec
While the maple leaf graces the Canadian flag, the syrup industry is heavily concentrated in Quebec.
More than 70 per cent of North American production is in the province, according to the industry group's report, released Thursday.
When production, processing, and specialized equipment manufacturers are included, the maple syrup industry contributed $1.21 billion to the gross domestic product in 2025, the report said.
In total, the sector employs more than 10,000 full-time equivalent workers and generated $285 million in tax revenue, excluding municipal taxes and fees for the lease of public lands.
This figure does not include the sugar shacks that many Quebecers visit in the spring.
"Sugar shack operations are more akin to the restaurant industry," Turenne said.

The maple syrup producers' group used the recent election campaign to highlight the industry's importance as an employer and economic driver, and Goulet says the candidates were often surprised by the important role it played.
In some municipalities, "if you take away maple syrup production, you might as well shut down the villages," Goulet said.

articles.title: Petition urges McGill to allow convicted murderer on day parole back into law classes
articles.summary: Some students and alumni in McGill University's law faculty have signed a petition calling for the school to allow Jeffrey George Ewert, a convicted murderer on day parole, to return to campus.

image.caption: A petition signed by more than 100 students and alumni in McGill University's law faculty argues the exclusion of Jeffrey George Ewert from campus undermines his access to education and rehabilitation. (Kolya Hubacek-Guilbault/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal·New
Some students and alumni in McGill University's law faculty have signed a petition calling for the school to allow Jeffrey George Ewert, a convicted murderer on day parole, to return to campus.
Law school grapples with fallout after paroled murderer excluded from campus
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 19, 2026 1:16 PM EDT | Last Updated: 20 minutes ago
Now in his 60s, Ewert was convicted of second-degree murder and attempted murder for two attacks in B.C. in 1984.

He sexually assaulted and killed one woman and, less than six weeks later, beat and choked a 15-year-old so severely that she was paralyzed and disabled for life, according to a summary of his case in his parole board file.

Ewert is serving a life sentence and was granted day parole in 2025. While various clinical assessments ranked Ewert’s risk of reoffending as moderate to high, official parole documents say with close supervision at a halfway house and clinical follow-up, that risk “seems to fall more into the moderate risk category.”
Ewert is currently living in a halfway house. He declined an interview with CBC.

items: Convicted killer attending McGill law school divides students over safety, 2nd chances

blocks.text: He began attending law classes at McGill in August, but has not been seen on campus since early October, according to students. McGill's provost also confirmed that timeline in a letter Friday to students and alumni.
In a story published Friday, students told CBC News they were upset the university had not disclosed their peer’s violent history and some expressed feeling unsafe.
But the petition, signed by more than 100 students and alumni, argues the exclusion undermines Ewert's access to education and rehabilitation as an Indigenous man and a survivor of the Sixties Scoop.
Jeffrey George Ewert began attending law classes at McGill University in August. Some students told CBC they were upset his violent criminal past was not disclosed. (Name withheld/Instagram)
The petition, addressed to the university provost, the dean of the law faculty and the dean of students, acknowledges student safety concerns but says Ewert should not be excluded from campus.
"We are asking that Jeff be given the chance to do what the rest of us are doing, which is to attend class and learn," the petition says.
"A ban from the premises, with no conversation beforehand and no finding of misconduct, takes that chance away."
Debate among students
The CBC report has sparked heated debate among faculty, students and alumni.

An online discussion on Facebook features McGill law students on all sides of the controversy: some argue their peers should be more compassionate toward those convicted of a crime, while others say there should be more respect for students who feel unsafe.

"I can recognize the importance of reintegration, while also questioning how our university is handling the situation for students with such trauma," one person posted anonymously in the Facebook discussion.
"You never know what someone has been a victim to in their life and how that might impact their reaction, especially after having experienced such violence firsthand."
The administration, meanwhile, has tried to calm concerns among the student body.

items: Have a story worth digging into? Reach out to CBC Montreal Investigates

blocks.text: Tina Piper, the law faculty's dean, said in a letter to students that the university took "prompt action as soon as we became aware of this situation earlier this month."
Piper said she has been working with the administration on next steps.
"I want you to know that my highest priority is to ensure the safety and well-being of all members of our faculty," Piper said in the note, obtained by CBC.
"This situation is not unlike one you may encounter in your future legal career and now is a good time to practise how you want to be in the world."
In a separate email, McGill provost Angela Campbell also tried to reassure the university community.
She wrote that when information came to their attention about a situation that could "compromise a safe learning environment," the university took measured, decisive action.
Convicted killer attending McGill law school divides students over safety, 2nd chances
Ewert 'an example of rehabilitation,' lawyer says
Ewert’s lawyer, Nora Demnati, said his admission to McGill’s law program was a continuation of two decades of legal advocacy while he was in prison.
Ewert heads the Canadian Prisoners’ Labour Confederation, a group that advocates for labour rights for inmates.
She said the situation has “put tremendous stress on someone who’s like, honestly, an example of rehabilitation,” said Demnati.
While Demnati said she understands the concerns of some students, she believes they come from an “uninformed” reading of the parole decisions.
“Parole is based on progress and work and it’s on merit," said Demnati in an interview with CBC last week.

When Ewert’s parole was extended in June, some of his conditions included not to enter a drinking establishment, to immediately report all sexual and non-sexual relationships with women and to allow his case management team access to all his telecommunication activity.

That latter condition was added by the parole board because Ewert had been viewing women’s profiles on social media, starting discussions with them and exploring a dating site without notifying his case management team.
He was reprimanded by the parole board in 2025 after he had contacted and collected the phone numbers of multiple women.
As parolees are adjusting to life outside prison, Demnati said it’s normal for there to be occasional breaches.
“People on parole have breaches a lot of the time,” she said. “It does not lead necessarily to an increase in the risk and it does not lead to a conclusion that the risk cannot be managed anymore.”
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Benjamin Shingler is an investigative reporter based in Montreal. He previously worked at The Canadian Press, CTV and the New Brunswick Telegraph-Journal. You can email story ideas or tips to montrealinvestigates@cbc.ca, or reach out on Signal at @bshingler.67

articles.title: Vinted blocks French looters listing stolen goods for sale
articles.summary: The platform said since the weekend it had "taken immediate action to idenitify and remove listings linked to looting".

blocks.text: Vinted says it has removed listings of items believed to have been looted from shops during the ongoing riots in France.
The second hand re-selling platform said following the weekend's disorder it had "taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to looting".
Shops across several French cities were broken into and ransacked during the outbreak of riots over the weekend.
"The sale of stolen goods, or soliciting them, is strictly prohibited on Vinted, and we have zero tolerance for it," a spokesperson for the company said.

Widespread looting was reported across Paris, Marseille and Lille, as well as other areas after protests against the cost of living and public spending turned into riots, leading to the arrests of at least 1,200 people.
More than 2,000 businesses were directly impacted by the weekend's violence, according to the head of the Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI).
Alain Di Crescenzo told France's broadcaster RTL that the riots led to hundreds of millions of euros worth of damage.
Groups of rioters, some wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings as well as looting businesses.
Those that stole goods now appear to be looking to sell them on fast.
"Since this weekend, our teams have taken immediate action to identify and remove listings linked to the looting, and we have stepped up monitoring of suspicious listings," Vinted told the BBC.
"When our rules are breached, we act against the accounts involved, up to permanent bans."
The company said it was working with French authorities and the police, and was adapting its "processes to detect and counter emerging risks and malicious behaviour".

eBay has not noted any increase in listings linked to the looting in France, but said it works with law enforcement to investigate suspected stolen goods and takes appropriate action, including removing listings and taking action against sellers, when authorities confirm an item is stolen.

articles.title: Warning signs over threats to Australian politicians were rising before MP hit by car
articles.summary: The apparent attack on MP Helen Haines suggests the worst fears of politicians and public figures appear to have been realised.

blocks.text: As increasingly frequent acts of violence against politicians have shocked the globe in recent years, Australia has watched on with a contradictory feeling: that attacks like that could not happen here, and that it was only a matter of time until they did.

Australians will tell you this is a largely peaceful society with a comparatively civil public discourse. Violence targeting politicians has been rare, the bungled assassination of Labor leader Arthur Calwell in 1966 now a distant and fleeting memory.
But MPs and public figures – backed by experts – have been warning of a volcano of threats against them as social cohesion cracks, polarisation intensifies and the tone of debate grows hotter.
And on Monday, their worst fears appear to have been realised.
Independent MP Helen Haines was struck by a car and severely injured outside her office in the regional Victorian town of Wangaratta.
Police say a 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and a knife seized, but they have not said Haines was hit deliberately.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, however, swiftly described the incident as an apparent attack.

He was briefed by federal police – whose counter terror squad is helping state officers investigate – and told the national broadcaster: "This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear."
Though he stressed no motive had been confirmed, Albanese earlier got emotional as he talked about the growing fear amongst MPs that they would end up targets.

Earlier this year Albanese himself was evacuated from his official residence over a bomb threat. As of August, about 20 cases in which people were accused of making violent threats against him were winding their way through courts around the country.

In recent years, politicians here have been mailed bullets. Female MPs – and in some cases their children – have been threatened with sexual violence. A Jewish MP's office has been firebombed, a Sydney mayor's car has been torched and countless other politicians have had their workplaces vandalised.

Just last week Small Business Minister Anne Aly said she had received a wave of death threats after a politician from the opposition said she should be "shamed and stoned in the square" over a tax policy.
According to government statistics, there were 1,067 reports of "harassing and threatening behaviour" against "high office holders" in the year to June: an increase on last year.
"We tend to bury our head in the sand and say, 'Not here', but this has been happening now for well over a decade," Josh Roose, a Deakin University Professor on violent extremism, tells the BBC.

Socioeconomic strain, growing mental health problems in the community, "grifters" who benefit politically or financially from whipping up further discontent, and a "carcinogenic" online environment are drivers of the trend, he says, which has dramatically escalated since the pandemic.
But the political class must also take responsibility for their role, he adds.

"We've seen a willingness to cross previously sacred terrain - you know, not targeting individuals, not targeting their families - but we now see that this is part and parcel of Australian political life.
"This is occurring at both ends of the political spectrum."
And experts like him warn it is not just politicians who are vulnerable: it is members of the media, academics, court officials and other public figures too.
Mike Burgess, the head of Australia's spy agency, has warned for years that the spectre of political violence is looming in Australia.

"Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack," he said in his annual threat assessment for 2026.
And the Federal Police have said it is not just ideology motivating cases in recent times. "Grievance" is radicalising people.
"They're feeling distanced, they're feeling alone, they're looking for something to attach to, to give them meaning and purpose," Commissioner Krissy Barrett told the ABC earlier this month.

There have been frustrated rumblings in Canberra from some MPs who say security arrangements have not changed with the climate and – if a political motivation for this incident is confirmed – one of the greatest tenets of the nation's political culture could now be at risk.
It is not abnormal for you to run into your local member at the shops, or chat to them at the footy, and many open up their offices for constituents who want to raise concerns or share ideas.
Haines is particularly renowned and respected for that, Albanese said on Monday night.
"Here in Australia, it is a good thing that politicians are able to go about their community and engage with people," he said.

"I don't want to see a political system in which you can't have conversations with people at the supermarket, in the street, at street meetings, public forums – that's an important part of our democracy."

articles.title: Ex-OpenAI worker accused of planting device had Saudi support says court filing
articles.summary: The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.

blocks.text: A Saudi national charged with secretly planting a recording device in one of OpenAI's meeting rooms has been accused of having "considerable support" from the Saudi government, according to a court filing, external in California.

US prosecutors claimed Abdulrahman Alfozan, who worked for the AI firm, was in "frequent communication... with a member of the Saudi royal family", and say a member of the country's military paid for a one-way flight to Saudi Arabia for his wife and son after his arrest.
It was argued the 35-year-old engineer therefore posed a flight risk and should be detained, pending trial.
The Saudi government did not immediately respond to BBC requests for comment.
Alfozan had worked at OpenAI for around a year before he allegedly made his attempt to plant an audio recorder.
The AI company discovered the device, which was plugged into the back of a TV in a conference meeting room and covered up with toilet paper, on 30 September.
A camera was placed in the room and on 5 October, Alfozan was filmed entering and appearing to look behind the television where the audio recorder had been inserted.
He was arrested by the FBI on 9 October and his contract with OpenAI was terminated.

The court filing claimed the suspect's alleged conduct could pose "a danger to the national security of the United States", because executives from the tech firm met with government officials in the room during the days the device was believed to have been installed.
It said Alfozan's arrest came three days before he was scheduled to fly from San Francisco to Riyadh on a one-way itinerary with his wife and son.

Following the arrest, the document claims the defendant's wife told FBI agents who interviewed her that "her US visa was expiring" and so she and her son were "permanently moving back to Saudi Arabia", and her husband intended to do the same.

On 10 October, the day after Alfozan was arrested, his wife and son flew from San Francisco to Doha, Qatar. They travelled on a one-way business class ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official.
"Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through," the prosecutors argued.
The FBI investigation is ongoing.
Alfozan is scheduled to ‌appear ⁠in federal court in San Francisco later on Monday. If convicted, he faces a maximum penalty of five years in prison and a $250,000 (£188,000) fine.

articles.title: Houthi missile strike on Yemen camp kills 50 security recruits, local authorities say
articles.summary: Three missiles hit a camp in government-controlled Shabwa province that officials say was being used as a training centre for new recruits.

blocks.text: More than 50 security personnel have been killed and 200 injured in a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's central province of Shabwa, local authorities say.

A spokesman for the Saudi-backed Yemeni armed forces said the Iran-backed group launched three ballistic missiles at al-Alam camp near Ataq city, which was being used as a training centre for recruits to the security forces and police.
The head of Yemen's Presidential Leadership Council, Rashad al-Alimi, condemned what he called the "criminal attack" and promised a "firm response".
The Houthis' military spokesman said they had targeted "Saudi enemy concentrations".
Yemen's devastating civil war has flared up in recent months.
At the start of October, pro-government forces launched a major offensive that aims to retake territory in western Yemen that is controlled by the Houthis.

With air support from a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states, they managed to regain control of territory on the Red Sea coast that overlooks the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, which the Houthis captured in a surprise assault in September.
However, fierce fighting is continuing there, as well as around the besieged government-controlled city of Taiz, and to the north in Marib and al-Jawf provinces.
The Houthis have also responded to the Saudi air strikes by launching missiles and drones at airports, energy facilities and military bases in neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
Monday's attack in Shabwa is one of the deadliest reported since the start of the escalation.

Shabwa province's media office said in a statement that ballistic missiles struck the Martyr Ahmed al-Sulaimani Training Centre, where recruits from several provinces were undergoing training to be members of the internal security forces. According to a preliminary assessment, 53 were killed and more than 200 injured, it added.
A video posted on social media appeared to show several bodies scattered across the ground.

Shabwa's deputy governor, Fahad al-Khalifi, told AFP news agency that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to neighbouring Hadramout and Aden, where the government is based. Some of them were in a critical condition, he said.
Information Minister Moammar al-Eryani said the attack constituted a war crime because the internal security forces training centre was not a military target.

He also accused the Houthis of "attempting to fabricate a false media victory, boost the morale of its collapsing elements, and cover up the defeats and setbacks it is suffering across various combat axes".
The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, said in a statement that the missiles targeted a gathering of "Saudi enemy" forces at al-Alam camp, which he said was run by Saudi officers.
There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities.

In a separate development, Houthi-run media reported that a Saudi air strike on a home in the Sahar district of the Houthi-controlled northern province of Saada on Sunday killed at least 10 people and injured 23 others, many of them women and children.
According to the Houthi-run health ministry in north-western Yemen, a total of 141 people had been killed in Saudi strikes over the past seven weeks.
The government's health ministry, meanwhile, said last week that at least 1,282 people had been killed in the conflict across Yemen since 6 August.
In Saudi Arabia, at least 19 people have been killed in Houthi attacks targeting the kingdom's airports since the beginning of October.

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.
The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

articles.title: Obama blasts federal probe of congresswoman Ilhan Omar as 'so appalling'
articles.summary: Obama says federal agents' search of the Democrat's home was an effort to intimidate a Trump critic.

blocks.text: Barack Obama has said congresswoman Ilhan Omar is under federal criminal investigation simply because she's an outspoken critic of the President Donald Trump.

"The full weight of the federal government is being brought down on a law-abiding elected official because she has dared to criticize the president," the former US president wrote on X, calling the probe "so appalling".
The White House defended the inquiry, saying the justice department was "focused on restoring law and order".

Last week, homeland security agents searched the Minnesota Democrat's Washington DC home as part of an investigation into her immigration status. Born in Somalia, Omar moved to the US with her family as a child.
US media outlets have reported that the probe is tied to her American citizenship and whether she lied about her age when she arrived in the US in 1995.
Questions have been raised about whether the age listed on Omar's citizenship application differed from her actual birth date.
Obama said in his X post on Sunday that her father became a naturalised citizen when she was 17, and not yet legally an adult, which then gave her citizenship.

"Now the Administration is actively trying to deport Congresswoman Omar, seemingly based solely on the unsubstantiated theory that she was actually 18 when her father was naturalized, and therefore is not a citizen," he wrote.
"If this becomes the new normal," he added, "there's no reason to believe it will stop with her - or that future presidents, in either party, won't do the same."

According to the US Citizenship and Immigration Services, a child born outside of the US automatically becomes a citizen when he or she has at least one parent who is a citizen by birth or naturalisation, or he or she is under the age of 18, and is a lawful permanent resident living in the custody of a citizen parent.
White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis denied the investigation was politically motivated.
"Unlike Joe Biden, President Trump has not weaponized the Department of Justice against his political foes," she said in an emailed statement to the BBC.
"The Department is focused on restoring law and order and keeping Americans safe."
Trump has often argued that federal criminal investigations against him as he campaigned for re-election were politically motivated.

The investigation into Omar could lead to the justice department seeking to "denaturalise" her, or revoke her citizenship. It would have to prove there were material lies in the naturalisation process.
In 2023, Republicans removed Omar from the House Foreign Affairs Committee for comments and tweets she made about Israel, which drew bipartisan criticism.
Omar has said that Trump has targeted her for years with "baseless lies and smear campaigns" and called the investigation "the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation".
But Trump has said the investigation had "nothing to do" with him, while describing Omar as a "terrible person" and a "complainer".
Federal agents reportedly seized her phone, computers, notebooks and passport in the raid a week ago.

Her lawyers have demanded the government return her belongings, CBS News, the BBC's US partner, has reported, arguing in a letter sent on Friday that the seizure of property had violated restrictions put in place by a judge to protect her work as a federal lawmaker.

The lawyers also alleged agents did not duly notify Omar or the House of Representatives general counsel that a search would be taking place and kept her from contacting her attorney for more than an hour, according to CBS.

Democrats characterised the raid as the president attempting to interfere with the legislative branch of government. Republicans, meanwhile, have said Omar should be treated the same as anyone else under the law.

When Obama first ran for president, and throughout his two terms in the White House, Trump repeatedly raised questions about his citizenship, asserting he was not born on American soil and was disqualified from serving in office. Obama released two records proving he had been born in Hawaii.
Obama did not mention that history in his X post on Sunday.

articles.title: Kenyan starvation cult leader guilty of murder of 190 children and one adult
articles.summary:
Paul Mackenzie and his church set up sect that ordered followers to starve themselves and their children, say prosecutors

A Kenyan court on Monday found starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie…

blocks.text: A Kenyan court has found the starvation cult leader Paul Mackenzie and about 30 others guilty of murder over the deaths of ⁠190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult-related disasters in recent history.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast ⁠in south-eastern Kenya.

Prosecutors say Mackenzie and ⁠his Good News International Church organised ​a Christian doomsday sect in which they ordered followers to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve but the ⁠court rejected that argument.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered from the Shakahola forest. Many were severely decomposed, and only 26 of them were able to be identified.
Monday’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into the other deaths are continuing.
Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

blocks.caption: Kenyan high court judge Diana Kavedza Mochache on 19 October. Photograph: EPA

blocks.text: Mackenzie was in ​court, wearing a striped polo shirt and red trousers, sitting alongside his wife, ‌one of the co-accused.
He was silent, ‌staring into space before the ruling was handed down.
Relatives of some of those who died in the forest gathered to hear the judgment at Mombasa high ‌court.
Francis Wanje, 62, lost eight family members including two grandchildren to the cult.

Speaking before the verdict, he said: “It has been really a heavy thing [for] us as a family, and it has really taken us very far in terms of psychological problems … I was hoping for this particular day.”
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the coastal forest more than three years ago.

It raised questions over how Mackenzie was able to continue to operate despite having been on the radar of the authorities since 2017 when his premises were searched by police. In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.

blocks.caption: A Kenyan national youth service officer talks to a woman while on guard at the entrance to the Mombasa law courts on Monday 19 October. Photograph: Simon Maina/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Kenya’s president, William Ruto, said in 2023 that government agencies should have been ​able to prevent the deaths. He said he took responsibility as president.
People with direct knowledge of the cult’s activities said Mackenzie planned the mass starvation in three phases: first children, then women and young men, and finally the remaining men.

Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic, some of his followers told Reuters for a 2023 article.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene ⁠sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.

blocks.caption: Paul Mackenzie and his co-accused during their court appearance on 19 October. Photograph: Simon Maina/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in mid-March 2023, when a local man told ​police that his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives say he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police ​arrested him again in April 2023 and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths including terrorism-related ones, which he has denied.
Prosecutors say while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles (30km) from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.
