articles.title: Senators grill DENR on El Niño response
articles.summary: During the Department of Environment and Natural Resources budget hearing yesterday, senators grilled agency officials about the country’s El Niño response, including the deployment of…

blocks.text: October 20, 2026 | 12:00am
A farmer walks over cracked soil on a dried up Nueva Ecija field in this file photo.
Krizjohn Rosales

MANILA, Philippines — During the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) budget hearing yesterday, senators grilled agency officials about the country’s El Niño response, including the deployment of water impounding facilities and the closure of non-essential water services like resorts and fountains.
Sen. Risa Hontiveros led the budget hearing and asked Jose Salonga, chief of the DENR-attached agency Local Water Utilities Administration (LWUA), about its water conservation policy.
Salonga cited the LWUA memorandum circular, which considered water sprinklers on golf courses, swimming pools in water parks and fountains in resorts as non-essential water uses.

When Hontiveros asked if the LWUA can mandate their temporary closure until the “super El Niño” lapses, Salonga said the memorandum circular includes the possible temporary closure or easing of these non-essential services, but not the whole business.
The water valves of government offices may also be closed outside work hours, Salonga added.
DENR Secretary Juan Miguel Cuna said the President has directed a comprehensive communications plan for the public to be informed about water conservation.

“The President has called several times already the task force El Niño. And one of the agenda items that was taken up is a comprehensive comms plan that we’re already working on with the other agencies. So that as you said, people will know how they can contribute to at least easing the effects of the super El Niño,” Cuna said.
In an interview after the hearing, Salonga clarified that the LWUA cannot forcefully close non-essential water services like resorts and water parks.
But the agency can have these businesses reduce their non-essential water consumption for swimming pools and fountains, he added.

The Senate finance committee tackling their budget also learned from the DENR that based on their spatial assessment and geographic information system analysis, there are 34 percent or 14,434 barangays nationwide deemed “high priority” in the government’s El Niño response; 23 percent or 9,685 barangays deemed low priority and only two percent or 883 barangays deemed “not affected.”

articles.title: Kenya: Cult leader guilty of murdering 190 children, 1 adult
articles.summary: Preacher Paul Mackenzie was accused of encouraging his followers to starve themselves to death. He ran a Christian doomsday cult called the Good News International Church that claimed the end of the…

image.caption: Paul Mackenzie arrived at court under police escort ahead of the verdictImage: Laban Walloga/REUTERS

blocks.text: A court in Mombasa, Kenya, on Monday found self-proclaimed preacher Paul Mackenzie and 28 associates guilty of murdering 190 children and one adult as part of a notorious Christian starvation cult.
Mackenzie established his so-called Good News International Church in 2003 and was alleged to have incited his followers to starve themselves to death in order to "meet Jesus."
He was arrested in April 2023 after a rights group informed authorities.
Some of his acolytes were rescued but the subsequent police operation exposed hundreds of mass graves at a forest site near the Kenyan beach resort of Malindi.
Local media dubbed the case the "Shakahola Forest Massacre."
Shakahola Forest Massacre: What did the judge say?

"I am satisfied that the prosecution has proved the case against all the 29 accused persons for the murder of 190 children and one adult," said Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache after a hearing which lasted over eight hours.

blocks.caption: Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache delivered the verdict Image: Laban Walloga/REUTERS

blocks.text: The prosecution had said Mackenzie "initiated and directed" extreme fasting at his 800-acre (325 hectare) ranch in Shakahola Forest, claiming there was a "structured hierarchy of death" which said children should die first, followed by teenagers, women, and then men.
Post-mortems and police reports revealed that the children mostly died from starvation, but also from "asphyxia, neck compression and traumatic head injury," prosecutors said.
The court in Mombasa also heard that, in some cases, children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
"This is a very, very important day," said Francis Wanje, 62, who lost eight family members, including his daughter and two grandchildren, at Shakahola.

"We are expecting a ruling that will be a lesson to the whole public, so that such kinds of things will not happen again," he told the AFP news agency, expressing anger over the government's initial inaction.
Will Kenya's cult leader be found guilty of manslaughter?
Mackenzie facing even more Shakahola charges

Since the initial discovery of the graves, even more bodies of children, women and men have been unearthed, bringing the total to well over 400. The soaring death toll has even required sporadic pauses in excavations as local morgues ran out of space.
In January 2026, Mackenzie was charged over a further 52 bodies found at a nearby village.
There have been calls in Kenya for tougher regulations on religious organizations after it emerged that Mackenzie had been arrested twice in the past but released.
He was arrested in 2017 on charges of "radicalization" but was acquitted. He was arrested again in 2019 in relation to two child deaths at Shakahola, but released on bail.
His sentencing will take place on November 6.
How do radical churches get people to follow their beliefs?

articles.title: Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited
articles.summary:
More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces

At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile…

blocks.text: At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.

The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.

There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attacks. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.

Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.

Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.
He had already on Monday phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.

The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin Al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals.

The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.
Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.

The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in the Al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilizations, including Saudi officers.

“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”
Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of the Yemeni city Taiz, and citizens have been calling for greater air protection.
Southern forces were said to be making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.

The Saudi Armaco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they are not yet going to resume using Riyadh airport. The airport formally reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month.
Hans Grundberg, the UN envoy for Yemen, is due in London to meet ministers on Tuesday.

articles.title: Former journalist Pamela Wallin resigns from Senate
articles.summary: Sen. Pamela Wallin has resigned from the Upper Chamber.

image.caption: Sen. Pamela Wallin speaks at a media conference in Ottawa on Feb. 1, 2024. (Patrick Doyle/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·Breaking
Sen. Pamela Wallin has resigned from the Upper Chamber.
Former journalist represented Saskatchewan in the Red Chamber
The clerk of the Senate received a resignation letter from the longtime Saskatchewan senator effective Sunday, Oct. 18, according to the Senate of Canada.
The reason for her resignation, which was first reported by iPolitics, is not yet known. Wallin turns 75, the Senate's mandatory retirement age, in 2028.
Wallin was appointed to the Senate on the advice of Prime Minister Stephen Harper in 2009.
More to come
With files from Chris Rands

articles.title: Canada: Alberta votes on holding independence referendum
articles.summary: Canada's oil-rich western province of Alberta is not deemed likely to vote in favor of a real breakaway plebiscite. Nevertheless the separatist movement hopes to gain leverage over Mark Carney's…

image.caption: Alberta is a vast, resource, rich state with a population slightly smaller than Finland or New ZealandImage: Jeff McIntosh/PA Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: Residents of Alberta in Canada are voting in a referendum on whether the province should begin a process that could ultimately lead to independence.
The motion does not appear likely to succeed but the vote taking place at all signifies economic and political grievances gaining some sway in the vast oil-rich region.
Separatist leaders hope that a comparatively strong showing for their cause could nevertheless pressure Prime Minister Mark Carney's government in Ottawa to pay them more heed in future.
What will happen during the vote?
Polls opened at 9 a.m. local time in the provincial capital Edmonton (1500 GMT/UTC) on Monday.
They are scheduled to close at 8 p.m. that evening (Tuesday, 0200 GMT/UTC).
Results will then be published as they come in.
At least based on opinion polls, the yes/no result is in no real doubt, but as many as 1 in 3 voters might support the proposal.

blocks.caption: The 'no to the nine' campaign urges voters to refuse all nine proposal up for debate, not just the most significant one on setting the wheels in motion for a potential independence referendumImage: Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: What has led to the vote?

Monday's referendum is the first on the notion of breaking away from Canada in a province other than majority French-speaking Quebec, which has a better-known separatist movement founded in language and cultural differences.

The vast oil-rich state is almost double the size of Germany in terms of land mass, but is much more sparsely populated with around 5 million residents. Almost half of them live in its two main cities, Edmonton and Calgary.
Alberta's provincial government is led by Danielle Smith of the United Conservative Party while Mark Carney's Liberal Party lead the national government.

Smith herself does not advocate independence and has urged voters to oppose the motion. But she has nevertheless authorized the vote, seemingly in a bid to assuage an increasingly vocal flank within her own ranks.

Independence advocates accuse the government of stifling Alberta's oil industry, for instance through environmental regulations, and also say they contribute disproportionately to the national public purse.

"Canada has an imbalanced system which feeds the central population and government at the expense of the outlying producing provinces such as Alberta," said Cory Morgan, founder of a pro-separation organization called Pathway to Independence.

blocks.caption: PM Carney has been campaigning in Edmonton and elsewhere, trying to maximize turnout among those who favor staying part of CanadaImage: John Ulan/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Canadian sovereignty under pressure from within and without

Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has spent much of the past week campaigning for the "stay" campaign, appealing to national pride and urging supporters to vote to provide as resounding a result as possible — even in what might not be a close race.
The renowned economist and central banker often argued that the separatist cause might be guilty of overlooking matters more significant than dollars and drilling permits.
"Canada is not a transaction between provinces. It's not about gross and net, gives and gets," he said at an event in Red Deer on Friday.

Although polls in French-speaking Quebec suggest that enthusiasm for independence — typically a minority cause — is lower than usual during Carney's premiership, the issue is never very far from the political debate. The success of the separatist Parti Quebecois in local elections this month served as a reminder of this.
Carney is also trying to maintain national unity amid pressure from Canada's nearest neighbor and biggest trade partner.
US President Donald Trump is conducting characteristically combative trade talks with Canada that have seemed in danger of breaking down in recent months.
When at his most agitated, Trump has even called for Canada to become the "51st state" of the US. He has also tried to rename bodies of water like Lake Ontario.
Why Canada's trust in the US may not recover anytime soon

articles.title: Can diplomacy stop another Ethiopia-Eritrea war?
articles.summary: Ethiopia has installed a new administration in conflict-hit Tigray after federal forces pushed back Tigrayan fighters. But tensions with Eritrea continue to raise fears of a wider regional war.

image.caption: Ethiopia has installed an interim administration in Tigray tasked with holding elections and rehousing displaced peopleImage: Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed on Friday announced an interim government in the country's northern Tigray region and gave it six months to prepare for regional elections and restore stability.

Abiy's announcement followed a military offensive launched in September by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and six other armed groups. They were ultimately forced to retreat and lost control of the region.

"To attain the peace that has long eluded them, to secure their right to self-administration, ​and to finally enjoy the fruits of development — which have been out of reach for many years — the people of Tigray must break free from this cycle ⁠of conflict," ​Abiy said in a statement posted on X.

Shishay Amare, the new mayor of the regional capital Mekelle, said: "Our role is to create the right conditions for elections by ensuring peace and stability across Tigray," reported French news agency Agence France-Presse (AFP).

"I am confident that this will be done within six months, according to our plan," Amare said, adding that their priorities included restoring peace, helping displaced residents return home, reopening markets and ensuring humanitarian assistance reached those in need.
Why relations with Eritrea matter

The fighting has revived concerns about a return to the devastating 2020–2022 Tigray war. Around 1 million people remain displaced from that conflict. The African Union has estimated that the war resulted in around 600,000 deaths from combat, famine and the collapse of healthcare.
The new administration faces unresolved disputes over political authority and territory, including western Tigray, which is claimed by both Tigray and neighboring Amhara state.

blocks.caption: Egypt and Ethiopia have repeatedly clashed over the construction of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD)Image: Brian Inganga/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ethiopia and Eritrea were once bitter enemies but signed a peace agreement in 2018. Eritrean forces later fought alongside Ethiopian federal troops during the Tigray war. The countries' relationship has since deteriorated.
Addis Ababa accuses Asmara of supporting Tigrayan forces and violating Ethiopian territory. Eritrea has denied the accusations.
Reports of Eritrean troop movements near the border have heightened concern, although the extent of any current deployment remains disputed.

Tsedale Lemma, journalist and publisher of the prominent Addis Standard magazine, told DW earlier this month that the danger reflects years of unresolved tensions and failures to implement the November 2022 Pretoria Agreement, which ended the previous Tigray war.

Asked whether the international community was underestimating the threat, Lemma said: "It is absolutely underestimating it." She argued that international actors had failed to ensure effective monitoring of the agreement and respond adequately as the peace process weakened.
A wider regional risk
The confrontation comes amid instability across the Horn of Africa, including Sudan's war and tensions between Ethiopia and Egypt over the Nile mega-dam project.
Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again
Last year, Ethiopia inaugurated the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), a move that was not well received by neighboring Egypt and Sudan, both downstream countries.
Competition over access to the Red Sea adds another strategic dimension: Ethiopia became landlocked when Eritrea gained independence in 1993.

Journalist Martin Plaut, who specializes in the Horn of Africa, has warned that the region faces a crossroads. He has raised the possibility of Ethiopian forces entering Eritrea, but an invasion remains a scenario, not a confirmed decision by the Ethiopian government.

Any wider conflict could threaten regional trade and maritime security. The Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait connect shipping routes between Europe and Asia, making the region strategically important well beyond Africa.
Can diplomacy avert war between Ethiopia and Eritrea?
The United States and the United Kingdom have called on Ethiopia and Eritrea to exercise restraint and return to dialogue under their 2018 peace framework.
Speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews on Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that the military buildup on the Ethiopia-Eritrea border could escalate into a wider conflict.
Rubio said Washington hoped lifting some sanctions would improve communication with both sides and stressed the need for a "wise and measured" response to avoid a broader regional war.

A UK government spokesperson said in an October 15 statement that: "We urgently call for de-escalation and a return to dialogue. We reiterate our support for the African Union's role in facilitating this."
For now, the recapture of towns in Tigray has changed the military balance but has not resolved the tensions surrounding the region.
Whether international pressure can prevent a wider war will depend on whether the governments involved choose dialogue over further escalation.
Negash Mohammed, Tamirat Geleta and Christine Mhundwa contributed to this report.

articles.title: Strait of Hormuz scoured for spilt cargo after Iran attacks container ships
articles.summary:
At least 15 vessels struck in waterway in past 10 days, with rumours spread that they carried valuable goods

People have been scouring the strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran…

blocks.text: People have been scouring the strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacked at least 15 container ships traversing the crucial waterway in the past 10 days.
Some ships have been hit by drones, others by mines. On Sunday, a ship was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade launched from a small boat 120km (75 miles) north-east of the Saudi port of Jubail.

The rise in Iranian attacks appears to have helped resolidify Tehran’s disputed control over the strait, as well as pushing up the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil close to $108 a barrel on Monday morning.

blocks.caption: A container from the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride floats after the ship sank off the coast of Oman on 14 October. Photograph: Social media/Reuters

blocks.text: Last Wednesday a ship travelling from Karachi to Fujairah in the United Arab Emirates sunk after hitting a mine, according to Iranian state TV. All 21 crew members were evacuated and no injuries were reported. Dozens of its 2,500 containers were seen floating in the water. Rumours that iPhones and other expensive goods were among its cargo – fuelled by fake AI-generated photos published on social media – prompted fishers and others to investigate.
One fisher told an Iranian reporter: “The Arab boatmen, who were closer to the ship, arrived earlier than the Iranians. They used stonecutters to cut the container and took whatever was there.”

Col Javad Mokhtar Rezaei, the deputy head of cultural and social affairs for Iran’s cyber police (Fata), told the Tasnim news agency: “In some cases, the phones offered may actually exist, but exposing electronic components to saltwater and extreme humidity can cause corrosion of internal components, damage to the boards, battery and display, and cause hidden malfunctions in the device’s performance.”
Meysam Doost-Mohammadi, a spokesperson for the Iranian mobile association, said it would be unusual for valuable phones to be transported by ship.

The bulk of the recent spate of attacks have occurred close to the coast with Oman, a route that Iran regards as unauthorised. In the seven days to Friday 16 October, 12 vessels were attacked, according to the UK Maritime Agency (UKMTO).

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says it has the right to attack any ship that seeks to traverse the strait without its permission or with its transponders off. The officials have also ordered local fishers not to pillage the sea for luxury items, saying the goods are the property of the state.

Two oil tankers were hit on Saturday, including a supertanker carrying 2m barrels of oil, according to the IRGC. The Fars news agency also published a video that appears to show the tanker burning, but which cannot be independently verified. A third tanker was hit late Sunday.

It is disputed how many ships have been hit by mines or IRGC shelling. UKMTO’s weekly overview recorded 254 transits of the strait (125 outbound, 129 inbound) in the week to 14 October, approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels.

blocks.caption: A satellite image shows containers and items floating in the water after the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride sank off the coast of Oman on 14 October.  Photograph: European Union/Copernicus Sentinel-2/Reuters

blocks.text: Dr Devaraj Asir Ramesh of Anna University in Chennai, India, warned that the region’s marine habitats faced threats from toxic debris and oil spills, while noise might have disturbed marine life. Iranian strikes on the Emirates, he said, were likely to have contaminated seagrass beds with hydrocarbons and caused auditory damage to cetaceans – marine mammals such as dolphins and porpoises – which are sensitive to loud noise that travels through the sea.

Ramesh also said oil released by attacks on tankers at Fujairah could have caused ecological harm. “Oil spills, chemical leaks and acoustic disturbances have impaired biodiversity, fisheries, aquaculture, desalination, and eco-tourism,” he wrote in the International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Sciences.

blocks.caption: Vessels at the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman, 19 October. Iran has offered to open the strait in six days in return for sanctions relief. Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: On Friday the Iranian president said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had inflicted a significant toll on nature that extended beyond borders and required “international solutions”.

“What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned,” Masoud Pezeshkian said. He argued that countries subjected to economic sanctions or military aggression should not be forced to shoulder the financial burden of environmental damage resulting from conflicts they did not initiate.
Successive studies, mainly by US universities using satellite imagery, have warned of the dangers facing the strait.

The renewed concern over the environmental impact of the war in the strait came as the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, visited Tehran offering to act as an intermediary between Iran and Donald Trump, especially over the issue of Iran’s nuclear stockpile, an issue that the US president insists must be addressed before he lifts his threat to attack Iran again.
Iran has offered to open the strait in six days in return for sanctions relief.

Russia has offered to take Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium, but Iran is reluctant to make a commitment on its nuclear programme and has not given the International Atomic Energy Agency access to its bombed nuclear sites since June 2025. Lavrov also proposed a trilateral summit between China, Russia and Iran to agree new security architecture for the strait. He said the region was on the verge of a full-scale crisis.

Tehran is braced for another attack soon, especially after the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, launched a new national security doctrine on Sunday that included a new emphasis on prevention and offence, including pre-emptive strikes on potential threats.

articles.title: Germany news: Emergency at Leipzig airport sparked by novice driver
articles.summary: Two men breached a fence at the Leipzig/Halle airport while practicing for a driving test. Meanwhile, the "Invest in Germany Summit" is set to kick off as the government looks to fill gaps in public…

image.caption: Leipzig/Halle airport was already on high alert after bomb-laden drones were discovered there in AugustImage: Tobias Junghannß/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Published October 19, 2026last updated October 19, 2026
Novice driver caused fence breach at Leipzig/Halle airport: Police

blocks.caption: The breach in the fence triggered a major police operationImage: Erik-Holm Langhof/EHL Media/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Two men have admitted to breaking through a fence at Leipzig/Halle airport while one of them was practicing for a driving test, an incident that triggered a major security operation, police said on Monday.
The two, aged 20 and 32, handed themselves in to the police on Sunday evening, following the incident. The broken fence was first discovered by airport staff late on Saturday.
Police said the 20-year-old had been at the wheel despite not having a valid license.
An investigation was opened into the learner driver for fleeing the scene after breaking through the fence.
The mass-circulation Bild newspaper reported that the car involved, of which fragments were found at the site, was an Audi.
The airport was the site of a security scare in August, when an explosives-laden drone was found there near Ukrainian cargo planes.
German officials accused Russia of having planned an attack, something Moscow denied.

articles.title: Drone attack near market kills 80 in Sudan
articles.summary:
Witness says drone struck twice at transport hub in al-Dibab, in one of deadliest single attacks of war

A drone strike near a market in southern Sudan on Sunday evening killed 80 people,…

blocks.text: A drone strike near a market in southern Sudan on Sunday evening killed 80 people, mostly commuters catching rides home.
Ahmed Wadi, a witness, said the attack in the town of al-Dibab in West Kordofan state left “50 bodies who I helped bury, one of them my own brother Mohamed”.

Using a satellite internet connection to circumvent a communications blackout, Wadi also said 47 other people were transported to the nearest town, al-Mujlad. A medical source, requesting anonymity for his safety, said 30 of them died from their injuries.
The medic said: “A total of 80 people were killed in the drone strike on al-Dibab, and another drone strike on al-Mujlad injured four who are currently being treated.”
Wadi said the drone struck twice, 10 minutes apart, “on a transport hub where people gather to travel back to their villages after the market day ends”.

The attack is one of the deadliest single strikes since war broke out in April 2023 when a power struggle between the Sudanese armed forces (SAF), headed by Gen Abdel Fattah al-Burhan, and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), led by Mohamed Hamdan Dagalo, erupted into violence in the capital, Khartoum.
The RSF-declared administration, known as Tasis, accused the army of carrying out Sunday’s strike. All of West Kordofan state is under RSF control.

Sudan has witnessed an escalation in the use of drones in the war. Between January and April, drone strikes accounted for at least 880 civilian deaths, more than 80% of all conflict-related civilian deaths in Sudan.

After drone strikes on a busy livestock market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur state, on Friday, the SAF said they had killed RSF fighters, but the RSF accused the military of killing 30 civilians.
The fighting in Sudan has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced many more. It has been fuelled by foreign powers with vested interests who are supporting sides in the conflict.

Last week, Rosemary DiCarlo, the undersecretary-general for political and peacebuilding affairs at the UN, warned the security council that the conflict and humanitarian crisis was deteriorating “with no breakthrough on the horizon”.

She said: “They [the warring parties] are not moving closer to dialogue. On the contrary, they seem to believe that they can make greater gains on the battlefield and that continued external support will allow them to pursue their objectives by force.”
AFP contributed to this report

articles.title: Houthi strike on Yemen government military camp kills at least 50
articles.summary: The Iran-backed group has claimed responsibility for the attack which killed new recruits at a military camp. The strikes follow deadly attacks over the weekend blamed on Saudi-led forces.

image.caption: The Houthis began a new offensive against the internationally-recognized Yemeni government in September [FILE: October 7, 2026]Image: Osamah Abdulrahman/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: At least 50 Yemeni government forces were killed in a strike by Houthi rebels on a military camp in the south of the country on Monday, military officials said.
The group fired three ballistic missiles at the al-Alam camp in the province of Shabwa. Some 200 recruits were also wounded, according to the provincial government.
The Houthis confirmed that they had targeted the camp.
Deadliest attack in recent surge of violence in Yemen
Military sources had originally put the death toll at 30, but this rose to at least 50 later in the day, with the Associated Press giving a toll of 53 and citing provincial authorities.
"The death toll has risen to at least 50, with more than 100 people injured, some of them in critical condition," Fahad al-Khalifi, deputy governor of Shabwa said, according to AFP.
Al-Khalifi added that local hospitals had been overwhelmed and some of the more seriously wounded had been transferred to facilities in other provinces.
The increased death toll makes Monday's attack one of the deadliest in the recent uptick of violence in Yemen.
Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis?
Yemeni government vows response to Houthi attack

Fighting in Yemen between the Iran-backed Houthis and the Saudi-backed government has been going on for years, but the US-Israeli war on Iran and other factors have sparked renewed fighting in the peninsula, with the Houthis also carrying out major attacks on Saudi Arabian soil.
Officials said that the soldiers who were killed and wounded in the attack had been recruits for a new Rapid Intervention force which is supposed to defend the local area.
The missiles reportedly struck while they were lining up in formation ahead of training.

Rashad al-Alimi, head of the ruling Presidential Leadership Council, vowed a "firm response" for the killing of the recruits and said the attack reflects the Houthis' "approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter."
Monday's strikes follow several attacks over the weekend that killed more than 30 people in Houthi-held areas. The Houthis have blamed Saudi-led forces for the attacks.
Saudi Arabia on the backfoot in the war against the Houthis

articles.title: US airman dies as daredevil descent goes wrong before Texas college football game
articles.summary: The game continued after the incident. The American Conference said the decision was made before his death was known.

blocks.text: A member of the US Air Force died after he fell while abseiling from the ceiling of a Texas stadium ahead of a college football game.

Footage shows the serviceman plummet feet first to the turf midfield at San Antonio's 170ft (52 metre) high Alamodome on Saturday during a ceremony ahead of the game between the University of Texas at San Antonio and the Naval Academy.
The airman, identified, external by the military as Sgt Ian Patterson, a Tactical Air Control Party instructor at Joint Base San Antonio, died in hospital.
The incident is being investigated. The game between the UTSA Roadrunners and the Navy Midshipmen continued as planned following the tragic incident.
A collegiate athletic association said the decision to press ahead with the fixture was made before the airman's death had been confirmed.
"We extend our deepest condolences to his family, friends, teammates and members of the 57th Wing," the American Conference, external said in a statement.
US Air Force Brig Gen Scott Mills said in a statement issued by Nellis Air Force Base: "This tragedy is felt deeply across the 57th Wing.
"Tech Sgt Patterson and his service mattered immensely to our wing."
Patterson, from Fort Stewart, Georgia, had served in the US military for 15 years, according to Nellis Air Force Base.
He held multiple military decorations and was in 2022 named the Air Force Special Warfare Enlisted Instructor of the Year at the Headquarters Air Force level.

UTSA president Taylor Eighmy said: "I want to extend my deepest and most heartfelt sympathies to the service member's family, his fellow airmen, squadron and all those whose lives have been touched by this heartbreaking tragedy."

articles.title: Catalonia's former rebel president can return to Spain, court rules
articles.summary: The court upholds a decision to lift an arrest warrant for Carles Puigdemont linked to the independence bid he led in 2017.

blocks.text: Spain's Supreme Court has ruled the former president of Catalonia, Carles Puigdemont, can return without fear of arrest nearly a decade after going into self-imposed exile having led a failed independence bid.
The court upheld a decision to lift an arrest warrant for him linked to the referendum his regional government organised in 2017, in defiance of Madrid.

Direct rule was imposed on the region soon after the vote and Puigdemont fled to Belgium, where he has been based ever since - with a surprise appearance in Barcelona in 2024 prompting a police manhunt.
But the Spain to which he may return is much different from a decade ago, with Catalan independence now a marginal political issue.
Monday's ruling brings to an end a lengthy legal wrangle between the Spanish judiciary and the former Catalan president.

In 2024, Spain's socialist government introduced a controversial amnesty for dozens of Catalan politicians and activists who were involved in the secession drive, but the Supreme Court said Puigdemont and several of his colleagues should be excluded.
It argued this was because of the charges against them of alleged financial crimes around staging the referendum.

The Constitutional Court overruled that interpretation earlier this month, and on Monday the Supreme Court rejected an appeal by the far-right Vox party against lifting national arrest warrants for Puigdemont, as well as his former ministers Lluís Puig and Toni Comín, paving the way for their return to Spain.
Puigdemont was elected as a member of the European Parliament (MEP) in 2019 and to the Catalan parliament in 2024 as leader of the region's centre-right Together for Catalonia (JxCat) party.
He had campaigned in the south of France, where he held rallies attended by supporters who travelled across the border to see him.

Puigdemont is known to have made at least one brief return to Spain since leaving the country, addressing a crowd of supporters in Barcelona prior to disappearing and escaping back over the border to France before he could be detained.
While he was living in Waterloo, Belgium, nine of his former colleagues were jailed for their role in the events of 2017. They were released when the Spanish government pardoned them in 2021.
Puigdemont has remained an active political presence, travelling across Europe to espouse the Catalan independence cause and fiercely criticising Spain's democratic institutions.
In a video posted on social media just as the Supreme Court ruling was announced, Puigdemont spoke of his reasons for staying abroad.
"My role was to stir public opinion, internationalise the conflict and work from the heart of Europe to explain the reality of Spain," he said.
It is still not known when he might return to Spain.
Comín, his former regional minister for health, plans to travel this week to Madrid, where he is due to carry out administrative procedures linked to his status as an MEP.
The referendum sparked the country's biggest political crisis since democracy was restored following the death of Francisco Franco.

The banned vote was met with a heavy police crackdown. The region's separatist majority declared independence after the vote - Madrid then dissolved parliament, sacked its leaders and called a snap election.
But Catalan independence is now a relatively marginal issue in Spain, with housing and immigration dominating the political agenda.
The parliamentary support of Puigdemont's JxCat party was instrumental in allowing current Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez to form a new left-wing Spanish government after the 2023 election.
But within Catalonia, JxCat has been struggling, with a far-right, pro-independence party, Catalan Alliance, taking many of its voters.
And next month, Spain's general election could see the far right enter government for the first time.

articles.title: Canada-wide support grows for CFB Wainwright victims as 50 investigators probe deadly fire

image.caption: Minister of Emergency Management Eleanor Olszewski speaks to the media during a cabinet retreat in Banff, Alta., on Sept. 11. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: 'My heart just dropped,' says mother of Pte. Aidan Goulding
Sonia Monk had just returned from grocery shopping on Vancouver Island when her son Wylder texted her: "Do you know what's happening at Wainwright right now?"
"My heart just dropped," Monk told CBC Radio's As It Happens.

She spent the rest of the night anxiously watching the news and waiting for the phone to ring with an update about her son, Pte. Aidan Goulding. She knew people had died in the fire, but her husband felt sure that Goulding would be OK.
Then, at 11 p.m., there was a knock at the door.
"I didn't want to open the door, because I just knew," she said.
When she opened it, she was greeted by three military officers and a chaplain.
"They said, 'I'm very sorry to tell you that your son, Aidan Golding, has been killed,'" she said. "Honestly, I don't know what they said after that."
When Goulding first told her in December that he was going to quit his job as a mechanic and enlist in the military, she says she tried to talk him out of it.
But Goulding was determined. She says he felt strongly that he had only one life to live, and he wanted to dedicate his life to protecting his country.
"That's the thing about Aidan," she said. "If he had a goal, he will accomplish it."
While she awaits details about the fire, she says she can't stop thinking about what happened to her son in his final moments.
"My greatest fear is how Aidan died. That is my nightmare. That is why I can't sleep, because I just think: Did a fire engulf him?" she said, her voice trembling. "Aidan's life was cut so short."

articles.title: What health-care promises have B.C. parties made ahead of the provincial election?
articles.summary: B.C.'s provincial parties are sharing their priorities for health care ahead of the Oct. 24 election, with promises ranging from more recruitment, to accelerated training for international graduates,…

image.caption: B.C.'s provincial parties are campaigning on a variety of health care promises, from recruiting more doctors and nurses, to speeding up international credentials to new health centres. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia

B.C.'s provincial parties are sharing their priorities for health care ahead of the Oct. 24 election, with promises ranging from more recruitment, to accelerated training for international graduates, to new health centres.
Parties outline health-care priorities from more recruitment to accelerated training and new clinics
B.C.'s provincial parties are sharing their priorities for health care ahead of the Oct. 24 election, with promises ranging from more recruitment and accelerated training to new health centres.

Several changes have been introduced to tackle B.C.’s health-care challenges in recent years, including a new family doctor payment model as an alternative to the older fee-for-service system, and a streamlined process for internationally trained physicians to work in the province.
The B.C. NDP also launched the Health Connect Registry, an online portal linking patients to care providers, and expanded pharmacists’ ability to treat minor ailments and prescribe contraceptives.
The party says it’s attached 700,000 more people to a family doctor or nurse practitioner in the last three years.
But challenges remain as staffing shortages force regular ER closures in some communities and more than 1.2 million British Columbians remain without a family doctor.
So what are some changes parties are proposing for health care this provincial election?
B.C. Conservatives
The B.C. Conservatives say they are standing firm on keeping B.C.'s system universal and publicly funded, despite the NDP warning the Conservatives will move towards health-care privatization.
"I want a fully public system that everyone in this province can access, said leader Lorne Doerkson at the leaders’ debate on Wednesday.
The party says within its first 100 days, it will launch an expert commission to bring proven solutions from other public systems to B.C.

items: Lorne Doerkson talks values as he leads B.C. Conservatives into election

blocks.text: B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson says he supports a public health-care system and is focused on hiring and retaining more doctors. (Nav Rahi/CBC)
On Thursday, the party pledged a new women and children’s hospital in Surrey, so families no longer have to travel to Vancouver for care.
It's also vowing to keep emergency rooms open, hire and retain more doctors and nurses, and speed up international credential recognition for Canadians who studied abroad.
The party says it will support rural medical practices at risk of closing, and invest $50 million into what it is calling an emergency fund.
"We will protect health care funding, recruit and retain more doctors and nurses, and cut wait times. Your health card will always be all you need," the party said in a statement.
B.C. NDP
B.C. NDP Leader David Eby said he is committed to public health care and has echoed the shortage of health-care workers as a major challenge.
"We’ve got to recruit more doctors. That’s why we are tripling our recruitment of American health-care workers," Eby said at the leaders' debate, noting 800 U.S. workers have been hired so far.

The party said it will launch an accelerated training program for international medical graduates already living in B.C. and add 1,000 more training seats for nurses, nurse practitioners, allied health workers and care aides, including a 20 per cent increase in nursing seats.

items: B.C. NDP Leader David Eby talks Trump, Conservatives and LNG ahead of Oct. 24 election

blocks.text: B.C. NDP Leader David Eby's priorities include tripling the recruitment of U.S. health-care workers and creating regional surgical waitlists. (Nav Rahi/CBC)
The party is proposing new regional waitlists that offer patients the earliest surgery date possible in their region or, if they prefer, to still choose a specific surgeon or hospital.
Currently, surgery wait times can depend on the surgeon patients are referred to, the NDP said.

items: As Eby warns against health-care privatization, Conservatives say he's 'fearmongering'

blocks.text: Promises also include eight new MRI machines and 10 CT scanners, 20 additional team-based primary care clinics, and the opening of Canada’s first perinatal mental health unit at B.C. Women’s Hospital.
"We will pay for these actions by asking the top four per cent of earners in B.C. to pitch in a little bit more. Ninety-six per cent of people will see no change in their taxes," the party said.
B.C. Greens
The B.C. Green Party is pledging funding that establishes community health centres in every riding in the province.

"That would mean you could walk into your neighbourhood and you would have access to a physician, a nurse practitioner and imaging all under the same roof," said leader Emily Lowan at the leaders' debate.

items: How Emily Lowan’s B.C. Green Party plans to tackle affordability and the climate crisis simultaneously

blocks.text: B.C. Green Party Leader Emily Lowan has pledged funding for community health centres in every riding. (Nav Rahi/CBC)
The party’s platform online also includes increased funding for nurses in the public system to support safe nurse-to-patient ratios and end reliance on private agency nurses.
It also wants to centralize referrals for surgeries, and non-surgical and pre-surgical care rather than using distributed lists.
CentreBC
CentreBC has set a goal of providing a family doctor or nurse practitioner to anyone wanting one by the end of 2031.
Leader Elenore Sturko’s promises include 600 more nurse practitioner positions by 2030 and 100 more medical residency spots by the same year.

"A family doctor or nurse practitioner team for everyone who wants one, shorter waits that people can see for themselves, treatment for mental health and addiction when people ask for it. We are committed to public health care, not private pay," the party said in a statement to CBC News.

items: Elenore Sturko, CentreBC strive to give voters a centrist option in upcoming B.C. election

blocks.text: CentreBC Leader Elenore Sturko's promises include adding more nurse practitioners and doubling B.C.’s assessment program for internationally trained family doctors, (Ben Nelms/CBC)
The party wants to increase the assessment program for internationally trained family doctors, from 96 to 200 positions a year by 2028.
To help keep emergency rooms open, CentreBC is pitching an ER Accountability Act to cut unplanned closures in half by 2029/30 while allocating $25 million a year to stabilize rural ERs.

items: Rural emergency room closures put pressure on B.C. paramedics: union

blocks.text: Pledges also include the creation of a single public health dashboard showing surgeries, scans, specialists and ER statuses by hospital and region, five more MRI machines, and a new children’s hospital for Surrey and Langley with construction starting in 2031.
OneBC
OneBC is currently the only party platform listing support for private health care alongside fully-funded public health care.
The party wants to shift administration and HR spending to front-line employees.
It wants to repeal the Health Professions and Occupations Act (HPOA), which regulates health professions in B.C.

items: OneBC's Dallas Brodie aims to balance budget, repeal SOGI and unite the right in Oct. 24 election

blocks.text: OneBC says it would support private health care alongside fully-funded public health care. Leader Dallas Brodie is pictured. (Mike Zimmer/CBC)
OneBC says it also wants to adopt the findings of the Allison Inquiry into COVID-19 vaccine injuries to help shape B.C.’s vaccine protocols.
The inquiry, held in September by Conservative MP Dean Allison, did not hear from Health Canada and was unsanctioned by the federal government.
The inquiry's website says, "it will not make findings of fact or reach conclusions. The focus is to listen to Canadians."
Voters can have their say on health care in B.C. on Oct. 24.

items: What’s one issue you’d like to hear more about from the parties before election day? Click "Join the Conversation" below. On the app? Tap here.
