One effect is that the number of hot meals that are currently being provided by community kitchens will be cut from 250,000 to 150,000 each day.
Families living in hard-to-reach areas, for example near the so-called Yellow Line, which demarcates Israel's area of military control, will receive a meal every other day instead of daily.
Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million population remains displaced and two-thirds rely on food aid to survive.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mervat al-Satari, a mother-of-five, says the cuts are a "disaster"

blocks.text: Mervat al-Satari, a mother-of-five, says the cuts are a "disaster"

"It's a disaster! What will we do with these reduced rations? How will we provide for the little ones?" said Mervat al-Satari, a displaced Palestinian mother-of-five at a camp in the al-Mawasi area of Khan Younis after being told of the WFP's news. "Sometimes we wait for these meals to eat."

"This will affect us a lot. The daily aid was somehow ticking the box but now it will be every two days," said Sawsan Bahloul, who is also from al-Mawasi and is a mother of three. She added that the portions given by the community kitchen - usually pasta or lentils with occasional potatoes and aubergines - were already too small to feed her family.
The Palestine director for the WFP, Shaun Hughes, is clear that the cuts are being made because of finances, and "not because the needs are coming down, or because we don't have access - we do."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million people are displaced, with many living in camps like those in al-Mawasi

blocks.text: Nearly all of Gaza's 2.1 million people are displaced, with many living in camps like those in al-Mawasi

Already, since July, there have been reductions in cash transfers provided to some half a million people, meaning they have less money to buy food in local markets. The number of Gazans given bags of flour and ration boxes by the WFP will now fall from 1.1 million to 600,000 each month.

The WFP received less than half as much funding for its Palestinian operations in 2026 as in previous years. The agency says it urgently needs $450m (£338m) to maintain "critical" operations over the next six months.
Despite a ceasefire between Hamas and Israel that was agreed a year ago, humanitarian conditions in Gaza remain dire.

There has been no reconstruction and little recovery, with Israel tightly controlling the entry of goods through crossings. While food markets are now well stocked, few can afford to buy from them. More than 80% of people in Gaza are unemployed so most of the population relies on aid.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Two-thirds of the population relies on food aid to survive, according to UN-backed experts

blocks.text: Two-thirds of the population relies on food aid to survive, according to UN-backed experts
Families currently receiving the WFP food handouts complained to the BBC that already these were insufficient and gave them little diversity in their diets.

"The flour isn't enough and the food boxes aren't enough either," said Dalal al-Dahdouh, who is living in the ruins of her home in Gaza City with her family of eight. She fears the new cuts will have "a major impact".

The mother draws a contrast between the current desperate situation and life before the war. "In the past, thank God, we had our own home and a wonderful life. We had fresh vegetables, proper sanitation facilities and our own land," she said. "Now we live entirely on aid, including WFP vouchers."

There is no cooking gas available in Gaza because the Israeli government considers it a "dual use" item that could be used by Hamas for military purposes. Wood is expensive, so many families send their children into the street to find plastic and cardboard to burn as fuel to make bread or heat food.

"It's still a very concerning humanitarian situation, people living in brutal conditions, most people still without a proper home, living in tents, poor access to water and sanitation and healthcare," Hughes of the WFP told the BBC. "Cuts to food assistance are going to compound that hardship that families have been facing for three years now."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Families, including Sawsan Bahloul's, are forced to burn plastic and cardboard as fuel for cooking

blocks.text: Families, including Sawsan Bahloul's, are forced to burn plastic and cardboard as fuel for cooking
Humanitarian workers say that despite a modest improvement in Gaza compared to a year ago, acute food insecurity and the risk of famine returning continue to loom over the territory.

In July, the Integrated Phase Classification (IPC) - the world's foremost experts on food security - reported that two-thirds of the population - 1.4 million people - were "expected to face crisis or worse levels of acute food insecurity in July-December 2026".

For now, the WFP says it can continue supporting bakeries that provide one-third of Gaza's bread needs and provide nutritional assistance to about 300,000 women and children. It also delivers health food snacks to some 200,000 children.
In the occupied West Bank, the WFP is continuing to give assistance to some 200,000 Palestinians, having halved the number of recipients in September.
The agency says food insecurity is rising in the territory mostly due to increased Israeli settler violence and Palestinian displacement.

articles.title: What Earth's sixth mass extinction event means for humans
articles.summary: Human activity is driving plants and animals to extinction at an unprecedented rate. As countries meet in Armenia to discuss ways to reverse nature loss, DW reveals how declining biodiversity is…

image.caption: From tiny bees to big whales, all of the players on nature's team are essentialImage: Yonhap News/IMAGO

blocks.text: From the tiniest microbes in the human gut to giant whales in the ocean, biodiversity is the sum of all life on the planet. It's another word for nature. And because nature is like a team, every player has a job.

When various species from trees to animals work together, they regulate weather, maintain soil health, purify water and support food production. These benefits are known as ecosystem services and they underpin human wellbeing.

"It is really an abstract concept, but we experience it absolutely every day," said Rebecca Shaw, chief scientist at conservation group WWF "And we almost never think about it when nature is functioning."

blocks.caption: Without biodiversity, the variety of food humans eat would not be available. Declining biodiversity is endangering crop productionImage: Burak Kara/Getty Images

blocks.text: But as it declines, she and other scientists are calling on the world to really think about it. Because biodiversity is struggling as humans push ecosystems to the brink through intensive farming, burning fossil fuels,and pollution from sources like plastic and chemicals.

Over the past 52 years, monitored vertebrate populations have collapsed by an average of 73%, while freshwater ecosystems are faring worst with a drop of 85%, according to WWF's recent Living Planet report.
It tallies with other studies that show a million animal and plant species face extinction unless humanity reduces its pressure on nature.

"It is a really steep decline," said Shaw. "What it's telling us is that nature is in trouble, and it's an early warning indicator of the fabric of life that we depend on for freshwater and food and for clean air is unravelling."

blocks.caption: Deforestation directly drives biodiversity decline because forests are home to more than 80% of all land-based speciesImage: Juancho Torres/AA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Thousands of policymakers, business leaders and civil society groups are meeting in Yerevan, Armenia over the next two weeks for COP17, the latest UN biodiversity summit, to advance commitments to reverse nature loss by 2030. But progress towards those targets remains insufficient, with funding and implementation among the biggest challenges.
What happens when ecosystem services decline or disappear?

Take wetlands as an example. Some 85% of these vital ecosystems disappeared between 1700 and 2000. One study from Canada's University of Waterloo found that habitats like marshes and swamps in Southern Ontario provide C$4.2 billion (€2.63 billion) worth of water filtration services each year, removing nutrients like phosphorus and keeping drinking water sources clean.
The study found that as they disappear, water quality worsens, which massively increases the cost of treating it.
Another example is the decline in pollinators like bees and bats. More than 75% of global food crop types rely in part on animal pollination.
Why climate change is driving species loss

At the same time, soil and ecosystem degradation coupled with storms and heat waves linked to climate change are already damaging harvests. A recent UK government report stated that every critical ecosystem is on a "pathway to collapse," warning that nature's decline posed a grave threat to global food supply and geopolitical stability.

"The UK, like many other countries, relies on imports for much of the food and so is reliant on ecosystems around the world," said Louise McRae, a research fellow at the Zoological Society of London, who also contributed to WWF's Living Planet report. "This is why we need to care about global biodiversity."
It also provides the basis for many modern human medicines, with some 50% coming from natural compounds.

blocks.caption: Poisonous frogs could be a source for new medications but as species disappear we could be missing out on novel drugsImage: Al Carrera/Zoonar/picture alliance

blocks.text: Penicillin, the first antibiotic, is produced by a mold and is estimated to have saved over 500 million lives. Before its discovery, a person could die from a simple cut. Around 70% of cancer drugs come from natural products or synthetic compounds "inspired by nature," according to the World Health Organisation (WHO).
As biodiversity disappears, humans risk losing access to undiscovered treatments.
Does it really matter if one species disappears?

To return to the "nature as a team" metaphor, if a player disappears, sometimes a species with similar functions in the ecosystem can jump in as a substitute. But not always, particularly if it's a "keystone species." They play a disproportionately large role in their environments, and their disappearance has significant knock-on effects.
The oyster is one such species. Wild oyster populations are facing massive declines, while 85% of their reefs have been lost worldwide. An adult oyster filters up to 50 gallons of water a day.

"No one would ever think, they did anything but sit in a shell and be slimy," said Shaw. "But you lose oysters, you can lose water filtration and clean water, you can lose the habitat for many other species that we interact with or sometimes consume."

blocks.caption: People around the world rely on oysters and other marine life for their livelihoods and as a food source. Oysters are also a keystone speciesImage: Misper Apawu/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: And, said Shaw, the humble oyster protects coastal communities from storm surges. If you lose it "you lose the coastal protection."

The loss of a single species can also lead to more disease. One study suggests a decline in red foxes in North America is linked to the spread of Lyme disease, a tick-borne illness that also impacts humans.
Is humanity living through a sixth mass extinction and is it too late to prevent it?

The planet has experienced five mass extinctions when a large proportion of species globally disappeared over a short geological period. Extinction is a natural process. But the rate at which species are disappearing today, suggests Earth is experiencing a sixth event, driven largely by human activity, according to scientists.
Both McRae and Shaw called the declines extremely worrying, but said they shouldn't provoke despair.

Though she acknowledges that the underlying global trend is moving in the wrong direction and cannot be ignored, McRae says "the statistics are there to just motivate us to action rather than to cause alarm."
And the Living Planet report also highlights conservation successes, showing that nature can recover.

The number of green sea turtles, for example, had fallen significantly, but has now bounced back. This is thanks to a massive worldwide effort to protect nesting beaches and changes to fishing practices that reduce accidental capture.

blocks.caption: Since sea otters on the North American Pacific Coast have rebounded, so too have kelp forestsImage: Malcolm Schuyl/FLPA/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: Sea otters are another example. Prized for their fur, in the 1800s they were hunted to near extinction on the US Pacific Coast. When they disappeared, it meant sea urchins had no predators, leaving them free to decimate kelp forests.

That matters because as well as providing habitat for other species, these giant underwater groves protect coastlines from storm surges and absorb carbon, making them important for climate protection.
Following a ban on commercial hunting, sea otters have also rebounded, helping kelp forests recover.

"You can see that ripple effect that really had an obvious and a measurable impact. But critically, it can be reversed," said McRae, adding that biodiversity loss and climate change are intertwined and exacerbate each other but have joint solutions.
"We're learning how to turn things around at very small scales," said Shaw. "Now the real challenge is to turn things around at very big scale so we can see it in the global indicators."
Baltic seagrass: restoring a secret climate ally

articles.title: ‘This is not poker’: Alberta goes to polls in referendum that has exposed divisions, not least among separatists
articles.summary:
Voters to be asked whether province should remain part of Canada or hold second binding independence vote

Albertans are going to the polls to decide their place in Canada, in a referendum…

blocks.text: Albertans are going to the polls to decide their place in Canada, in a referendum that has exposed deep divisions within the province, not least in the separatist movement itself.
On Monday, voters will respond to the question of whether Alberta should remain in Canada, or hold a second binding independence referendum.

A minority have long argued that separation is the only way to address their belief that Alberta is short-changed by its financial relationship with Ottawa, and prevented from fully exploiting the province’s vast fossil fuel reserves.

Any enthusiasm either side might have held headed into the referendum was muted after a deadly fire broke out at a major military base in the province. On Saturday afternoon, a blaze tore through the CFB Wainwright and into the nearby town. Canada’s armed forces announced with “profound sadness” that there had been multiple deaths and injuries.
The premier of Alberta, Danielle Smith, argued for years that a referendum was not needed, but called one anyway after pressure from some within her United Conservative party.

blocks.caption: Alberta’s premier, Danielle Smith, called a referendum after pressure from some within her United Conservative party. Photograph: Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press/AP

blocks.text: Nevertheless, Smith did not campaign in favour of independence, saying in June she estimated the cost of separating at about C$400bn (£212bn) for the transition and another $25bn-$50bn in annual costs associated with starting a new country. Smith’s caution prompted some of her supporters to accuse her of betraying the independence movement.

Opponents of independence have focused heavily on the costs of separation, with the University of Calgary’s school of public policy saying in June it could be up to $170bn over a five-year period and be highly unpredictable in the long term.

The issue has not divided neatly along partisan lines. The former premiers Jason Kenney and Rachel Notley – from the rightwing Conservative and leftwing New Democratic party – have appeared on stage together, setting aside a bitter ideological rivalry that more usually defines Albertan politics.
Mark Carney, who grew up in the province, visited both Calgary and Edmonton last week to campaign for a united Canada.

“At this pivotal moment, Albertans have a choice: to build a stronger Alberta and a greater Canada to leave for our children, or to burden them with years of deep division and great uncertainty,” the prime minister told a raucous crowd.
Carney, who previously served as the governor of the Bank of England, saw first-hand the effects of the Brexit vote and the economic upheaval that followed.

“This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities,” he said. “Our country and your futures are too precious to play games with.”

blocks.caption: Mark Carney, who grew up in the province, visited both Calgary and Edmonton last week to campaign for a united Canada. Photograph: Megan Albu/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Carney, whom recent polls identify as the most popular politician in Alberta, joined the former deputy premier of Alberta Thomas Lukaszuk at a rally for the latter’s Forever Canadian group. Lukaszuk has driven more than 40,000km (24,855 miles) around Alberta in a 1992 motorhome named the Unity Bus and distributed at least 100,000 lawn signs.

Rather than campaigning frequently, Carney has pointed to big projects his government is looking to move ahead with that would benefit the province, including a pipeline to the Pacific coast to increase the flow of Alberta crude oil to Asia.
“I won’t sugar-coat it: some of those threads have needed to be repaired. The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” said Carney.

Energy policy has long been at the heart of Alberta’s grievance with Ottawa, stemming from the 1980 national energy programme, which sought greater federal control over the energy sector, provoked fierce opposition in Alberta and helped erode Liberal support across western Canada. The sense that the province’s wealth was being siphoned eastward is older still: a 1915 cartoon, “The Milch Cow”, depicted Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba as farmers feeding a cow whose milk was funnelled into buckets labelled Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal.

“Growing up, I remember. I remember how Ottawa made Albertans feel like our resources weren’t our own,” Carney told the crowd. “And more recently, we were made to feel that our energy contributions were running against the tides of history.”

blocks.caption: Energy policy has long been at the heart of Alberta’s grievance with Ottawa. Photograph: Jeff McIntosh/AP

blocks.text: The movement seeking to capitalise on those grievances, however, has been marked by competing interests, personal rivalries and allegations surrounding some of its leading figures. Jeff Rath, a bombastic lawyer linked to the Alberta Prosperity Project, is alleged to have mismanaged millions of dollars of First Nations trust funds, while David Parker, a longtime rightwing political organiser, was at the centre of a voter-data scandal that exposed the personal information of nearly 3 million Albertans and remains under investigation.

Keith Wilson, one of the principal intellectual and legal architects of the province’s modern separatist movement, recently published the Alberta transition plan, a 214-page blueprint for turning it into an independent country.

Rejecting comparisons to Brexit and the economic fallout, Wilson said: “Every single thing we found that needs to be addressed to do the transition is absolutely doable,” calling most of the tasks “super easy”.
Wilson dismissed the idea that negotiations between an independent Alberta and Canada’s federal government would be acrimonious and lengthy.

“It would be economic suicide for them to challenge Alberta,” he said. “You want to cut off trade with us? OK. By the way, go buy axes and chainsaws because you’re going to have to cut down all the maple trees to keep warm this winter because you’re not going to get our energy products.”

Even within the separatist camp, there are doubts about how quickly independence could be achieved. Bill Jones, a member of the Wildrose Independence party, said its leaders were moving too quickly without the institutions a new country would need, from a police force to a pension system.
“We – Alberta – were always meant to be a colony, to get resources that were here to go east,” said Jones. “And that mindset is still there.”
“I don’t see the evidence for our independence. If we go out today, we’d be a failed state for generations. The great-great-grandchildren would be still suffering. And that’s the problem.”
Monday’s referendum will also include nine other measures unrelated to separation, including proposals affecting social programmes, judicial appointments and the senate.

One remain campaign has distributed thousands of “no to the nine” lawn signs around the province. Even some separatists, angry at Smith, have started a “decline the 9” campaign. Smith, for her part, has pushed a “yes to the rest” message in response.
In Calgary, the city’s mayor said he was “duty bound” to speak out about the perils of an attempt to fracture the country.

“There will be catastrophic impacts that would arise from separation,” said Jeromy Farkas. “And the unfortunate bullshit implication of separation is that it’s invited a conversation about who is a ‘real Canadian’? Who is a ‘real Albertan’? If you are living here in Calgary, you are welcome here. We need to continue to signal that. We need to telegraph that stability.
“We stand to lose so much from simply even having this debate.”

In October, further details emerged about meetings between unelected Alberta separatists and both Republican operatives and staff at the US state department. Among items allegedly discussed were how oil royalties could be directed to the US in exchange for assistance establishing a new country. They also allegedly offered up Alberta’s fresh water resources.

No matter the results on Monday, the referendum could have looked far different if not for the intervention of First Nations, which successfully sued to force the Alberta government to either dismiss the question of separation or change the wording. Key to their argument was the fact that the land of modern-day Alberta is covered by five treaties signed with the crown before the creation of the province.

blocks.caption: Protesters highlight concerns about Indigenous treaty rights and the broader implications of Alberta’s separation. Photograph: NurPhoto/Getty Images

blocks.text: The president of the Blackfoot Confederacy, Chief Troy “Bossman” Knowlton, said: “These treaties are living documents, but the ignorance of the separatists, and their bigotry, does not allow their mind to accept the fact that they’re not symbolic documents. They have power, and the reality is Alberta does not have the constitutional right to separate.”

Knowlton said that if separatists had proactively reached out to First Nations before pushing ahead with independence, it might have led to a different outcome. “But they treated us as a speed bump they could just drive over.”

He added that the First Nations’ legal victory was followed by what he viewed as recriminations from the province, including an unexplained halt to talks on land claims and cooperation with Alberta’s government.

“At the end of the day, we want Alberta to continue to be a beacon of light,” he said. “Because when the first newcomers came to these lands centuries ago, that’s what our chiefs said: we’ll share these resources we have here. So do we want prosperity for Alberta? You’d better believe it.”

articles.title: Amelia Earhart researchers leave remote atoll empty-handed after ‘plane debris’ found to be a clump of trees
articles.summary:
Expedition was drawn to Nikumaroro after spotting what was described as a metallic glint in waters off uninhabited island

A US expedition that voyaged to a remote Pacific island in the hope…

blocks.text: A US expedition that voyaged to a remote Pacific island in the hope of solving the mystery of what happened to pioneering pilot Amelia Earhart has said an object they suspected to be her plane was a clump of washed-up trees.

“Unfortunately, we weren’t able to find that smoking gun,” said Steve Schultz of Purdue University, standing on the sand in front of a blue lagoon on the atoll of Nikumaroro, about halfway between Australia and Hawaii.

Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan vanished in 1937 during their attempt to circumnavigate the globe at the equator, leading to one of the largest air and sea searches in history. Nearly 90 years later, people are still looking, with Nikumaroro in the archipelago country of Kiribati emerging as a leading candidate for where they might have crash-landed.

Previous visits to the uninhabited atoll have found signs of a castaway camp, a 1930s-era woman’s shoe and other tantalising evidence attributed to the celebrity aviator, including glass from a cosmetics freckle cream jar.
The latest mission stemmed from 2020 satellite images showing an elongated, white object lying in the shallows of the island, near a sandy outcrop called the Taraia Peninsula.

Other longtime Earhart explorers quickly identified it as a fallen tree, but Richard Pettigrew, who heads the nonprofit Archaeological Legacy Institute, found other images, including aerial video showing what he suspected to be a metallic glint in the water.

After a multi-day voyage by ship and subsequent delays due to bad weather, the 17-person expedition managed to pass through the coral-encircled atoll and set up tents to conduct four days of research, including metal detecting. The crew was forced to sleep offshore, partly due to massive land-dwelling coconut crabs, known as “robber crabs” for their inquisitiveness when searching for food.
By Monday, Purdue University confirmed in a statement that the “visual anomaly” was “likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula’s sandspit”.

It said the glint was part of a natural process. “The fragment’s reflective surface, long associated with the idea that the object was a metallic substance, was due to its carbonate veneer. Other items found by the team were similarly coated with a shiny concretized amalgam of coral sand.”

The trip was partially sponsored by the university in Indiana, where Earhart once taught and mentored young female pilots, and which helped fund her modified Lockheed Electra 10-E, known as her “flying laboratory”.

“While we know this is disappointing to many, including us, this mission adds a new chapter in the quest to find the ultimate answer to the mystery of what happened to Earhart during her attempt to circumnavigate the globe nearly nine decades ago,” the university statement said.

The trip adds to a growing list of dismissed hypotheses, including that Earhart – who was the first woman to make a nonstop solo transatlantic flight – was captured by Japanese forces or that she survived and lived under an alias.

articles.title: Kenya pastor accused of ordering parents to starve their children to death faces verdict
articles.summary: Prosecutors say Paul Mackenzie lured the latest victims to their deaths by writing notes from his prison cell.

blocks.text: A Kenyan court is set to deliver a judgement in a mass murder case involving doomsday preacher Paul Mackenzie.
Mackenzie and 29 of his followers are being charged with the murder of 191 children.
His cult is alleged to have forced children to starve to death so that they could "meet Jesus". His doomsday doctrine said that education was forbidden and modern medicine was considered "evil".
Mackenzie and the 29 others have all pleaded not guilty to murder, repeatedly insisting that nobody was forced to die.
Mackenzie's former head of security, Enos Amanya Ngala, was initially accused but then entered a plea deal and became a witness for the prosecution.
Mackenzie and other leaders of the cult are facing a raft of other legal cases, including for terrorism, radicalisation and denying education to children.
But this is the first time the pastor will face a verdict on the most serious charges of murder.
Authorities said over 400 bodies were found in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast, where Mackenzie led his followers from across the country.
Seventeen men were hired from the nearby town for the horrifying task of digging up the shallow graves. Some were paid just $8 (£6) a day.
"Every grave we found had at least three bodies," James, one of the gravediggers, told the BBC. "Some of the remains were of children as young as a few weeks old."
"We once found 12 bodies of children in a line inside a grave. It was massive, the bodies were arranged like clothes. One on top of another."
Gravediggers described some of the bodies of children as having had their "hands and legs tied and bodies wrapped in bedsheets".
Mackenzie's son, Dan Paul Mackenzie, said he worked as a cameraperson in the church. "The children would sit at the back, adults in the middle, and everyone would sing worship songs all morning."
The pastor would start his fiery sermons at noon, some of which included "casting out demons".
The main church shut down in 2019 and Paul Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.

Peter Shukrani, 23, says his mother relocated to Shakahola with him at the time. He started going to Mackenzie's church when he was eight years old and described him as his "spiritual father", adding that he would "never say a bad word about him".
When in the forest, Shukrani fell ill and his condition deteriorated because medication was banned.
"My mother would throw away all the medicine I was supposed to take because she believe that only God could heal me," Shukrani said.
The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest. "We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," Shukrani said.

By March 2023 when the first remains were discovered by local herders, hundreds of people had died. "We would carry someone out of the forest but they were so frail that they would die in our arms," explained Salim Karisa, one of the gravediggers.
Shukrani was one of the men rescued from the forest in March 2023.
He was ill and bed-ridden for weeks until that point, but his condition worsened because his mother would throw away all the medication he needed to recover.
"My mother believed Pastor Mackenzie's doctrine that medicine was evil," Shukrani said.
"I would have died if I wasn't rescued from Shakahola forest."
In the 298 pages detailing the charges against him in the current case, all of the 191 victims Mackenzie and his followers are accused of murdering are children.
Many of the bodies are still unidentified, owing to their advanced state of decomposition.
In the court documents, several are referred to as "unknown male child" and identified by the location of their grave and date of their discovery.

Despite the suffering endured by Mackenzie's followers, men, women and children who died due to starvation, strangulation and even being bludgeoned to death, as well as his own suffering, Shukrani believes Mackenzie was "a good person who cares for me".
"Mackenzie didn't force anyone to fast. People made those choices by themselves because of their beliefs," Shukrani said.
"I still love him and he is still my pastor."
In contrast Dan Mackenzie believes his father should be found guilty of murder.
"He was the leader, he was someone who they were looking [up to]. So he is a murderer of mass killing."

articles.title: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff survives shooting in Mumbai
articles.summary: Video published by several news outlets shows gunmen firing multiple shots at a car while it is moving past a crowd.

blocks.text: Bollywood actor Tiger Shroff has survived a shooting in Mumbai and has not sustained any gunshot wounds, according to Indian police who are investigating the incident.
The 36-year-old was shot at on Sunday evening, while he was in a car that was leaving a football club in the suburb of Juhu.
Several news outlets have published a video showing at least two gunmen firing multiple shots at close range at the front passenger seat of a car while it is slowly moving past a crowd.
The incident has heightened concern about the safety of public figures in India, with some killed or injured in targeted attacks in recent years.
"These attempts to intimidate people will not be tolerated, and we will put an end to this hooliganism," said Eknath Shinde, deputy chief minister of Maharashtra state, where Mumbai is located.
He paid a visit to Shroff after the shooting on Sunday evening, and said the actor and his mother had been left "shaken" by the attack.
Police said two people were injured in the shooting, including Shroff's driver, local media reported.
This is the latest in a string of attacks on some of the country's biggest public figures in recent years.
In 2024, police in India arrested two members of a criminal gang for a gun attack targeting the home of Bollywood actor Salman Khan.
That same year, influential Indian politician Baba Siddique was shot dead in Mumbai.
The son of two actors, Tiger Shroff made his acting debut in 2014 with the romance film Heropanti and went on to star in several films.
He is also a football enthusiast who plays for the professional football club Mumbay FC.

articles.title: Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going
articles.summary: The US president blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect.

blocks.text: US President Donald Trump has said his decision to suspend several Russian sanctions is an effort to keep Moscow at the negotiating table.

"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine," Trump said on his Truth Social messaging platform, adding that he didn't want to "do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table".
Trump blocked numerous sanctions on Russia two days before they were due to take effect, as a row with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky deepened.
Zelensky told NBC News on Sunday that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake".

Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev has responded to Trump's order by calling it "an important and truly historic moment", and saying the sanctions would have inflicted "serious damage" on the US and global market.
Trump also claimed in his Truth Social post that Zelensky "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did", adding "he could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now".
Zelensky has pushed for an end to fighting, and has repeatedly said that Putin doesn't want peace, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Relations between Washington and Kyiv frayed after the US struck a controversial deal to import Russian diesel last week. Ukraine has accused the Trump administration of withdrawing key military support.
Since then, Zelensky declared it was nice to be among "real leaders" while addressing a European Union summit, after Trump said Zelensky was "more difficult to deal with" than Putin.

articles.title: Guardian reporter filmed masked militants seconds before West Bank attack on French mayor
articles.summary:
New video footage of Israeli settler assault on European delegation as Netanyahu attempts to raise doubt

Hours after

blocks.text: Hours after Israeli militants attacked a delegation of European diplomats, French clerics and a visiting mayor in the occupied West Bank, Israel’s leader, Benjamin Netanyahu, responded by questioning the delegation’s account of the assault.

“Serious accusations require serious evidence” was the all-caps headline of a social media post from the office of the prime minister. As news of the attack spread globally there was no pledge to find those accountable and bring them to justice.

Instead Netanyahu’s team dismissed video of Bernard Baudoux, the mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, on the ground grimacing in pain and shock, photos of the smashed window of a diplomatic car, and footage of masked men threatening diplomats and activists with sticks.
“These images alone do not establish the complete sequence of events or individual responsibility,” the statement said, warning of “concerns about a coordinated campaign to smear Israel”.

The prime minister’s office went on to cast doubt on the integrity of senior French, Belgian and Polish diplomats in Jerusalem and clergy from the Catholic church who witnessed and reported the attack.

“We call on the public and responsible journalists to demand verifiable evidence, reject hearsay and refuse to turn unproven allegations into a collective indictment of the Jewish residents of Judea and Samaria [the occupied West Bank],” it said.

Footage below filmed by the Guardian (no audio) shows the moments before Israeli settlers attacked the French mayor Bernard Baudoux, who was in the Palestinian town of Taybeh with a delegation of European diplomats. A second clip shows the immediate aftermath of the attack. The final section shows one group of settlers attacking the car carrying Baudoux and others.
Verifying the details of attacks can be painstaking journalistic work, seeking out eyewitness accounts, photos and videos for confirmation.

But this weekend the Guardian was in Taybeh, and witnessed the masked militants speeding up a hill in order to attack diplomats and French visitors who had spent a morning peacefully harvesting olives with Palestinians who own the groves.

Shortly after 1pm, they were warned that settlers had attacked Palestinians harvesting olives nearby. Keen to avoid confrontation, the group decided to leave and were approaching their vehicles as the militants closed in, masked, menacing and brandishing sticks.

The Guardian filmed the moments before Baudoux was assaulted, showing him approaching an SUV with his wife and Vincent Dollmann, the archbishop of Cambrai, escorted by diplomatic security. Our vehicle pulled away, making room for the two parked by the road to follow.
Moments later the settlers attacked, apparently determined not only to force the foreigners to flee but to extract a price for joining Palestinians on their land.

It was clear the group contained foreign dignitaries because the cars had diplomatic plates, and Baudoux was apparently targeted for his nationality, because he was wearing his mayor’s sash of office. One of the attackers aggressively shouted “France, France” before pushing him to the ground, eyewitnesses said.

Metadata from that video shows there were just 22 seconds between the last shot of Baudoux remonstrating with his attackers and footage of him slumped on the ground taken by activists in the second car.
The embassy security team then helped him into the vehicle but the attack continued as they drove off. Footage filmed from the hillside opposite shows the settlers attacking the SUV as pulls away.

The force of their blows smashed one of the reinforced windows at the back of the car, which can be seen intact in the first video. A photo of the crumpled pane taken minutes later in the relative safety of Taybeh shows the force of the impact.
If the militant settlers had broken one of the windows next to the passengers, it is unlikely those inside would have escaped injuries.

blocks.caption: Former Israeli ambassadors and employees demonstrated outside the foreign ministry, demanding the prime minister and his government ‘Stop Jewish Terrorism. It’s in your hands’. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: Israeli authorities have repeatedly attempted to obfuscate details of attacks on Palestinians and undermine survivor or witness accounts.
For the prime minister to deploy the same tactics on senior diplomats from European allies – however strained their current relationship – marks a new embrace of isolationist extremism.

A day earlier the American photojournalist Heidi Levine was hospitalised after a brutal attack by Israeli militants blocking the Palestinian olive harvest in another village. Netanyahu’s office described it as an “alleged assault” and a “disputed incident” adding “the facts … remain unclear and are under investigation”.
The message from the very top of Israel’s government, that the state was reluctant to impose consequences or seek justice for that attack, may have emboldened the attackers on Saturday.

blocks.caption: The protest outside the foreign ministry in Jerusalem drew a response from conservative passersby. Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The Guardian

blocks.text: There was one unprecedented response in Jerusalem, however. On Sunday, more than a dozen of Israel’s top former diplomats gathered outside the foreign ministry where they had all worked for decades for an unprecedented protest.

Two former directors general, one deputy director general and a host of ambassadors held up signs calling for action on the campaign of terror by Israelis against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.
“Bibi [Netanyahu], foreign minister [Gideon] Sa’ar. Stop Jewish Terrorism. It’s in your hands,” read one banner.

articles.title: France: Young voters blase about Glucksmann's Socialists
articles.summary: Raphael Glucksmann wants to lead France's Socialists to power without working with the left-populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, who is particularly popular with young voters. How can the center-left…

image.caption: Glucksmann has a difficult campaign ahead as the Socialist candidateImage: Raphael Lafargue/abaca/picture alliance

blocks.text: The historically working-class Parisian neighborhood of Belleville has gentrified in recent years. It was here that Raphael Glucksmann, a member of the European Parliament for France's center-left Socialists, celebrated his victory in the party's presidential primary on October 11.

Two rounds of voting had been anticipated, but the 46-year-old son of philosopher and essayist Andre Glucksmann triumphed in the first round with a convincing 66% of the vote and will be the Socialist candidate in France's 2027 presidential election.

As he left the Cantine de Belleville restaurant, Glucksmann was flour-bombed by an unidentified assailant. The following morning, he called on his rival, the left-wing French populist Jean-Luc Melenchon, to condemn attacks carried out by his supporters, though it is not clear that the attacker was indeed a supporter of Melenchon's La France Insoumise (LFI).
The incident has highlighted the issue set to dog Glucksmann's presidential candidacy over the coming weeks: How can he win over Melenchon's supporters if he refuses to work with their candidate?

blocks.caption: Glucksmann was flour-bombed while leaving his victory celebrationImage: Raphael Lafargue/abaca/picture alliance

blocks.text: Gluckmann's rapid rise

"Where do you stand on Melenchon?" That was the question that dominated much of the Socialists' primary campaign. Party leader Olivier Faure spoke in favor of leaving the door open for cooperation with the LFI, but Glucksmann called for a clear break with the far left. His decisive victory is therefore also seen as a vote in favor of a clear demarcation.

The other primary candidates questioned Glucksmann's political experience. Segolene Royal, a previous presidential candidate, compared his bid for the Elysee with that of an "intern" wanting to take charge of a company. She said Glucksmann had no experience in government or even running a local authority.

Despite Glucksmann's victory in the primary, his starting position is a difficult one. A poll by Toluna Harris Interactive, published the day after his win, projects that he would win 10–11% of the vote. The same poll put Melenchon on 18%, meaning the far-left man would be much more likely to reach the runoff. But the survey was conducted before Glucksmann won the primary, and so does not take into account any potential boost the nomination may give him. Still, 10% would be an improvement on the Socialists' performance in the last presidential election in 2022, when their candidate Anne Hidalgo won just 1.75% of the national vote.

There is also the complication that the Socialists are banking on a man who is not even a party member to lead them from irrelevance. Raphael Glucksmann actually belongs to a small center-left party called Place Publique.
France students demand better schools
Melenchon's youth appeal

Glucksmann has his work cut out for him — especially with young people. In an Ipsos survey in September, which posited Glucksmann as the social-democratic candidate and Edouard Philippe as the only candidate from the political center, Melenchon scored 41% among the under-25s. Meanwhile, 20% of this age group supported the far-right nationalist Marine Le Pen. France's young electorate is politically divided, but Melenchon still dominates on the left.

The 75-year-old is currently rallying alongside the students whose protests have drawn international attention. At a rally near Clermont-Ferrand in central France , he expressed solidarity with their movement and reiterated his calls for lowering the voting age to 16 and abolishing Parcoursup, France's national admissions procedure for higher education.

In an analysis for the Fondation Jean-Jaures, a Socialist-aligned think tank, the political scientist Antoine Bristielle distinguishes between a core group of committed LFI voters and the broader left. Melenchon's most loyal supporters, he says, are often young, educated city-dwellers, and many are under a lot of financial pressure. Four in ten households in this group live on a net monthly income of less than €2,000 ($2,200).

Bristielle estimates that just under a third of the left-wing electorate in his study care more about a left-wing victory than their allegiance to any particular party. Almost half of the people in this group are younger than 35, and would consider voting for the Socialists, the Greens, or LFI. Redistribution and an active government are important to them, but most would prefer politicians who are willing to compromise.

blocks.caption: Melenchon in Paris during a public sector strike on September 29Image: Tom Nicholson/REUTERS

blocks.text: Glucksmann's youth efforts

The pattern recently observed in Germany, where young women are more likely to vote for the left and young men for the right, does not apply in France. Political scientists Anja Durovic, Nonna Mayer and Noemie Piolat found that in the 2024 European and parliamentary elections, young French women were not significantly more likely to vote for the left, or less likely to vote for the far right, than men of the same age. It remains to be seen whether this pattern will be replicated in the 2027 presidential election.

Glucksmann says he would ease the burden on earned income by reducing France's CSG social security tax while increasing taxes on inheritances worth more than €2 million. He also presents himself as a committed supporter of European integration, while Melenchon has called the EU a neoliberal institution. Glucksmann's political profile combines social policy demands with foreign policy positions that could also appeal to voters from the camp of the current president, Emmanuel Macron.

France's Ukraine policy is one such issue. Glucksmann favors decisive support for Kyiv. Manon Aubry, a member of the European Parliament for Melenchon's LFI, says her party supports military assistance only under certain conditions, namely: The provision of aid to Ukraine must first be subject to democratic debate; it must not enable attacks deep inside Russian territory; and it must not weaken France's own defense capabilities. In 2024, LFI MPs voted against the French–Ukrainian security agreement.

The tension between the parties of the left was once again apparent in the aftermath of the flour attack in Belleville. The LFI MP Sebastien Delogu posted a declaration of support on X for the taxi driver who was going to have to clean his car.

Glucksmann must win over a lot of voters from Melenchon's camp if he is to have a chance of winning the presidency. This is likely to prove a much more difficult task than simply distancing himself from Melenchon.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV thanks wellwishers in first event after cancer surgery
articles.summary: The Pope's first event since his lung cancer diagnosis and surgery saw him recite the traditional Angelus prayer from the balcony of the Apostolic Palace.

blocks.text: Pope Leo XIV held his first public engagement since his lung cancer surgery on Sunday, as he recited the Angelus prayer from the window of Vatican's Apostolic Palace.
The surgery had taken place just a few days before, after Pope Leo had been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer.
After the prayer, he thanked the people who have prayed for him in recent days and said he appreciated the support. He added he will now gradually return to his commitments as he recovers.

articles.title: Parisians wake up to protest damage and looted shops
articles.summary: Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against conditions in schools and the cost of living.

blocks.text: Violence broke out across France on Saturday during the latest day of demonstrations against conditions in schools and the cost of living.
At least 1,200 people were arrested during what the French government described as an "escalation in violence", as shopfronts were smashed and stores looted.
For shop owners, this morning marks the start of clean-up efforts, with some reporting damages and stolen goods amount to €100,000 (£85,000).
The BBC's James Waterhouse reports from the streets of Paris outside damaged buildings.

articles.title: Is Germany's eight-hour workday under threat?
articles.summary: Would you work 12 hours straight? The CDU/CSU and SPD are locked in a dispute over reforms to the Working Hours Act. Workplace flexibility, collective bargaining agreements and worker protection…

image.caption: Leuna, in Saxony-Anhalt, has become one of Germany's major hubs for the chemical industry and oil refineriesImage: Annegret Hilse/REUTERS

blocks.text: The town of Leuna, in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt, is one of the country's largest chemical industry hub, where more than 100 companies have established operations. Among them is the Finnish biotechnology group UPM, which has recently built a biorefinery for wood-based chemicals in Leuna. It's now hiring.

One of the job listings is for a chemical technician to oversee the rollout of new facilities. But to qualify, candidates must be willing to work 12-hour shifts. Is that legal? According to German law, standard working hours are limited to eight hours per day. It is permissible to extend this to ten hours, provided that workers receive compensatory time off for the overtime, and there must be at least 11 hours of rest between two shifts.
Twelve-hour shifts? What German law permits
Business associations and the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) parties have long called for these rules to be made more flexible.

Rainer Dulger, president of the Confederation of German Employers' Associations (BDA), points to the European Working Time Directive, which allows for a maximum weekly working time of 48 hours. "The allowance is being taken advantage of almost everywhere else — except here," Dulger told the dpa news agency in August.

Companies say they often find the existing rules too rigid, particularly in industries with seasonal fluctuations — such as tourism — or in project-based work, or during irregular peaks in workload, such as in the restaurant industry. They could deploy their staff more efficiently, says Dulger: "The Working Hours Act dates back to the era of fax machines and rotary-dial phones. It knows nothing of laptops or daycare hours."
4-day workweek: A model for the future?
CDU and SPD divided on working hours

In their 2025 coalition agreement, the CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) agreed to reform the Working Hours Act. "In keeping with the European Working Time Directive, we want to allow for a maximum weekly rather than daily working time — also and especially to promote a better work-life balance," the agreement said.

The SPD would have preferred to leave the law unchanged, but had to accept the conservative parties' plans. The Social Democrats pointed out that longer working hours are already permitted in exceptional cases, such as in emergency services, the health care sector and security services. Workers in power plants, refineries and the chemical industry are also allowed to work up to 12 hours at a time.
A surprise for Chancellor Friedrich Merz

Even Chancellor Friedrich Merz himself seemed unaware of this exception until quite recently. After visiting the UPM refinery in Leuna in September, he recounted to business leaders at the German Employers' Day in Berlin that he was "completely surprised" to learn that the facilities operate on a continuous 12-hour shift schedule, thanks to the approval of the works council.

Merz recounted the shift supervisor describing the work schedule as "really great" — with three-day work weeks. "He said we have plenty of time for our families — it's a great way to organize things." Merz went on to conclude that this demonstrates the benefits of relaxing the Working Hours Act.

"Working more than eight hours is not exploitation. Rather, it can be a good opportunity to organize working hours more flexibly — both for businesses and for the people working there," the chancellor said. "We should do it."
SPD agrees to longer working hours, but with conditions

But there is resistance from within the SPD and from trade unions opposed to amending the Working Hours Act. The trade union Verdi argues that significantly longer workdays would have negative consequences for employees' health and would disadvantage people with family and caregiving responsibilities. In certain industries, employees could also be put under pressure to accept longer shifts.
An initial reform draft was drawn up in June 2026 by the Labor and Social Affairs Ministry, headed at the time by Bärbel Bas, an SPD politician who has since resigned for personal reasons.

The draft includes some conditions, including a collective bargaining agreement between employers and unions if any schedule changes were made, as well as health and safety regulations, and working hours to be tracked electronically.

blocks.caption: Bärbel Bas' reform plan had the CDU up in armsImage: Christophe Gateau/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Dispute over collective bargaining rights and worker protection

Annika Klose, spokesperson for labor and social policy for the SPD parliamentary group, explained the thinking behind the idea. Flexibility, she said, is "not a one-way street." The coalition agreement explicitly aims to promote a better balance between family and work. "So that it's sometimes possible to take your child to football practice in the afternoon and then continue working afterward — but not that my boss tells me against my will: 'You're working the shift from 9 a.m. to 10 p.m. tomorrow.'"

The CDU/CSU immediately rejected the draft. Businesses were also up in arms. "This draft must be withdrawn and completely revised," demanded Dulger in a statement, saying it was "steeped in mistrust." The German Confederation of Skilled Crafts (ZDH) spoke of a "breach of the commitments agreed to in the coalition agreement." The reform has been on hold ever since.
Why the reform stalled
At the Employers' Day event, Merz held out the prospect of progress. "This is indeed long overdue. I believe we can accomplish this relatively quickly and create flexibility in the labor market."

It remains to be seen, however, whether the new SPD Labor Minister, Alexander Schweitzer, shares this view. In early October, his party released a paper on reforming working hours that read like a declaration of war against the CDU. "Self-determination, Not Deregulation" is the title of the seven-page document that was signed by the SPD working group on labor, the youth organization Jusos, the "60plus" working group and the women's wing of the SPD.

In the paper, the Social Democrats not only reiterate the points that already appeared in Bas' draft back in June. They also demand that, in the future, employers and employees should decide on working hours "jointly and by mutual agreement." They argued that it is not "in the spirit of a modern reform of working time law" if only employers can determine when employees finish work.

From a political perspective, the dispute over reforming work hours has long become more than just a debate over legal provisions. It is a fundamental dispute over how much flexibility workers should be expected to tolerate in the future and to what extent the state should protect them. And it is yet another stumbling block for the already beleaguered government in Berlin.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: Hilarious quips and ‘100,000-volt’ energy: the hypemen (and women) redefining Afrobeats music
articles.summary:
Style of emceeing based on high-octane, ad-libbed vocals has flourished thanks to its unique way of captivating crowds

For the 2015 freshmen cohort of the history degree programme at the…

blocks.text: For the 2015 freshmen cohort of the history degree programme at the University of Lagos, their classmate’s first-semester presentation was so captivating that they began calling him Toby Shang, after the 16th-century Chinese dynasty he had focused on.

His crowd engagement that day had been harnessed from his high school days as a ginger-man (energiser) in a three-man band and as a private tutor. By his final year at university, his viral catchphrases and infectious energy had resulted in a hit song, Shedibalabala. Today, he is one of the self-acclaimed “evangelists and pioneers” in the Afrobeats sub-genre some are now calling Afrohype or lamba.

blocks.caption: Toby Shang by the waterfront in the Lagos suburb of Akoka. Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The Guardian

blocks.text: “Even my mother calls me Shang now,” the 32-year-old, born Tobi Michael Adeyeye, said in an interview near the university’s lagoon waterfront, where he once emceed gatherings.
Since then he has hosted his own rave, released two EPs and run four editions of his School of Hype – a one-day masterclass with online mentoring that has launched several rising stars.
Allow TikTok content?

This article includes content provided by TikTok. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Hypemen neither sing nor rap entirely, but perform high-octane ad-libbed vocals “and onomatopoeic sounds” over fresh beats or popular instrumentals such as Dorime, a made-in-Nigeria version of 1996’s Ameno by the French group Era, a song that has become a continental nightclub classic. In response, nightclub patrons donate or spray money – the Nigerian custom of throwing or placing money on someone to celebrate them.

Hype is now omnipresent at wedding after-parties, raves and corporate parties. On Instagram, one teenage sensation is now known for recording 30-second hypes for birthday celebrants at the request of friends or relatives.

blocks.caption: Toby Shang made a name for himself while still a student at the University of Lagos. Photograph: Sogo Oladele/The Guardian

blocks.text: “Hypemen have the gift of the gab and fine mic control,” said the London-based doctor and cultural critic Dami Ajayi, who encountered one at a party in Tirana last month. “He used the spaces between lyrics for hilarious quips, many of which were frontally risque and misogynistic,” he said.

Despite being a male-dominated sub-genre, a few women have made their mark, such as the Yaoundé-based bikutsi artist Lady Ponce, known as the “100,000-volt lady” because of her energy. Other notable female figures in the scene include Deborah ‘Hype Queen Baddy’ Francis – an alumnus of Shang’s school who died in September – and the radio presenter Melody “M.I.A” Adigo, both from Lagos.

The art of hyping as it is known in west and central Africa has its roots in praise-singing and call-and-response music styles ingrained for centuries in Black populations on both sides of the Atlantic. In west Africa, this tradition took the form of oral historians known as griots. In the US, it was sustained by negro spirituals, sacred folk songs created by enslaved African Americans.
after newsletter promotion
These styles laid the foundation for the atalaku (meaning “look here, look at me” in the Kikongo language of the DR Congo) tradition that came alive in 1980s Kinshasa, followed by today’s hype scene.
Exponents of this style include the American gospel singer Kirk Franklin as well as the Congolese rumba bandleader Koffi Olomide and the Congolese singer Awilo Longomba.

The success of Olomide and Longomba at the turn of the 21st century set off a craze in Côte d’Ivoire, where coupé-décalé music embraced the atalaku trend alongside farotement, the act of showing off by throwing cash at performers or guests at parties.

blocks.caption: The Congolese singer Koffi Olomide performing at a festival in Abidjan in September 2021.  Photograph: Sia Kambou/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: A line encouraging audiences to gallop like a horse in the Ivorian star DJ Arafat’s 2003 viral homage to a late friend – “Tout le monde galope, kirikata kirikata” – influenced later hits from Nigerian Afrobeats musicians Flavour N’abania and Skales.

Côte d’Ivoire’s national television network, RTI, ran an atalaku talent hunt for several years. Lili Djely, an Ivorian woman of Malian origin, won the 2006 edition with a mix of Ivorian nouchi and French, defeating men to take the crown. In recent years, an MC/hypeman of the year category was introduced at the Ghana DJ awards as hype flourished there too.

Thanks to the success of Afrobeats, Afrohype is now widely recognised as a full-time career. As artists became more expensive to book after Covid-19, promoters turned to hypemen – previously criticised for simply doing voiceovers. Some are now reportedly paid as much as 5-8m naira (£2,844–4,550) for a 30-minute or one-hour performance.
Some observers, however, say hype is a nuisance, amping up noise levels at events or encouraging fraudulent lifestyles, and that many performers do not customise language and tempo to fit the event.

blocks.caption: The Congolese musician Awilo Longomba performing at the All Africa music awards in Lagos in November 2019.  Photograph: Pius Utomi Ekpei/AFP/Getty

blocks.text: Nevertheless, hypemen are now a permanent fixture on the entertainment scene. For Shang, they are helping fun-seekers and club-goers get back on the dancefloor.

“People are facing a lot of challenges … they need somebody to tell them money is coming in the new week,” he said. “Also, everybody wants to press their phones or show Birkin bags in clubs. Nobody wants to dance because dancing is seen as for small kids. You need a hypeman to bring out that childlike part in every person. A 60-year-old woman can start dancing like a young girl if the hype is good enough.”

articles.title: How reliant is Ukraine on the US-controlled Starlink internet service?
articles.summary: Kyiv keeps issuing warnings that the satellite internet system Starlink is being restricted in Ukraine. How dependent is the country on the system, and what would happen if it went down?

image.caption: The Starlink satellite internet system has become a core component of Ukrainian defenseImage: Adam88/Pond5 Images/IMAGO

blocks.text: Few technological systems have played such an important role in the war in Ukraine as Starlink, central to the communications, reconnaissance and drone operations of the Ukrainian armed forces. There are currently widespread concerns that Elon Musk's satellite internet service in Ukraine may be restricted or even switched off. In recent days, Kyiv has repeatedly reported disruptions and restrictions affecting its use.
How Starlink enables communications

Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has made extensive use of the satellite internet service, which is operated by the US company SpaceX. With it, military personell can continue to communicate and exchange data, even when infrastructure has been destroyed or cellphone networks are down.

According to the Center for Security Studies (CSS) at ETH Zurich, around 50,000 Starlink terminals were in use in Ukraine in 2025. These are the system's specialised receiving and transmitting devices, which enable communications on the battlefield. They are also used to relay orders between command levels and receive drone footage.

The importance of the Starlink network can in part be explained by events at the beginning of the war. According to a CSS analysis, the KA-SAT satellite system previously favored by Ukraine was targeted in a cyberattack just hours before Russia's invasion. Starlink quickly became a vital alternative.
Starlink and Starshield: civilian versus military use
When discussing current affairs, the terms "Starlink" and "Starshield" are often used interchangeably.

blocks.caption: There are around 50,000 Starlink terminals in UkraineImage: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: However, Starlink is SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, whereas Starshield is specifically designed for governmental and military use. While based on the same technological infrastructure, it is designed for security and defense applications.

This distinction matters, because the latest reports of restrictions seem to primarily concern systems used for military purposes. Elon Musk recently stated that Starshield systems are controlled by the US government, whereas Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX.
The role of Starlink in drone warfare
Alongside communications, Starlink is mainly used for drone operations. The system provides an internet connection for ground, naval and aerial drones.

This connection means video footage can be transmitted almost in real time, while drones can be controlled over long distances. Ukraine uses these systems for reconnaissance and attacks deep behind enemy lines.
According to ETH Zurich, images and GPS coordinates of Russian positions are also transmitted via these communication channels. The data is sent to artillery units and used to coordinate operations.
What throttling Starlink would mean

According to Ukrainian media reports, on Tuesday night, SpaceX temporarily introduced a speed restriction for Starlink terminals in Ukraine, limiting terminals in motion to a speed of about 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph).

Such a restriction has direct consequences for fast-moving Ukrainian drones, some of which travel at speeds of up to 300 kilometers per hour (186 mph). If the connection to the drone is lost, live video footage can no longer be transmitted, and the systems can no longer be controlled in real time. The drones effectively have to continue their mission while flying blind.
Did someone order Ukraine's high-speed Starlink shutdown?
Restricting or even shutting down a Starlink network would therefore not only make communication more difficult. It would also affect Ukrainian drone operations, and other military activities.
More than just satellite internet

However, Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, are only one essential component of Ukraine's defense system. Ukraine also receives reconnaissance data from western partners, including information about Russian air attacks, missile launches, troop movements and anti-aircraft positions, as well as potential routes to avoid them.

This information helps with air defense and offensive operations. Without this intelligence, it would be significantly harder for Ukraine to carry out long-range drone operations against targets in Russian territory.

The two elements are particularly effective when combined. Reconnaissance data provides information about potential targets and routes, while Starlink ensures that this data can be quickly relayed to units.

This is why reports that the US is limiting access to its reconnaissance data are as worrying as the possibility that Starlink might be throttled. Other NATO countries, such as the United Kingdom and France, can also provide reconnaissance data, but not to the extent as the United States.
Strategic dependence
Europe has several alternatives to Starlink, including Eutelsat/OneWeb. However, their ability to match Starlink's performance in wartime conditions has not yet been tested on a large scale.

blocks.caption: Starlink terminals enable mobile internet connection on the battlefield for the operation of dronesImage: Yasuyoshi Chiba/AFP

blocks.text: The recurrent concern about possible restrictions makes clear that satellite communications have become a central component of Ukrainian defense. And while relying on a single provider simplifies operations, it also shows how dependent modern armed forces have become on private technology companies. Experts say this marks a fundamental change in warfare.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's successful use of Starlink has helped the system to achieve global recognition.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: ‘4,000 people minding our own business’: four decades on, Falklands again face a hostile Argentina
articles.summary:
Facing a slump in the polls, Argentina’s president is making economic attacks on the islands’ oil industry, and suggesting its key fisheries industry could be next

A dozen local people and…
articles.byline: Daniel Boffey in Port Stanley, Falkland Islands; photographs and video by Sean Smith

blocks.text: Facing a slump in the polls, Argentina’s president is making economic attacks on the islands’ oil industry, and suggesting its key fisheries industry could be next

A dozen local people and a uniformed military police officer (“Do you mind if I sit in?”) took their seats at the back of the handsome wood-panelled courtroom that doubles as the Falkland Islands’ legislative assembly. Outside, it was a typically blowy early evening. It may nominally be spring in the south Atlantic, but Stanley harbour, with its dark grey water speckled with historical shipwrecks, was a cauldron of swells and churn.

Six of the assembly’s eight members – five men, one woman – waited patiently at a row of desks and microphones. The heating had been turned up to just short of uncomfortable. Behind them, a portrait of King Charles. From the other walls, dusty photographs of governors, of varying popularity, gazed disinterestedly at the scene.

blocks.caption: The Falkland Islands, home to approximately 3,600 residents

blocks.text: Proceedings started at the raised hand of a bored-looking young man wearing headphones in the corner. He was transmitting the question and answer session via radio across the dozen or so inhabited islands that make up the 778-strong archipelago.

It was not clear how many of the Falklands’ 3,600 residents were listening in from their farm houses out in the diddle-dee shrub that coats much of the islands, or in the front rooms of Port Stanley’s white clapboard cottages with the pretty coloured roofs; likely not on a par with the number who learned 44 years ago from the Falkland Islands broadcasting station that their lands had been invaded.
“There’s no turning back, we can expect them by dawn,” the governor, Rex Hunt, had said then.
But for those who did tune in on Monday evening, there was much to dwell on. Not so much the answers about the local internet contract or the consultation on the contentious plan for a salmon farm.

“I have another one for you,” piped up one enthusiastic quizzer with a heavy local accent, a West Country burr with a slight antipodean lift. That intervention prompted a little shuffling of tired bums. But a rather more significant announcement was to come.

blocks.caption: Assembly members Roger Spink, Stacy Bragger and Lewis Clifton before the monthly meeting.

blocks.text: Lewis Clifton, an assembly member who can date his family’s residence on the Falklands to the late 1870s, advised the islanders that an unprecedented economic war was being waged against them – a community no bigger than an English village – by a country of 46 million people.

“I am concerned that the level of Argentinian thrust this time has been at a different level,” Clifton said. “Perhaps a more vehement and belligerent tone than [seen since] 1982, because it has the potential to threaten our very economic development.”

Facing a downturn in his domestic polling and with an upcoming election, Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has legislated to criminalise companies and individuals involved in the Falklands’ nascent oil industry, and suggested the fisheries industry on which it currently relies for its prosperity could be next.

The British forces capability at Mount Pleasant airbase – 1,800 personnel there and on Ascension island, four typhoon jets, a ground-based air defence system and with HMS Medway patrolling the waters – makes a military threat from Argentina largely hypothetical. But Buenos Aires has launched a full spectrum attack of another sort.

blocks.caption: Aerial view of a new port and floating jetty being built in the Falkland Islands.

blocks.text: In response this week, Andy Burnham and his foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, restated the UK’s solidarity with the islanders’ desire to remain British, and promised legislation that might offer some protection against the financial damage imposed by Argentina’s economic sanctions. Interpol received Foreign Office representations suggesting they reject an Argentinian request for arrests relating to the dispute.

For the islanders, it was a welcome show of muscularity. They have never felt entirely confident in the spine of those in power back on the homeland. It was arguably the indifference of Westminster that led Argentina to launch its invasion in the first place back in 1982.

“I have never trusted the Foreign Office and I have been proven right,” said Norma Edwards, 84, whose husband, Roger, 80, a former Royal Marine, was attached to the SAS in the 1982 conflict. “Catching up time,” said Clifton, of what he saw as a belated toughness from London this week. But things remain precarious.

blocks.caption: Ricky Evans, who runs a guesthouse and other businesses, carries post and supplies for Stanley.

blocks.text: The Falkland Islands might be described as a British success story. Four decades ago, there were 1,800 inhabitants, and its tiny wool-centric economy, 300 miles (480km) east of mainland South America, was dependent on UK government handouts.

Today the population, growing at 3% year-on-year in recent times, includes about 70 different nationalities, attracted by the 26% top rate of tax, good pay and opportunities in a growing and entirely self-reliant economy.

There are Zimbabweans who came to de-mine after the war. Construction workers from South Africa who came to rebuild. Chileans who found something they liked after taking a Latam Airlines flight. The largest minority group is the Filipinos, who came to work in social care and the service industry in the late 1980s and 90s.

blocks.caption: Chilean tourists pose for a photograph outside the Stanley post office.

blocks.text: Working behind the bar at Groovy’s, a Nepalese waiter said he had come from Dubai. The money was better in the Falklands, he said, and “the people are nicer”. “The locals start at Deano’s bar, then it’s the Victory bar and here – then it is the Globe, for dancing,” he said with a smile. “After that they go to house parties.”

Such has been the Falklands’ success in attracting people that a permanent residency scheme, capped at 90 people a year, has been frozen for 12 months. The islands, for all their challenges, are somewhere people want to be.

blocks.caption: John Barton, chair of the Falkland Islands fishing companies association and James Bates, the executive secretary.

blocks.text: All of this had been made possible because of squid, said John Barton, chair of the fishing companies association. “It has been transformational,” he said.

In 1986, the UK allowed the Falklands to establish a 200-nautical-mile exclusive fishing zone in which those wanting to operate had to be licensed by the islands’ government. Licences sold to fleets of Spanish, Korean and Taiwanese “jiggers” have delivered major revenues, but the locals are increasingly running the vessels too.

The islands’ gross domestic production per capita soared as a result, from about £2,000 in 1982 to £85,000 in 2025, putting the islands sixth in the world league table, just behind Norway. The tourism industry is also going strong, with 75,000 or more people spilling out of cruise ships every year at Stanley port, but that is at best a nice addition.

blocks.caption: James Wallace, who runs the Fortuna fishing company, onboard his harbour launch.
A worker packs filleted toothfish into plastic bags at a Falkland Islands processing factory.

blocks.text: James Wallace, 41, is chief executive of Fortuna, the largest fishing company on the island. It is a growing operation, which last year acquired Cornwall’s oldest fishing business, the Ocean Fish Group. But he is diversifying his business for a reason.

The squid populations in the Falklands waters, on which his company and the islands rely, are hugely variable and it is clear that “catches are declining”, he said. “We have commissioned a bunch of inshore work to see what is happening but the answer is that we don’t yet know,” he said. But there is another natural resource on which the islanders’ hopes are pinned.

blocks.caption: A bust of Margaret Thatcher by the 1982 war memorial.

blocks.text: About 136 miles north of the Falkland Islands, work is continuing at pace on the Sea Lion oil project led by Israeli firm Navitas and its British partner, Rockhopper Exploration.

Independent estimates suggest the offshore oil field could triple the Falkland Islands’ GDP and deliver a Norway-style sovereign wealth fund. The companies involved remain confident that drilling will commence within months. A new jetty is busy with activity. But the impact of Argentinian pressure cannot be discounted. Two major contractors recently pulled out of the project.

blocks.caption: Chief executive of the Falklands government, Andrea Clausen, in the room where Argentinian forces surrendered.

blocks.text: Andrea Clausen, as chief executive of the Falklands government, its top civil servant, works from a building on Thatcher Drive. Her office is opposite the room where Brig Gen Mario Menéndez signed Argentina’s letter of surrender on 14 June 1982. The letter remains on the wall.

Clausen was 10 at the time of the invasion and remembers the Argentinian solders’ arrival. She also recalls cowering with her family in their home in Goose Green, 60 miles west of Stanley, as the British Harrier jets came in with their cluster bombs. “Even now I struggle to cope with the sound of fast jets,” she said.
